title: Hand Clinic Workflow
heading: Order favorites — follow Dr. Barrera's preference list
text: Set this up once and you inherit all of Dr. Barrera's pre-built imaging, medication, lab, and OT-referral favorites: Open the Order Preference List — the three-line (hamburger) button next to Add Order . Click + Follow Users (top right of the order search). Add Barrera . His favorites now appear under My Favorites — imaging, meds, labs, and the specific OT referrals above. What you get. Imaging (XR / MRI / US upper extremity), procedures (brace, EMG), the full set of OT and ortho referrals, common labs, and the standard hand-clinic medications — all pre-set so you don't build orders from scratch.

title: Hand Clinic Workflow
heading: Per-patient workflow
text: Staff every patient See the patient, then staff with the chief, fellow, or attending before finalizing the plan. No patient leaves without being staffed. Discuss operative cases Any patient who may be a surgical candidate gets reviewed with the fellow or attending before you commit to a plan or book a case. Steroid injections Prep the standard injection and document it (see recipe and documentation note below). Confirm the plan when you staff the patient. Enter the diagnosis & sign the note Enter the diagnosis, then sign the note only — do not sign the encounter . Billing / level of service: OK to skip; the attending sets the charge.

title: Hand Clinic Workflow
heading: Steroid injection recipe
text: Standard steroid injection 1 cc Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 0.5 cc 1% lidocaine Document every injection with .procdoc . Any injection you give must have the .procdoc phrase in the note — this captures the procedure, consent, site, and medication for billing and the legal record.

heading: Questions (attempt before viewing answers) › Replantation
text: A 28-year-old factory worker sustains a clean-cut amputation of the right dominant thumb at the MCP level 2 hours ago. Cold ischemia time. What are your indications for replantation, what’s your acceptable ischemia window, and what’s the post-op monitoring regimen? Answer Key (open after attempting all questions) Flexor zones: Zone I: distal to FDS insertion on middle phalanx — only FDP Zone II: FDS insertion to distal palmar crease (A1 pulley) — “no man’s land”; both FDS + FDP Zone III: distal palmar crease to distal edge of transverse carpal ligament — lumbricals originate here Zone IV: within the carpal tunnel Zone V: proximal to the carpal tunnel (forearm) Carpal tunnel contents: 4 FDS + 4 FDP + 1 FPL + median nerve = 10 structures . FCR sits in its own sheath outside the canal. Palmaris longus, ulnar nerve/artery, and radial artery are all outside. Intrinsics by nerve: Median (recurrent motor branch): APB, opponens pollicis, FPB superficial head, lateral 2 lumbricals (index + middle) Ulnar (deep motor branch): all other intrinsics — hypothenar (ADM, FDM brevis, opponens digiti minimi), all 4 dorsal + 3 palmar interossei, medial 2 lumbricals (ring + small), adductor pollicis, FPB deep head Cutaneous innervation: Radial dorsum: superficial radial nerve Palmar thumb–index–long–radial half of ring: median Dorsal small + dorsal ulnar ring: dorsal cutaneous branch of ulnar Palmar ring (ulnar half) + small: ulnar FDS vs FDP isolation: Hold all non-tested fingers in full extensi

title: Session 2 — Fractures & Dislocations
heading: Questions › Mixed decision-making
text: List the common complications after distal radius ORIF and the warning signs for each (EPL rupture, flexor tendon irritation/rupture, median neuropathy, stiffness, CRPS). Answer Key Acceptable reduction (distal radius): Radial height: within 2-3 mm of contralateral (~11 mm normal) Radial inclination: ≥ 15° (normal ~22°) Volar tilt: neutral to 10° dorsal acceptable (normal 11° volar); any dorsal angulation > 10° is concerning, especially in younger patients Articular step-off: ≤ 2 mm (some accept ≤ 1 mm for younger/active) DRUJ congruent Frykman uses two axes: intra-articular vs extra-articular (radiocarpal +/- DRUJ), and ulnar styloid involvement (yes/no). Eight types total, evens = ulnar styloid fx, intra-articular rising with number. Scaphoid anatomic location: Proximal pole (~10%): worst blood supply (retrograde flow via dorsal ridge branches of radial artery); highest nonunion rate Waist (~70%): most common; moderate healing Distal pole / tubercle (~20%): best blood supply, usually heals with casting Blood supply: dorsal carpal branch of radial artery enters the dorsal ridge and flows proximally — proximal pole is end-vascular. Eaton-Littler (PIP fracture-dislocation): <30% articular involvement: stable → extension block splint, early motion 30-50%: tenuous → often surgical (hemi-hamate or dynamic ex-fix) >50%: unstable → hemi-hamate autograft or volar plate arthroplasty; dynamic ex-fix for comminution Thumb metacarpal base fractures: Bennett: intra-articular 2-part fract

text: Deep-dive library. This page is no longer an assignment. The required curriculum now runs on a weekly schedule (7-week resident track, 4-week intern track). Everything below is optional extra depth.

title: Session 3 — Tendon & Nerve Injuries
heading: Questions › Anatomy & classification
text: Name the 5 flexor tendon zones and state the single most important anatomic feature of each zone for repair. List the annular (A1-A5) and cruciate (C1-C3) pulleys, and identify which two pulleys are biomechanically most important to preserve. Classify jersey finger (Leddy). Which type needs repair within 7-10 days and why? Name the extensor tendon zones (Doyle) for the finger and the thumb. What is the classic injury at each even-numbered zone in the finger? Compare Seddon and Sunderland classifications. Which Sunderland grades recover spontaneously and which need surgical repair?

title: Session 3 — Tendon & Nerve Injuries
heading: Questions › Board-style
text: The PRIMARY blood supply to the flexor tendons in the digit comes from: Intrinsic circulation within the tendon Vincula longa and brevia from the digital arteries The palmar arch Synovial diffusion alone A patient has a laceration at the wrist with loss of thumb opposition and loss of sensation over the palmar index and long fingers, but preserved wrist flexion and finger flexion. The most likely injured structure is: Median nerve at the wrist Anterior interosseous nerve Recurrent motor branch of median only Ulnar nerve at Guyon’s Answer Key See templates/flexor-tendon-repair-handout.md for in-depth answers on questions 1-3 and 9. Summary answers: Flexor zones: Zone I: only FDP (distal to FDS insertion on middle phalanx). Jersey finger territory. Zone II: “no man’s land” — A1 pulley to middle phalanx; both FDS + FDP in a narrow sheath under pulleys. Historically poor outcomes → Bunnell’s original injunction against primary repair; now primary repair is standard with early active motion. Zone III: palm (distal TCL edge to A1) — lumbrical origins; outcomes good. Zone IV: within the carpal tunnel — must protect median nerve, may need TCL release/repair. Zone V: forearm — often with nerve injuries; outcomes good if no nerve involvement. Pulleys: A1-A5 + C1-C3. A2 and A4 are biomechanically most important — venting one pulley partially is usually OK, but loss of both causes bowstringing. Modern teaching allows partial venting of A2 and A4 to facilitate repair. Leddy classification

title: Session 4 — Compressive Neuropathies & Common Electives
heading: Questions › Anatomy & classification
text: List the 9 structures that pass through the carpal tunnel and name the one whose compression causes CTS symptoms in the radial 3.5 digits. Walk through the CTS-6 score — the 6 items, their weights, the cutoff, and what the score means for needing EDX. Five anatomic sites of potential ulnar nerve compression at the elbow (cubital tunnel). Name them in order from proximal to distal. Grade cubital tunnel severity (McGowan + Dellon). What’s the clinical threshold for operative treatment, and for transposition vs in situ release? Name the Eaton-Littler stages of thumb CMC arthritis and state the dominant treatment for each stage. Name the cords of Dupuytren’s disease anatomically (pretendinous, spiral, lateral, central, retrovascular) and identify which cord displaces the neurovascular bundle centrally and superficially.

title: Session 4 — Compressive Neuropathies & Common Electives
heading: Questions › Board-style
text: The most sensitive provocative test for CTS is: Phalen’s Tinel’s at the wrist Durkan’s (carpal compression) Semmes-Weinstein monofilament The most common iatrogenic injury during an open carpal tunnel release is to the: Motor branch of median (recurrent) Palmar cutaneous branch of median Ulnar nerve at Guyon’s Superficial palmar arch Answer Key See ~/JanosClaude/templates/compressive-neuropathies-handout.md for detailed references. Summary answers: Carpal tunnel contents: 4 FDS + 4 FDP + 1 FPL + median nerve . Median nerve compression causes the radial-3.5-digit symptoms; palmar cutaneous branch travels over the TCL so it’s spared (palmar thumb base sensation intact in classic CTS — helpful differentiator from a high median nerve lesion). CTS-6 (Graham et al., 2006; Fowler et al., 2023): | Item | Points | |—|—| | Numbness in median nerve territory | 3.5 | | Nocturnal numbness | 4.0 | | Thenar weakness / atrophy | 5.0 | | Positive Phalen’s | 5.0 | | Loss of 2PD ≤ 5 mm | 4.5 | | Positive Tinel’s at wrist | 4.0 | Max 26. Cutoff > 12 = ~80% probability of CTS → EDX may not be needed if clinical picture is consistent. ≤ 12 → get EDX. Cubital tunnel — 5 sites of compression (proximal → distal): Arcade of Struthers (~8 cm proximal to medial epicondyle) Medial intermuscular septum Medial epicondyle (retrocondylar groove) Osborne’s ligament (between the two heads of FCU) Deep FCU fascia (distal edge) Cubital tunnel grading: McGowan I: subjective symptoms only (paresthesias) — non-op,

title: Week 1 · Hand Exam & Consult Survival
heading: Run the check-in
text: Book 15-20 minutes with Dr. Barrera (default: Friday after 6:00 rounds). You present, he asks. Bring one real consult from your week. Cases to walk through: The ED calls: “volar forearm laceration from glass, bleeding controlled.” Talk through your bedside exam from the doorway to the phone call back to your senior: what you inspect, every motor and sensory test you run, and how you report it. A 62-year-old woman fell on an outstretched hand. Wrist films are read as negative but she is tender in the snuffbox. Walk through your exam, what you tell her, and how she leaves the ED. You are asked to “rule out flexor tenosynovitis” in a swollen finger. Walk through the exam that confirms or excludes it and what else is on your differential for a red, swollen digit. Rapid-fire: Normal 2PD at the fingertip? (Report digits thumb to small.) How do you perform and interpret an Allen’s test? How do you isolate EIP from EDC? title: Week 1 · Hand Exam & Consult Survival
heading: Self-test (attempt before opening the key)
text: Name the 5 flexor tendon zones and the anatomic landmark that bounds each. What are the 10 structures that pass through the carpal tunnel? List the intrinsic muscles of the hand by nerve supply (median vs ulnar). What is the cutaneous innervation of the hand: which nerve supplies the radial dorsum, the palmar thumb through radial ring, the dorsal small finger, and the palmar ulnar ring and small? How do you isolate FDS from FDP on exam? What is the pitfall with the small finger? A patient cannot lift the thumb off a flat table but can still extend the thumb MCP. Which tendon is out, and what muscle is compensating? Describe how you test the intrinsics in a suspected ulnar neuropathy. Be specific about finger positioning. Answer key (open after attempting all questions) Flexor zones: Zone I distal to the FDS insertion on the middle phalanx (FDP only). Zone II FDS insertion to the A1 pulley at the distal palmar crease (“no man’s land,” FDS + FDP). Zone III distal palmar crease to the distal edge of the transverse carpal ligament (lumbrical origins). Zone IV within the carpal tunnel. Zone V proximal to the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel contents: 4 FDS + 4 FDP + 1 FPL + median nerve = 10. FCR runs in its own sheath outside the canal; palmaris longus, ulnar nerve/artery, and radial artery are all outside. Median (recurrent motor branch): APB, opponens pollicis, FPB superficial head, radial 2 lumbricals (index + middle). Ulnar (deep motor branch): everything else: hypothenars, all 7

text: Name the four Kanavel signs. Which appears first and which is most specific? A patient punched someone in the mouth 18 hours ago and has a 3 mm laceration over the middle-finger MCP with pain on active flexion. Diagnosis, workup, and management? A painter has a pinhole entry wound at the index pulp from a paint gun 4 hours ago. The finger looks pink and pain is mild. What do you do and why? At what compartment pressure (or delta pressure) do you take a forearm to the OR, and what wins when the numbers and the exam disagree? Differentiate felon, paronychia, and herpetic whitlow: location, etiology, and the one you must NOT incise. Rapidly spreading erythema, dusky skin, crepitus, gas on x-ray, LRINEC 9. Next step, and what is the role of the ED vs OR here? State the absolute and relative indications for replantation, and the ischemia windows for a digit vs a muscle-containing part. Answer key Kanavel: fusiform swelling, flexed resting posture, tenderness along the flexor sheath, pain with passive extension. Fusiform swelling and sheath tenderness tend to appear early; pain with passive extension is the most specific . FTS is a surgical urgency: IV antibiotics, hand elevation, and OR sheath irrigation for the established case; a very early presentation (< 24 h) can occasionally be trialed on IV antibiotics with serial exams by the surgical team. title: Week 3 · Fractures I: The Wrist
heading: Run the check-in
text: Cases to walk through: ★ A 62-year-old woman falls on an outstretched hand at home. Dorsally angulated intra-articular distal radius fracture. Take it from ED reduction (your technique, your block) through the surgery-vs-cast conversation, and defend your recommendation with the trial data. A 24-year-old fell playing basketball, has snuffbox tenderness, and films are negative. Walk through your plan, including exactly what you write in the discharge instructions and why you will not be talked out of immobilizing him. A 30-year-old high-energy fall has a “sprained wrist” per the outside read. You notice the capitate is not seated in the lunate on the lateral. What just happened, what do you do tonight, and what is the definitive plan? Rapid-fire: Acceptable dorsal tilt before you recommend surgery in a young patient? Which scaphoid fracture location can go in a cast, and for how long? Patient 8 weeks out from a nondisplaced distal radius fracture suddenly cannot lift the thumb off the table: diagnosis and fix? What makes a distal radius fracture “unstable” on the initial films? Name the carpal bone fractured by a direct blow to the hypothenar palm and the view that shows it.

title: Week 3 · Fractures I: The Wrist
heading: Self-test (attempt before opening the key)
text: State the acceptable reduction parameters for a distal radius fracture: radial height, radial inclination, volar tilt, articular step-off. Why do proximal-pole scaphoid fractures behave differently from distal-pole fractures? Describe the blood supply. Snuffbox tenderness with a “normal” x-ray 4 days after a fall: what is the sensitivity of the initial film, and what are your two acceptable pathways? A 55-year-old independent, right-hand-dominant woman has an intra-articular distal radius fracture with 3 mm step-off and 25 degrees dorsal angulation. What do you recommend, and what did the WRIST trial show for patients over 60? What is a Galeazzi fracture, a Monteggia fracture, and an Essex-Lopresti injury? List the common complications after distal radius ORIF and the warning sign for each. Name the Mayfield stages of perilunate instability and the radiographic finding that gives away a perilunate dislocation on the lateral view. Answer key Radial height within 2-3 mm of contralateral (~11 mm normal); radial inclination >= 15 degrees (normal ~22); volar tilt from neutral to 10 degrees dorsal acceptable (normal ~11 volar); articular step-off <= 2 mm (<= 1 mm for young, active patients); DRUJ congruent. The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters at the dorsal ridge and flows retrograde, distal to proximal , so the proximal pole is end-vascular: highest nonunion and AVN risk. Distal pole/tubercle fractures have the best supply and usually heal in a cast. Initial x-ray

heading: Run the check-in
text: Cases to walk through: ★ A 19-year-old punches a wall: small-finger metacarpal neck fracture, 50 degrees angulated. The ED wants to reduce and cast. Talk through your evaluation (especially rotation), your actual treatment, and the conversation with the patient about the bump on his hand. A 20-year-old has a thumb metacarpal base fracture with a small retained volar-ulnar fragment and a proximally displaced shaft. Name it, draw the deforming forces, and take it to the OR: reduction maneuver, fixation choice. A 35-year-old caught a ball wrong 3 weeks ago; the ring-finger PIP is swollen and she cannot fully extend it. Films show a dorsal fracture-dislocation with 45% volar lip involvement, still subluxated. Options, your pick, and why the 3-week delay matters. Rapid-fire: Angulation tolerance in the index vs small metacarpal neck, one sentence. What deforming force does APL exert on a Bennett fracture? title: Week 4 · Fractures II: The Hand
heading: Self-test (attempt before opening the key)
text: State the acceptable apex-dorsal angulation for a metacarpal neck fracture of each finger, index through small, and the finding that is never acceptable. What is the difference between a Bennett, a Rolando, and a reverse Bennett fracture? Name the deforming forces on a Bennett. How does percentage of articular involvement guide treatment of a dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation? A 35-year-old has a dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation with 45% volar articular involvement. What are the three surgical options and which is the modern choice? How do you examine a thumb UCL injury, what laxity is diagnostic, and what is a Stener lesion? How do you clinically check rotational alignment of a finger fracture? Board-style: a 19-year-old punches a wall, closed small-finger metacarpal neck fracture, 45 degrees angulated, no rotational deformity. Operate or not? Same fracture in the index? Answer key Roughly 10-15 degrees index, 15-20 middle, 30-40 ring, 40-50 small (increasing CMC mobility compensates ulnarly). Any rotational deformity is a surgical indication. Dr. Barrera’s practice for the classic boxer’s fracture without rotation: angulation up to ~70 degrees is treated with buddy taping and early motion (Martinez-Catalan RCT showed equivalent outcomes to reduction and casting). Bennett: two-part intra-articular thumb metacarpal base fracture; the volar-ulnar beak fragment stays reduced (anterior oblique ligament) while APL pulls the shaft proximally and radially and adductor pollicis adducts

heading: Run the check-in
text: Cases to walk through: ★ A 22-year-old football player grabbed a jersey; he cannot flex the ring-finger DIP and there is a tender mass in the palm. Diagnosis with Leddy type, the timeline conversation, and your OR plan including how you retrieve and fix the tendon. A 35-year-old chef cut the middle finger over the proximal phalanx 6 hours ago and cannot flex either joint. Walk from the ED exam (what confirms both tendons are cut) through your zone II repair and the exact splint and therapy prescription he leaves with. A 40-year-old jammed his finger a month ago and now has a droopy DIP; a fresh film shows a dorsal base fragment with the distal phalanx subluxated volarly. What changed the plan, and what do you offer? Rapid-fire: Which two pulleys do you protect, and how much can you vent? Leddy I repair window and the reason for it. Elson test: how and why? Sagittal band rupture: which finger, which side, and the nonoperative window? What position is the dorsal blocking splint, and when does therapy start?

title: Week 5 · Tendon
heading: Self-test (attempt before opening the key)
text: Name the annular and cruciate pulleys and the two that matter most biomechanically. How much venting is acceptable? Classify jersey finger (Leddy I-IV). Which type must be repaired within 7-10 days and why? Name the Doyle extensor zones and the classic injury at zones I, III, and V. What percent laceration of a flexor tendon warrants formal repair, and what is the trap with partial lacerations under A2? Describe the OR plan for a zone II flexor laceration: anesthesia, exposure, core and epitendinous technique, pulley management, splint position, and rehab start. A closed soft-tissue mallet with 25 degrees of lag: treatment, duration, and the operative indications for mallet injuries. Why does early active motion beat immobilization after a modern multi-strand repair? Answer key A1-A5 and C1-C3. A2 (proximal phalanx) and A4 (middle phalanx) prevent bowstringing. Modern practice tolerates venting up to ~25% of A2 or all of A4 to let a repair glide. Leddy I: FDP retracts to the palm, both vincula torn, no nutrition, the muscle shortens: repair within 7-10 days . II: retracts to PIP (long vinculum intact), weeks of grace. III: bony fragment caught at A4. IV: fracture plus tendon avulsed off the fragment; fix both. Odd zones sit over joints: I DIP = mallet; III PIP = central slip (boutonniere; test with Elson); V MCP = sagittal band rupture (traumatic) or fight bite (assume the joint is violated until proven otherwise). title: Week 6 · Nerve: Injury & Compression
heading: Run the check-in
text: Cases to walk through: ★ A 55-year-old woman has a year of nocturnal numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers; Durkan and Phalen positive, early thenar atrophy, CTS-6 of 18. Take her from clinic to the OR: do you order EDX, how do you consent her, open vs endoscopic, and what does recovery look like? A 60-year-old diabetic has progressive ring and small finger numbness, weak grip, intrinsic atrophy, positive Froment and Wartenberg. Grade it, choose your operation, and defend in situ vs transposition. A 45-year-old sustained a sharp volar forearm laceration; median motor and sensory are out. Walk through acute repair principles (timing, technique, what “good” looks like under the microscope) and how you will follow recovery month by month. Rapid-fire: CTS-6 items and cutoff, from memory. What does the palmar cutaneous branch spare in CTS, and why is that useful? Nerve regeneration rate, and how you use Tinel progression clinically. Night splint position for cubital tunnel? Most common iatrogenic injury in open carpal tunnel release?

title: Week 6 · Nerve: Injury & Compression
heading: Self-test (attempt before opening the key)
text: Compare Seddon and Sunderland. Which grades recover spontaneously, and at what rate does an axon regenerate? Walk through the CTS-6: the six items and the cutoff, and what the score means for ordering electrodiagnostics. Name the five sites of ulnar nerve compression at the elbow, proximal to distal. Grade cubital tunnel severity (McGowan). When do you operate, and when do you transpose instead of decompress in situ? How do you distinguish AIN palsy from a high median nerve injury on exam? Durkan, Phalen, Tinel at the wrist: technique and rough sensitivity of each. A median nerve repaired at the mid-forearm shows no thenar recovery at 6 months. Why are motor nerve transfers usually off the table by then, and what is the workhorse reconstruction? Answer key Neurapraxia (Sunderland I): conduction block, full recovery in weeks. Axonotmesis (II-IV): II recovers by regeneration at ~1 mm/day; III is variable (endoneurial scarring); IV is a neuroma-in-continuity that needs surgery. Neurotmesis (V): transection, always surgical. I-II recover spontaneously, III is variable, IV-V need repair. Numbness in the median distribution (3.5), nocturnal numbness (4.0), thenar weakness or atrophy (5.0), Phalen positive (5.0), 2PD loss (4.5), Tinel positive (4.0); maximum 26. Score > 12 means CTS is likely (~80%) , and with a consistent clinical picture electrodiagnostics are not required before offering release; 12 or less, get EDX. text: Final session is half cases, half debrief. Cases to walk through: A 50-year-old has a middle finger that locks in flexion every morning and needs the other hand to unlock it. title: Week 7 · Electives & Wrap-Up
heading: Self-test (attempt before opening the key)
text: Grade trigger finger (Green). What is first-line treatment, how effective is it, and when do you operate? Describe Dr. Barrera’s corticosteroid injection formulation and technique for a flexor sheath injection. How do you differentiate De Quervain’s tenosynovitis from thumb CMC arthritis on history and exam? Name the Dupuytren cords and identify the one that endangers the neurovascular bundle. What makes a patient operative? Compare collagenase, needle aponeurotomy, and limited fasciectomy for a combined MCP + PIP contracture. Stage thumb CMC arthritis (Eaton) and give the treatment ladder for stage III. Dorsal wrist ganglion: origin, exam finding, and the recurrence rates for aspiration vs excision. Answer key Green I pre-triggering pain, II active triggering, III locking requiring passive unlocking, IV fixed contracture. First-line: corticosteroid injection into the sheath (~80% success first injection, ~50% second). Up to two injections, then A1 pulley release; go to surgery sooner for grade IV and consider a lower injection threshold in diabetics. 0.75 mL 1% lidocaine + 0.25 mL Kenalog 40 mg/mL (10 mg triamcinolone), 1 mL total, for every injection site; never Depo-Medrol. Trigger finger: into the sheath at A1; if you feel doughy resistance you are in the tendon, back out slightly until it flows. De Quervain’s: dorsoradial pain at the first dorsal compartment over the styloid, positive Finkelstein/Eichhoff, younger patient, classically postpartum. CMC arthritis: pain at t

title: Lower Extremity Flap — Dangle Protocol
heading: Completing the protocol
text: Once the patient is tolerating 30 min TID for 3 days , the protocol may be discontinued and the patient can dangle ad lib .

title: Lower Extremity Flap — Dangle Protocol
heading: If not tolerated
text: If a dangle is not tolerated ( evidence of venous insufficiency ), stop the protocol and re-initiate the following day at the frequency used prior to that day. Example: if on POD 9 there is venous insufficiency, stop the dangle and re-start at 5 min TID the following day, then ramp back up.

title: Lower Extremity Free Flap Pathway
heading: Discharge (usually POD#7) › Discharge activity (both flap types)
text: No pressure on the flap lower extremity Keep the flap lower extremity in the splint at all times Strict flap lower extremity elevation at all times No weight bearing on the flap lower extremity Continue lateral transfers to chair, wheelchair, and commode while keeping the flap lower extremity elevated at all times Continue anti-foot-drop PT (peroneal strengthening, stretching) Notes. Daily changes (the new order for that day) are highlighted. **Always ask, don't assume: criteria for JP drain removal in the lower extremity are usually ≤ 25 mL/day × 3 consecutive days. Compiled by Dr. Janos Barrera (NYU Langone) as a teaching/workflow aid. Always defer to the operating surgeon's specific orders.

text: Apply Adaptic over muscle flap + skin graft Cover with ABD pads Loosely wrap with Kerlix around splint Do this for all transfers (hospital → SNF, SNF → clinic, home → clinic, etc.). Leave Coverlet dressing on until seen in clinic STSG donor — Ioban with Mepilex (default): leave the dressing in place and remove POD#14 . Reinforce the edges with Tegaderm to prevent leakage. STSG donor — Xeroform: outer ACE and gauze already came off on POD#1. Leave the Xeroform in place, open to air, and let it dry and separate on its own. Do not peel it off. If it is still damp at discharge, the Bair hugger stays directed at it until dry.

title: Lower Extremity Free Flap Pathway
heading: POD#0 (day of surgery)
text: Flap checks Q1h × 24h, then Q2h × 24h, then Q4h until d/c (color, temp, turgor, cap refill, doppler) Labs CBC and BMP immediately in PACU Pain meds PCA Antibiotics Kefzol or Clinda × 24 hrs, unless abx indicated for infection DVT prophylaxis Hold — start Lovenox on POD#1 Wound care — muscle flap Bacitracin + Xeroform over muscle flap + skin graft, BID Wound care — STSG donor Ioban with Mepilex (default): placed in OR — leave intact, remove POD#14. Reinforce edges with Tegaderm to prevent leakage. If Xeroform instead: leave the outer ACE + gauze intact today. Wound care — skin flap Xeroform to flap edges BID × 48 hrs Drains All JPs and Penrose stay Diet NPO IVF Continue mIVF Foley Gravity Activity Strict bedrest. Strict flap + donor leg elevation SCDs On non-operative leg Bair hugger Over the flap: on until POD#4, tent at 42°. text: Text a wound photo + one line: mechanism, bone, Gustilo grade, perfusion (well-perfused vs. diminished/asymmetric)

title: Orthoplastic Pathway — Open Extremity Fractures
heading: 5. Incision & fasciotomy planning
text: Medial and lateral fasciotomy incisions facilitate recipient-vessel access during free-flap coverage — these incisions can be planned together. Medial (posteromedial) incision — preserves the posterior tibial perforators (local fasciocutaneous flaps) and gives access to the posterior tibial vessels as free-flap recipients. Lateral (anterolateral) incision — decompresses the anterior and peroneal compartments. title: Orthoplastic Pathway — Open Extremity Fractures
heading: 4. Initial management (reference — per BOAST-4 / AAOS)
text: Antibiotics — within 1 h Type I/II: cefazolin Type III: add piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn) Soil / farm / crush: add high-dose penicillin Penicillin allergy: clindamycin + a gram-negative agent Plus tetanus prophylaxis ER Control hemorrhage Remove gross debris only — no aggressive ER irrigation Splint Debridement Radical, to healthy bleeding tissue, within ~12 h Copious saline (high- vs low-pressure equal — FLOW) Antibiotic beads / NPWT to bridge to coverage Imaging Plain films + CT Hard signs (pulseless limb, expanding hematoma) → OR, not imaging IIIB/IIIC: CTA after provisional fixation — reduction clarifies perfusion and maps flap recipient vessels Cultures low-yield Pre-op flap labs CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags (PT/INR, PTT) HbA1c, pre-albumin

title: Orthoplastic Pathway — Open Extremity Fractures
heading: OTA Open Fracture Classification (OTA-OFC)
text: Grades five components 1–3; higher grades carry higher risk and more often need orthoplastic coverage. Component 1 2 3 Skin No major degloving Limited degloving Extensive degloving Muscle Intact function Loss but functional, focal necrosis Dead/nonfunctional, compartment loss Arterial No injury Injury without distal ischemia Injury with distal ischemia Contamination None/minimal Surface, removable Embedded or high-risk (barnyard, water, feces) Bone loss None Some contact retained Segmental loss Interpretation: a grade of 3 in any category marks a high-risk limb — muscle 3, arterial 3 (distal ischemia), or bone 3 (segmental loss) correlate with higher rates of amputation, infection, and the need for flap coverage. Grade 1 across categories generally behaves like a low-energy open fracture.

title: Orthoplastic Pathway — Open Extremity Fractures
heading: 3. Photography
text: Photograph at first exposure, before debridement, and again after debridement/fixation Remove gross contamination only; follow department policy; keep images in the record

title: Orthoplastic Pathway — Open Extremity Fractures
heading: 6. Timing targets & why early matters
text: Debridement within ~12 h Soft-tissue coverage within 48 h of definitive fixation (SPARTA) Definitive fixation + coverage within 7–10 days of injury (extended Godina window) Fix-and-flap in one sitting where feasible; a planned day-1 fixation / day-2 flap is a safe alternative to after-hours microsurgery BOAST-4–compliant early fixation and coverage: deep-infection rate ~ 2% vs. 16% with delayed care (D’Cunha, 12-year review) Orthoplastic approach: ~ 60% reduction in wound infection and osteomyelitis vs. traditional sequential care (Klifto meta-analysis)

title: Orthoplastic Pathway — Open Extremity Fractures
heading: 1. When to flag plastics
text: Open fracture that won’t close primarily — soft-tissue loss, degloving, or exposed bone, hardware, joint, tendon, or neurovascular structures Gustilo IIIB (needs a flap) or IIIC (vascular injury) Segmental, high-energy, or mangled extremity When in doubt, flag early — at first identification, before debridement. (Polytrauma/ATLS priorities first — “life over limb.”)

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4a. Mallet (Zone I — DIP) & Zone II (middle phalanx)
text: Phase Orthotic Exercises Precautions I — Immediate (day 1 to wk 6–8) DIP 10°–0° hyperextension. Tendinous mallet : 6–8 wk. Bony mallet : 6 wk. Op : 100% × 6 wk. Provide 2 splints (one for showering). Active PIP flex of affected finger with adjacent fingers held in extension. Daily skin check, DIP must stay extended. Consider taping DIP. If swan-neck → reduce passively, dorsal block PIP at 30°. II — Protective (wk 6 bony / wk 8 tendinous) Tendinous: orthosis 100% except exercise/hygiene. Bony: orthosis for strenuous activity + sleep × 2–4 wk. Remove orthotic. Gentle AROM DIP flex/ext: start 10° flex, progress 10° per week. Replace orthotic. Wk 8 : light activity out of orthosis if no lag. If DIP extensor lag ≥10° → orthosis 100% × 2–4 wk. III — Intermediate (wk 10) D/C during day. Night orthosis × 2 more wk. Fine motor, gradual flexion while maintaining DIP ext. Most zone 1–2 injuries finish with –10–0° extensor lag.

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4b. Boutonniere (Zone III — PIP)
text: Phase Orthotic Exercises Precautions I — Immediate (day 1 to wk 6) Orthosis or circumferential cast with PIP at 0°. Op: 100% × 6 wk. Active DIP flex of affected finger. If DIP hyperextension at wk 2 → reduce passively. II — Protective (wk 6) Convert to orthosis with PIP at 0°. Wk 7: reduce gradually as 0° PIP ext maintained. Light activity if no lag. Gentle active PIP ext to 30° flex, progress 10° per week. Replace orthotic. If PIP extensor lag ≥10° → orthosis 100% × 2–4 wk. III — Intermediate (wk 10) D/C. — —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4c. Zones IV–VIII (proximal phalanx through forearm) — Immobilization Protocol
text: Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1–6 Volar digit static, PIP at absolute 0°, or serial cast. Lateral bands repaired → include DIP at 0°. Lateral bands intact → DIP free. ROM may start wk 3–6 depending on healing. AROM PIP flex to 30°, progress 10–20°/wk if no lag, 10 reps hourly. Lateral bands repaired → tendon gliding wk 3. Intact → wk 1. No forceful flex. No gripping. Splint between sessions. Serial cast if PIP contracture, closed injury, or noncompliant. 6–8 Wean from splint during day. Night splint continues. AAROM or dynamic flexion splint may start. Composite wrist + digit flex. Light functional use out of splint (≤1–3 lb). 10–12 D/C splint. PROM / PREs. —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4d. Zones III–IV Alternative — Short Arc Motion (SAM) Protocol
text: Consider when broad tendon-bone interface in zone IV and adhesion risk is high. Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1 Digit volar immobilization: PIP & DIP at 0°, 24/7 except exercise. Two volar exercise splints: template 1 (PIP 30° flex, DIP 20° flex), template 2 (PIP 0°, DIP free). Remove immobilization hourly, AROM PIP & DIP, 10–20 reps in templates 1 & 2. Wrist held 30° flex, MP at 0°. Lateral bands repaired → limit DIP flex to 30–35° in template 2; intact → fully flex/extend DIP. PIP must be at 0° in immobilization splint to prevent extensor lag. 2 If no lag: progress template 1 → PIP 40–50°, DIP 30–40°. If extensor lag develops → smaller flex increments, focus on extension. If rupture suspected → MD. 3 If no lag: template 1 → PIP 50–60°, DIP 40–50°. — — 4 If no lag: template 1 → PIP 70–80°, DIP 50–60°. — If PIP stiff → intermittent splint into flex, continue static ext splint into wk 5–6. 5 Begin weaning. Composite flex and gentle PREs. Light functional activities out of splint. 6 D/C splint. Night PRN. PROM & PREs, reverse putty scraping. —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4e. Thumb Extensor (EPL) — Zones T1–T5 (BWH 2007)
text: Thumb zones differ from finger zones. EPL has its own zone map (T1–T5) and rehab protocols. Do not use finger zone I–VIII protocols for EPL repairs. Zone T1 (IP joint) — Immobilization Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1–3 IP at 0° or slight hyperextension, continuously. Op : 5–6 wk. Non-op : 8 wk. Provide 2nd splint for showers. None. No IP flexion. No gripping or pinching in splint. McConnell tape to hold digit during splint changes. 5–6 Op: remove for exercise, otherwise continuously ×2–4 more wk. Op : AROM IP flex in 20° increments/wk, modifying if extensor lag develops, 10 reps hourly. Non-op : no ROM yet. If extensor lag ≥10° → continuous splint ×2–4 wk, reassess. 8 Gradually wean during day. Continue at night. Op : AAROM if needed, provided no extensor lag. Non-op : initiate AROM IP flex in 20° increments. — 10–12 D/C splint. Op : PROM, PREs (light grip/pinch). Non-op : AAROM → PROM → PREs as tolerated. — Zone T2 (proximal phalanx) — Immobilization Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1 Hand-based static splint (short opponens): MP and IP at 0°, thumb in radial abduction. None. No active motion. 3 Same. Initiate AROM flexion at each joint; progress 25–30°/wk. Tendon-to-bone adherence may limit excursion in this zone. 4–5 Same. AAROM flexion, isolated and combined joint. Light prehension ADL out of splint. — 6 Begin to wean. Dynamic flexion splinting PRN. Moderate prehension ADL out of splint. — 8 D/C splint. PREs. Full function. — Zones T3–T4 (MP joint / metacarpal) —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 1. Flexor (FDS + FDP) — Early Active Motion · Zones 1–5
text: Therapy frequency : 1–2×/week × 8–12 weeks. Orthosis day 3. Phase Orthotic Exercises Precautions I — Immediate (day 3 to wk 2) Zones 1–3 : dorsal forearm-based; wrist 20° ext, MCP 30–40° flex, IP 0°. Zones 4–5 : dorsal forearm-based; wrist 0°, MCP 60–75° flex, IP 0°. Add pulley ring if pulley repaired. Passive DIP & PIP flex, active ext to orthosis. Passive MCP flex 60–80° with active IP ext. Passive wrist flex, active wrist ext to orthosis. Day 4–5 : after passive, active motion to 25% fist + active ext to orthosis. No passive wrist ext beyond 0° (zones 4–5) if median/ulnar n. repaired ×6 wk. Avoid place-and-holds (pulley buckling). Tendon weakest day 5–21. II — Protective (wk 2–4) Wk 4: transition orthosis to hand-based. Active to 50% fist (wk 2), 75% fist (wk 3–4). Wk 3: light fine motor out of orthosis in clinic. Wk 4: tendon gliding + isolated FDS glide to repaired finger, wrist 0°–20°; light fine motor at home. — III — Intermediate (wk 4–6) Gradually wean during day. Discharge orthosis by 6 wk. If IPs stiff at 6 wk: convert dorsal block → volar hand-based nighttime (zone 2) or volar forearm-based (zone 3). Tendon gliding wrist 20–30° ext. Wk 5 : DIP & PIP blocking. Wk 6 : progress functional activities. No composite wrist >30° + combined finger ext until 6 wk. Avoid PIP/DIP blocking of small finger (rupture risk). Weightlifting restricted. title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 2. Flexor (FDS + FDP) — Modified Duran · Zones 1–5
text: Use when EAM is deferred. Same orthotic, exercises are passive only in Phase I. Phase Orthotic Exercises Precautions I — Immediate (day 3 to wk 2) Same as EAM (zones 1–3 vs 4–5). Pulley ring if pulley repaired. Passive DIP & PIP flex, active ext to orthosis. Passive MCP block 60–80° with active IP ext. Passive composite fist. Passive wrist flex, active wrist ext. In clinic (orthosis off): passive wrist ext with fingers passively flexed; passive wrist flex with passive hook fist (prevent intrinsic tightness). No passive wrist ext beyond 0° (zones 4–5) if nerve repaired ×6 wk. Avoid place-and-holds. Reduced blood flow in zone 1. II — Protective (wk 2–4) Wk 4: hand-based. Wk 3: light fine motor out of orthosis in clinic. Wk 4: tendon gliding + isolated FDS glide, wrist 0°; light fine motor at home. — III — Intermediate (wk 4–6) Wean during day. D/C by 6 wk. Convert to nighttime orthosis if IP stiffness. Tendon gliding wrist 20° ext. Wk 5: DIP & PIP blocking. Wk 6: progress function. No composite wrist >20° + combined ext until 6 wk. Avoid small-finger blocking. IV — Minimal protection (wk 6–12) D/C night orthosis when digital ext = 0°. Wk 8: light graded strengthening, resisted isolated DIP/PIP flex. No resisted grip/pinch until 8 wk.

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 3. Flexor Pollicis Longus — All Zones
text: Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 0–3 Dorsal blocking: wrist neutral, CMC flexed/abducted under 2nd MC, MP full ext. Zone I only : add separate dorsal gutter blocking IP at 30° flex. Passive composite thumb flex / active ext to orthotic. Passive IP flex / active ext to orthotic. Gravity-assisted wrist flex / active ext. Tendon gliding digits 2–5. EAM (if cleared + 4-strand + epitendinous): place/hold thumb flex with wrist ext, start 48–72 hr post-op. No active thumb flex unless cleared EAM. No passive wrist ext. No passive thumb ext. No functional use. 3 Same. Add place/hold thumb flex with wrist passively extended (gentle). Continue prior. Avoid co-contraction. 4 Convert to hand-based. Active non-resistive thumb flex with wrist ext. Light prehensile in therapy. 5 D/C orthosis. Gentle blocking for thumb IP flex. — 6 Dynamic IP ext splinting PRN. Putty scraping PRN. May start NMES/US PRN. — 8 — Gradually add resistive exercises. —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: Key principles
text: Repair is weakest day 5–21 . Strong repair (4-strand core + epitendinous) is the prerequisite for EAM. Adhesions favor extrinsic healing; controlled motion favors intrinsic healing. Gap >3 mm → ↑ rupture and adhesion risk. Always cross-check with surgeon’s op note (suture configuration, pulley/nerve/vessel work).

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020)

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: Red flags at follow-up
text: Sudden loss of active flexion / extension after gain → assume rupture. Refer to surgeon. Extensor lag ≥10° → return to full-time orthosis × 2–4 weeks. PIP contracture developing → serial casting or static progressive splint, escalate therapy. No improvement in tendon glide after 6–8 weeks → discuss tenolysis (typically deferred to ≥3–6 months post-op). Persistent edema beyond 4 weeks → edema control, rule out infection.

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › AAOS Surgical Indications
text: Articular displacement > 2 mm Radial shortening > 3 mm Dorsal angulation > 10° Loss of radial inclination > 5° Plus: volar ulnar corner fragment, sigmoid notch involvement, associated fractures

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Two articular facets ( scaphoid + lunate ); ridge between = membranous SL ligament insertion Volar/ulnar bone densest → less comminution; ideal start point for ORIF reduction Volar radiocarpal ligaments : RSC, LRL, SRL — short, parallel to radius long axis, resist ulnar translation Dorsal extrinsic : dorsal radiotriquetral + dorsal intercarpal — oblique, V-shape over dorsal triquetral tubercle DRUJ stability = 20% bone + 80% soft tissue ; volar + dorsal radioulnar ligaments → fovea + ulnar styloid Distal oblique bundle of IOM present in 40% — additional DRUJ stabilizer (Moritomo) TFCC thickness inversely proportional to ulnar positive variance Coronal shift of distal radius predicts DRUJ instability more reliably than ulnar styloid fracture

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What are the AAOS surgical indications for distal radius fractures? A: > 2 mm articular step-off, > 3 mm shortening, > 10° dorsal angulation, > 5° loss of radial inclination. Q: Which tendon ruptures most commonly after nonoperative treatment of minimally displaced distal radius fracture? Treatment? A: EPL — EIP-to-EPL transfer (attritional, can’t primary repair). Q: What is the watershed line and why does it matter? A: Distal-most ridge of volar radius; plate placement distal to it predisposes to flexor tendon rupture (esp FPL, index FDP). Q: When is ulnar styloid fixation indicated after volar plate ORIF of distal radius? A: Only when clinical DRUJ instability after radius fixation; routine styloid fixation not needed. Q: What’s the most reliable radiographic predictor of DRUJ instability? A: Coronal plane shift of the distal radius (not ulnar styloid fracture presence).

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Classification
text: AO/OTA : A (extra-articular), B (partial articular), C (complete articular) Melone : based on fracture lines through scaphoid facet + lunate facet (± coronal split) Column theory (Rikli/Regazzoni): radial (scaphoid facet + radial half), intermediate (lunate facet + sigmoid notch), ulnar (distal ulna + TFC) — reconstruct intermediate first Volar marginal (volar ulnar corner) fragment = unstable, radiocarpal + DRUJ subluxation risk → always anatomic ORIF

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Distal Ulna
text: Reduced + aligned ulna can heal without internal fixation when radius stable on volar plate Unstable displaced ulnar head/neck → 2.0-2.4 mm plate (ulnar or volar position) Preserve ulnar head; resection = salvage

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › DRUJ Management
text: Examine contralateral side preop AND in OR after radius fixation Ulnar styloid fixation NOT routine after volar plate ORIF unless clinical DRUJ instability Options if unstable: foveal TFCC repair, ulnar styloid ORIF (hook plate / tension band), DRUJ cross-pinning, supination/neutral splinting If cross-pinning DRUJ: 0.062” K-wires, 4 cortices, neutral rotation, exit pin both sides of skin so a broken pin can still be retrieved

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Open wound near apex of deformity Acute CTS vs nerve contusion : contusion = immediate fixed deficit; acute CTS = evolving pain + paresthesia DRUJ stability check: always compare with contralateral side (clinic + preop)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: AP, lateral, oblique — measure ulnar variance, radial inclination (22°), volar tilt (11°), sigmoid notch obliquity Volar teardrop angle (Medoff) — confirms volar lunate facet reduction CT after reduction for articular or distal displaced fractures + comminution + associated carpal fractures

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Initial — All Fractures
text: Hematoma block with 1% lidocaine (rapid onset, resolves for post-reduction exam) Traction 8-10 lb with finger traps; palmar translation of neutral lunate is key Padded 3-point molded sugar-tong splint, wrist neutral One concerted reduction attempt; repeated manipulation causes harm without benefit in elderly

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes › Major Complications
text: Acute CTS — urgent release (distinguish from contusion — contusion is non-progressive) EPL rupture — most common after nonop, esp minimally displaced; treat with EIP-to-EPL transfer Flexor tendon rupture (FPL, index FDP) — too-distal volar plate (past watershed); use US to monitor (small plate-to-tendon ratio = urgent removal) Malunion — radial shortening + dorsal angulation most common Nonunion — rare; workup metabolic/mechanical/infection; vitamin D , smoking cessation CRPS 3-10% — aggressive rehab, neuropathic meds, sympathetic blocks, CTR Ligament injuries : SL 4.7-46%, LT 12-34%, TFCC 39-82% (peripheral with ulnar styloid usually doesn’t need repair)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Cast 3-4 wk → removable splint by wk 4 if alignment stable Pad DRSN + DUCN; avoid extreme flexion; ensure digital ROM Weekly films first 3-4 wk Elderly low-demand patient: gentle attempt at reduction acceptable; deformity well tolerated Combined distal radius + ulna fracture in elderly → consider surgery (loss of strut → significant deformity/nonunion)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Volar (FCR) Approach — Workhorse 8 cm incision over FCR Protect LABC nerve (radial), PCBM nerve (ulnar; may travel within FCR sheath or superficial — inspect fat carefully) Release distal BR insertion to reduce deforming force PQ released radially + distally Extended FCR (Orbay) : best visualization of volar ulnar corner Plate proximal to watershed line; distal pegs 75% of volar-dorsal distance Intraop fluoro views: AP, lateral, tilt views (10° lunate, 30° scaphoid), pronated + supinated oblique, dorsal tangential, near-axial sigmoid Subtract 1-2 mm from drill measurement to avoid dorsal prominence Dorsal Midline For complex articular fractures requiring direct joint visualization Protect SBRN + SBUN; 3rd compartment incision to retract EPL (transpose at closure) PIN neurectomy + ligament-sparing capsulotomy 2.0-2.4 mm dorsal plates; low profile, subperiosteal Fragment-Specific (Medoff) Multiple small plates form fixed-angle triangular constructs (plate proximal screws + K-wire through distal hole into opposite cortex) Excellent for highly comminuted; orthogonal plating common External Fixator / Dorsal Bridge Plate Severe comminution, soft tissue compromise, polytrauma needing weight bearing Index MC pins (2.5 mm Shanz; first at metaphyseal flare, second distal parallel) Radius pins through ECRL/ECRB interval (bare area, 4 fingerbreadths proximal to styloid) Check extrinsic tightness at end (passive IP flexion shouldn’t extend MCPs = no over-distraction) Bridge plate removed

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes › Outcomes (RCTs)
text: Surgical vs non-op in > 65 yo : better radiographs with surgery, similar function at 1 yr, more complications with surgery Pinning vs ex-fix : no difference Volar plate vs pinning : better DASH at 3 mo, equal at 1 yr Bridging vs non-bridging ex-fix : McQueen showed non-bridging better; later studies equivocal AAOS CPG : unable to recommend one technique over another

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Don’t miss volar marginal fragment — primary indication for ulnar-side approach (between flexor tendons + FCU) Coronal shift must be corrected to restore sigmoid notch + DRUJ tension BR tendon release dramatically reduces deforming force Hardware too distal (within 3 mm of volar lip) = flexor rupture risk Watch for prominent dorsal screws — Lister tubercle blocks them on standard lateral; use dorsal tangential view Younger active patients benefit most from surgery; very low-demand elderly accept deformity well Combined distal radius + ulna fracture in elderly = consider surgery despite age (loss of strut → high deformity + nonunion risk)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Volar plate: protected wrist motion + grip strengthening early External fixator removed ~6 wk in clinic Bridge plate at ~3 mo Maximum recovery 6-12 mo from injury

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: References
text: Berger RA. Anatomy of ligaments of wrist and DRUJ. Clin Orthop. 2001;(383):32-40. Medoff RJ. Essential radiographic evaluation for distal radius. Hand Clin. 2005;21(3):279-288. Souer JS, et al.
