title: Compartment Syndrome of the Upper Extremity
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Clinical signs have only 13-19% sensitivity individually — maintain high index of suspicion Pain with passive stretch is the earliest and most important sign Pulselessness is a late finding — compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis, not a vascular one Measure pressures at multiple locations; highest within 5 cm of fracture Volar forearm decompression is not complete without lacertus fibrosus AND carpal tunnel release Do NOT close fasciotomy wounds primarily — this recreates the compartment syndrome “Found-down” extremity from drug overdose is increasingly common and carries unknown ischemia time Children cannot describe paresthesias — watch for agitation, restlessness, escalating analgesia needs

title: Compartment Syndrome of the Upper Extremity
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Physiology
text: Normal resting pressures: 0-8 mm Hg (forearm), <15 mm Hg (hand interossei) Cascade: increased pressure → venous obstruction → capillary leak → further pressure → decreased arterial inflow → ischemia → necrosis Tissue perfusion ceases when interstitial pressure = diastolic BP (Dahn) Matava: critical threshold = 20 mm Hg below diastolic BP

title: Compartment Syndrome of the Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Preoperative
text: Limb at or slightly below heart level (improves perfusion via gravity) Remove constrictive bandages/splints Aggressive fluid + BP resuscitation; oxygenation Monitor CPK, urine myoglobin Mannitol diuresis reduces incidence post-revascularization

title: Compartment Syndrome of the Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Pressure Measurement
text: Indications: equivocal exam, obtunded patients Diagnostic threshold : absolute >30 mm Hg OR within 30 mm Hg of diastolic BP Stryker handheld manometer most common; side-port needle most accurate Measure at multiple locations — significant variability (pressures higher within 5 cm of fracture) Stryker handheld manometer used to measure forearm tissue pressure after trauma. ## Etiology Most common: forearm fractures (18% of all forearm compartment syndromes) Fasciotomy in 1.6% of all forearm fractures ; open fracture = 5x higher likelihood Risk factors: male, younger, OTA type C, both-bone forearm, substance abuse Other: reperfusion injury, IV extravasation, drug injection, coagulopathy, “found-down” extremity (increasingly common with drug overdose)

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Systemic autoimmune inflammatory synovitis; ~1% US prevalence Autoantibodies: RF + ACPAs (anti-citrullinated protein antibodies) Wrist: 50% within 2 yr, >90% at 10 yr Reactive synovium erodes ligaments, cartilage, tendons, bone DMARDs have dramatically reduced surgical volume

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: Which DMARDs should be continued perioperatively in RA? A: Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. Q: What is Vaughan-Jackson syndrome? A: Sequential attritional rupture of extensor tendons starting with EDM/small EDC due to caput ulna dorsal prominence. Q: When is Sauve-Kapandji preferred over Darrach? A: When ulnar translocation of the carpus is present — Darrach worsens instability. Q: What deformity is pathognomonic for psoriatic arthritis on x-ray? A: “Pencil-in-cup” deformity (proximal phalanx tapered, distal expanded). Q: What is the Mannerfelt lesion? A: Attritional FPL rupture over a scaphoid osteophyte in RA.

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Volar/dorsal swelling, crepitus (tenosynovitis) Prominent distal ulna → impending extensor rupture Bunnell test for intrinsic tightness (PIP flexion limited with MCP extended) Check for CTS from flexor tenosynovitis

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Workup › History
text: Disease duration, prior surgeries, current DMARDs Cervical spine instability — mandatory preop assessment

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Standard wrist series; Larsen grading MRI/US helpful to distinguish tendon rupture DDx (sagittal band, PIN palsy, cervical)

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Classification › Larsen Radiographic Score
text: Grade Description 0 Normal 1 Periarticular osteoporosis + swelling 2 Mild narrowing + erosion 3 Moderate destruction 4 Severe destruction + joint space loss 5 Arthritis mutilans

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Splinting, activity modification, steroid injection for early synovitis Team approach: rheumatology, primary care, hand therapy Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo). Useful early for isolated tenosynovitis or single-joint synovitis before surgery is warranted

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Treatment › Operative — Staged Proximal to Distal
text: Wrist Tenosynovectomy (dorsal compartments) — early intervention; doesn’t alter progression Chamay radiolunate fusion — radiolunate arthritis with midcarpal sparing; ~40% develop midcarpal degeneration but doesn’t cause failure Total wrist arthrodesis — end-stage; slight extension + ulnar deviation; most common salvage Total wrist arthroplasty — 4th-gen porous-coated; bilateral = dominant arthroplasty, nondominant arthrodesis DRUJ Darrach (distal ulna excision) — reliable pain relief; oblique cut beveled proximally on radial side Sauve-Kapandji — preferred over Darrach when ulnar translocation present; DRUJ fusion + proximal shaft pseudarthrosis (10-14 mm resection) DRUJ arthroplasty (Aptis/Scheker) — semi-constrained; for painful DRUJ or symptomatic Darrach stump Extensor Tendon Rupture Vaughan-Jackson syndrome : attritional rupture starting ulnar side (EDM/small EDC) Primary repair rarely possible — tendon transfers: EDM alone → side-to-side to ring EDC Ring → EIP to small EDC Long → FDS ring to ring/small EDC, EIP to long All EDCs + EIP → FDS ring + middle Flexor Tendon Rupture Mannerfelt lesion : FPL attenuated over scaphoid osteophyte FPL: ring/middle FDS transfer via extended CT approach MCP Joint Crossed intrinsic transfer — passively correctable ulnar drift without arthritis Silicone arthroplasty — subluxation + drift with arthritis; bone shortening + alignment + intrinsic release; favorable outcomes for pain/ROM/appearance Pyrocarbon: 32% complication, 29% reoperatio

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Workup › Other
text: 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria: active synovitis ≥ 1 joint + serology (RF/ACPA) + acute phase reactants SLICC criteria for SLE; CASPAR criteria for PsA

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Methotrexate + hydroxychloroquine continue perioperatively — all others hold Vaughan-Jackson starts ulnar-side — inspect EDM first Sauve-Kapandji over Darrach when ulnar translocation present Cervical spine clearance before any procedure under GA Pyrocarbon fails in RA — ligamentous laxity intolerance PsA can present before skin rash — check nails + DIP joints SLE deformities are soft tissue, not erosive — splint + rebalance before surgery

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Treatment › Perioperative DMARD Management
text: Continue Hold Methotrexate Sulfasalazine, azathioprine (1 wk) Hydroxychloroquine Leflunomide (1-2 d pre, restart 1-2 wk post) NSAIDs (D/C 1 wk) Etanercept (1 wk) Infliximab, golimumab (1 mo) Rituximab (2 mo)

title: Rheumatoid and Inflammatory Arthropathies
heading: Other Inflammatory Arthropathies › Psoriatic Arthritis
text: Seronegative; DIP most affected ; 20% present before skin rash CASPAR criteria (≥ 3/5): psoriasis hx, nail changes, dactylitis, RF-negative, juxta-articular new bone “Pencil-in-cup” deformity on x-ray DIP arthrodesis: K-wires × 8 wk or headless compression screws

heading: Other Inflammatory Arthropathies › SLE
text: 90% present with arthritis (joint laxity), unlike RA: bony destruction + tendon rupture uncommon Avoid wrist arthroplasty (soft tissue laxity) Silicone MCP arthroplasty for recurrent drift

heading: Classification › Wrightington Wrist Classification
text: Grade Pathology Surgery 1 Osteoporosis, cysts, erosion Synovectomy 2 Carpal instability Soft tissue + partial arthrodesis 3 Destruction + subluxation Arthroplasty or arthrodesis 4 Severe radial destruction Arthrodesis

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Systemic fibroproliferative disorder → palmar nodules → cords → flexion contractures Most common inherited connective tissue disorder Myofibroblast = characteristic cell; TGF-beta, EGF, PDGF, CTGF drive fibrosis Luck’s 3 stages : proliferative (hypercellular nodules) → involutional (aligned cords) → residual (hypocellular fibrotic) Type III collagen elevated in early stages, normalizes but never reaches baseline

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: Which cord displaces the neurovascular bundle and makes it vulnerable during surgery? A: The spiral cord — displaces the NV bundle midline and superficial (“spiral nerve”). Q: What is the recurrence rate of CCH at 5 years (CORDLESS)? A: 47%. Q: What defines Hueston diathesis? A: Family history, bilateral disease, knuckle pads (Garrod), Ledderhose (plantar fibromatosis) — predicts early recurrence. Q: What is Luck’s characteristic cell of active Dupuytren disease? A: The myofibroblast. Q: Why are revision fasciectomies higher risk? A: 10x arterial injury and 5x nerve injury compared to primary, due to scarring and distorted anatomy.

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Collagenase Injection (CCH)
text: FDA 2010; inject day 0, manipulate day 1-7 Two cords same session OK (Gaston RCT) Degrades collagen I + III; rare tendon/pulley rupture, CRPS, anaphylaxis Recovery: light activities < 1 wk, RTW 1-2d

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Cord-Contracture Map
text: Cord Contracture NV Bundle Risk Central MCP Safe (bundles lateral) Spiral PIP HIGH — displaces NV midline + superficial Retrovascular DIP Deep to NV bundle Natatory Webspace Low Spiral cord = key surgical hazard: NV bundle spirals dorsal-to-volar around cord Suspect spiral cord when subdermal cord passes beneath a soft compressible mass + tender on tensioning PIP contracture > 45° often involves retrovascular cord + multiple cords Digital cords may involve Grayson’s OR Cleland’s ligaments (contrary to older teaching)

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Dermofasciectomy
text: Fasciectomy + skin excision + FTSG — lowest recurrence in diathesis patients Tendon exposure up to 1 cm: skin graft on vascularized bed OK Recovery: light activities 4 wk, RTW 9 wk

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Epidemiology
text: Caucasian 3-6%; Hispanic 1/3, African American 1/5, Asian American 1/10 M:F ratio decreases with age: 30:1 at < 40 yo → 1:1 at 85 Ring + small fingers most affected (50-60%); thumb + index least (5-7%) Risk factors: diabetes, smoking, heavy ETOH, hyperlipidemia, psoriasis, manual labor RA and obesity are protective

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Diagnosis is clinical — no imaging needed Modified Tubiana stages (0/N/1/2/3/4) — total extension deficit per ray (MCP + PIP + DIP) Measure MCP extension with PIP flexed; PIP extension with MCP flexed Hueston table-top test — cannot place palm flat on table Document neuro + digital Allen test pre-procedure (especially in previously treated hands)

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Fasciectomy
text: Regional (all visibly diseased) — US standard; radical abandoned (high complications, no benefit) Incisions: Bruner zigzag, Watson V-Y, transverse (McCash open palm — less pain/hematoma) Dissection: magnification, known to unknown , do NOT skeletonize NV bundle Loose closure; sutures left 2-3 wk (abnormal wound healing biology) Recovery: light activities 2 wk, RTW 5 wk, full unrestricted 2 mo

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Fasciectomy Complications (Denkler)
text: Major: CRPS 6% , digital nerve 3%, infection 2%, hematoma 2%, arterial injury 2% Minor: wound healing 23% Revision = 10x artery injury, 5x nerve injury vs primary More complications with PIP > 60°

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Epidemiology › Hueston Diathesis (Predicts Early Recurrence)
text: Family history, bilateral disease, knuckle pads (Garrod), Ledderhose (plantar fibromatosis) Onset < 50, Peyronie, > 2 digits, male, Caucasian, thumb involvement

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Non-operative — Nodules
text: Do not excise isolated nodules — triggers inflammation + progression Intralesional corticosteroid for tender/itchy nodules Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo). Reserve intralesional steroid for symptomatic nodules without contracted cords

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Operative Indications (Hueston Table-Top Test)
text: MCP contracture ≥ 30° PIP contracture > 15° Adduction contracture Worse correction outcomes : MCP > 50°, PIP > 40°, composite > 90°

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Outcomes
text: MCP: 80-90% success (< 5° from full extension) — all methods comparable PIP: 25-50% success — all methods; small finger worst Fasciectomy > PNF/CCH for severe contractures CORDLESS 5-yr : 47% recurrence after CCH

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Spiral cord displaces the NV bundle superficially — palpate before any procedure PNF + CCH best for MCP; fasciectomy for PIP or severe contractures Nodule excision worsens disease — inject instead Revision surgery carries 10x vascular and 5x nerve injury risk PIP > 60° = suspect pseudo-boutonniere with central slip attenuation Anticoagulants safe for PNF Dermofasciectomy for young diathesis patients — lowest recurrence

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Percutaneous Needle Fasciotomy (PNF)
text: Hypodermic needle under local; cords tight, tendons loose on passive extension Work distal → proximal to preserve patient feedback (paresthesias) Complications: skin tears 8%, dysesthesia 3%, tendon rupture 0.2% Anticoagulants do NOT need to be held Recovery: light activities < 1d, RTW 1-2d

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Outcomes › Recurrence Rates (Per Year)
text: Method Rate Dermofasciectomy < 2%/yr Fasciectomy ~5%/yr CCH/PNF MCP ~10%/yr CCH/PNF PIP ~20%/yr “Recurrence is an inevitable consequence if the patient lives long enough” (Bulstrode)

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Secondary Deformities
text: Pseudo-boutonniere : PIP > 60° → central slip attenuation, lateral band subluxation, DIP hyperextension Secondary swan neck : chronic MCP contracture → PIP volar plate stretch

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Severe / Recurrent PIP Contracture
text: Routine open joint release NOT recommended (gains lost, flexion decreases) Two-stage for severe : external fixator (Digit Widget) for progressive lengthening → fasciectomy/dermofasciectomy Dorsal closing wedge osteotomy = ineffective Salvage: amputation, arthrodesis, middle phalangectomy

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Superficial palmar arch complete in 81.3% ; deep palmar arch complete in 95.2% Only 10-20% of normal hand blood flow for metabolic demands; 80-90% is thermoregulatory Endothelial regulation: endothelin (vasoconstriction) vs EDRF (vasodilation) Classification by etiology: embolic, thrombotic, systemic, iatrogenic Classification by arterial layer (Fuchs): endothelium → thromboemboli; intima → atherosclerosis; media → aneurysm; adventitia → arteritis

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What is the most common occlusive vascular disease of the hand? A: Hypothenar hammer syndrome — ulnar artery aneurysm/thrombosis at the hook of hamate. Q: What is the pathognomonic angiographic finding in HHS? A: “Corkscrew” tortuous appearance with alternating stenotic and ectatic segments. Q: What percentage of patients with systemic sclerosis develop digital ulcers? A: >40% (large multinational study). Q: What criteria distinguish primary from secondary Raynaud’s? A: Primary: bilateral symmetric, no necrosis, normal inflammatory labs, negative ANA. Q: What is the first-line pharmacotherapy for Raynaud’s phenomenon? A: Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine).

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Raynaud’s Phenomenon › CCB Outcomes (Cochrane 2017)
text: 38 RCTs, 982 patients: reduce frequency, duration, severity, pain, disability Greater effect in primary Raynaud’s

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: End-Stage Ischemia — Venous Arterialization
text: For failed revascularization or no distal arterial targets Reverse flow through veins delivers oxygenated blood Cephalic vein most common target; donor = dorsal radial, radial, or ulnar artery Selective side-branch ligation + valvulotomy forces flow distally Allows healing + collateral development; doesn’t preclude future AV fistula Long-term outcomes unknown

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Pallor, cyanosis, mottling, subungual hemorrhages, clubbing Brachial, radial, ulnar pulses Allen’s test Hand-held Doppler: palmar arch, dorsal radial artery, proper digital vessels Cold water provocation for Raynaud’s

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Workup › History
text: Pain, paresthesias, cold intolerance, color changes with cold/stress Digital ulcerations, necrosis, prior amputations Rheumatologic conditions, hypercoagulability, smoking

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Conventional angiography = gold standard (best detail; can use intra-arterial vasodilators) Digital brachial index (DBI) : normal 0.9; ≤ 0.7 = inadequate perfusion Doppler US for flow + thrombus + aneurysm characterization CTA/MRA for larger vessels; insufficient for digital arteries Echo for embolic source

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Hypothenar Hammer Syndrome (HHS) › Key Facts
text: Most common occlusive disease of the hand Ulnar artery aneurysm + thrombosis at hook of hamate Incidence 1.6-14% in manual laborers, craftsmen, athletes Mechanism: ulnar artery superficial + tethered by dorsal branch → repetitive trauma → media damage → aneurysmal dilation → thrombosis → distal embolization Angiography: pathognomonic “corkscrew” tortuous pattern with stenotic + ectatic segments

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Hypothenar Hammer Syndrome (HHS) › Non-operative
text: Activity modification, smoking cessation CCBs, alpha-blockers, aspirin/clopidogrel Stellate ganglion / brachial plexus block for acute critical ischemia Intra-arterial thrombolytics (bleeding complications up to 10%)

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Hypothenar Hammer Syndrome (HHS) › Operative
text: Indications: reconstructible lesion, acute ischemia, chronic ischemia with threatened tissue, failed medical management Resect diseased segment until normal tunica intima + media Reversed vein graft (volar forearm or saphenous) — most common reconstruction May need branched graft to reconstruct common digital vessels 8-0 nylon microsuture; end-to-side of common digitals into graft if needed

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Hypothenar Hammer Syndrome (HHS) › Outcomes — The HHS Paradox
text: 78% of grafts occlude by 10 yr (Endress) — yet patients remain satisfied Even with occlusion, temporary flow restoration allows tissue healing + collateral development → sustained symptom improvement Patent grafts = significantly less cold sensitivity Vein grafts outperform arterial grafts for patency

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: HHS is the most common hand occlusive disease — ask about occupational/sports hand-hammering “Corkscrew” on angiography = pathognomonic for HHS HHS grafts often occlude but patients still improve — don’t withhold surgery Primary Raynaud’s = bilateral, symmetric, ANA-negative, no necrosis Nifedipine first-line for Raynaud’s; botox emerging option Conventional angiography remains gold standard — CTA/MRA insufficient for digital arteries DBI ≤ 0.7 = inadequate perfusion

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Hypothenar Hammer Syndrome (HHS) › Post-op
text: Wrist splint × 2 wk; fingers free Heparin × 3-5 d; ASA × 1 mo

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Raynaud’s Phenomenon › Primary (Raynaud’s Disease)
text: Vasospasm without tissue injury Bilateral symmetric, no necrosis, normal inflammatory labs, ANA negative

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Raynaud’s Phenomenon › Secondary
text: Underlying systemic disease (SSc, SLE, MCTD) Progressive ischemia, ulcerations > 80% of SSc patients have Raynaud’s at diagnosis; > 40% develop digital ulcers

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Raynaud’s Phenomenon › Sympathectomy Outcomes
text: Ruch (22 pts, 46 mo): 82% decreased pain; 90% avoided amputation Hartzell (90 mo): 75% fewer ulcers or complete healing; 26% still required amputation Momeni: 92.3% pain improvement — advocates earlier surgical intervention

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Raynaud’s Phenomenon › Treatment — Non-operative
text: Lifestyle modification, cold avoidance, wound care, smoking cessation Nifedipine (CCB) = first-line pharmacotherapy PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) ACE inhibitors Botulinum toxin : 50 U/hand distributed across common digital and proper digital arteries; RCT shows improved QuickDASH + pain

title: Vascular Disorders
heading: Raynaud’s Phenomenon › Treatment — Operative
text: Periarterial sympathectomy (adventitial stripping 1.5-2 cm) 4 incisions: radial artery at wrist, ulnar artery at wrist, superficial arch + 3 common digitals (transverse mid-palm), radial artery in snuffbox Circumferential adventitia stripping; separate from venae comitantes; divide nerve branches Post-op: compressive dressing × 3-5 d; immediate digital ROM Counsel patients that recurrence after sympathectomy is common; a substantial percentage still ultimately need amputation (Hartzell: 26% required amputation at 90 mo) Earlier referral to surgery may be better than waiting for tissue loss (Momeni: advocates earlier intervention)

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Treatment › Amputation — Salvage Only
text: Recurrence in stump 43-82% ; phantom pain > 70% Indications: chronic infection, ADL-limiting contractures, weeping skin, edema

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Persistent extremity pain beyond cellular injury or nerve distribution Type I (RSD) : no identifiable nerve lesion Type II (Causalgia) : identifiable nerve lesion Pain pathway: transduction → A-delta (small myelinated) + C-fiber (unmyelinated) → dorsal horn → spinothalamic tract → cortex Peripheral sensitization: substance P, bradykinin, increased ectopic alpha-adrenergic receptors Cortical reorganization of somatotopic maps (Maihofner) — central component AV shunting → nutritional deprivation of tissues Inflammatory mediators: TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-2, IL-6

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What are the Budapest criteria categories for CRPS diagnosis? A: Sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema, motor/trophic — need symptoms in ≥ 3 of 4 and signs in ≥ 2 of 4, plus disproportionate pain and no alternative diagnosis. Q: What is the incidence of CRPS after distal radius fracture? A: 2-39%; risk factors include age < 60, psychiatric history, prior CRPS. Q: What is first-line pharmacotherapy for CRPS with bone resorption? A: Bisphosphonates (alendronate 40 mg daily × 8 weeks). Q: What distinguishes SMP from SIP? A: SMP responds to sympatholytic intervention (stellate block); SIP does not. Q: What is the classic radiographic finding in CRPS? A: Sudeck’s atrophy — periarticular osteopenia.

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Budapest Criteria (2010, Validated)
text: Continuing pain disproportionate to inciting event ≥ 1 symptom in ≥ 3 of 4 categories: Sensory (hyperesthesia/allodynia) Vasomotor (temp asymmetry, skin color) Sudomotor/edema (edema, sweating changes) Motor/trophic (decreased ROM, weakness/tremor/dystonia, skin/hair/nail changes) ≥ 1 sign at evaluation in ≥ 2 of 4 categories (same list) No alternative diagnosis

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Epidemiology
text: Incidence: 5.5-26.2/100,000; F:M 1.6-4.5:1; mean age 40 Type-I has genetic/familial component; 10% have no inciting event 2-39% after distal radius fracture ; 8.3% after carpal tunnel release Risk factors: migraine, female, postmenopausal, smoking (68% increased risk) , prolonged tourniquet, immobilization Implicated nerves: palmar cutaneous branch median, median, dorsal ulnar, superficial radial, ulnar at elbow, PIN CTR-associated CRPS at 8.3% warrants preop counseling. Risk factors include prior CRPS, psychiatric history, and fibromyalgia. Early recognition is the single best prognostic factor.

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Full upper extremity + cervical + contralateral assessment Pain: burning, throbbing, shooting — out of proportion, non-dermatomal (stocking-glove) Trophic changes : shiny/waxy skin, hair loss, nail changes, pulp atrophy Motor: weakness, tremor, dystonia (10-15% late stage) Vasomotor: asymmetric sweating, flushing, edema Check for adhesive capsulitis (shoulder-hand syndrome) Evaluate nociceptive foci: neuroma, compressive neuropathy, OC fracture Severe swelling → consider factitious behavior

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Treatment › Hand Therapy
text: Active + passive ROM within pain limits Edema control, contrast baths, desensitization, TENS Graded motor imagery (laterality recognition, mirror therapy, imagined movements) — equivalent/superior to medication in some studies Static + dynamic orthotic positioning

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Sudeck’s atrophy = periarticular osteopenia on x-ray (classic but late finding) Abnormal x-ray in 70-80% (low sensitivity, reasonable specificity) Bone scan: reasonable specificity, low sensitivity — not for routine diagnosis MRI not routinely indicated

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Treatment › Interventional
text: Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) — strong evidence for pain, QOL, satisfaction Dorsal root ganglion stimulation — newer; cost-effective for refractory Sympathectomy (RF or chemical) — short-term (6-12 wk then receptor upregulation)

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Workup › Other
text: Labs: CBC, ESR/CRP, HbA1c, autoimmune panel, HIV NCV/EMG to rule out compression/injury Stellate ganglion block (lidocaine): pain relief → SMP; no relief → SIP or alternate dx Continuous brachial plexus block — more reliable diagnostic + therapeutic

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Budapest criteria: pain + 3/4 symptom categories + 2/4 sign categories + no alternative Early recognition (< 6 mo) is the single best prognostic factor Bisphosphonates = first-line pharmacotherapy (especially with bone resorption) Graded motor imagery is underutilized and evidence-supported Cold skin = worse prognosis; warm = better response to DMSO Stellate block differentiates SMP from SIP — critical for treatment planning Amputation has 43-82% stump recurrence — use only as salvage Vitamin C prophylaxis is low-risk and reasonable for distal radius fractures

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Treatment › Pharmacologic — Strong Evidence
text: Agent Dosing Bisphosphonates (1st-line) Alendronate 40 mg PO daily × 8 wk Calcitonin 100 U/day SC × 4 wk (perioperative) Gabapentin 600-1800 mg PO daily × 8 wk Corticosteroids Prednisolone 30-40 mg/day × 3-4 wk (acute only) IV Ketamine Subanesthetic (refractory) Topical DMSO Warm-type Vitamin C : contradictory evidence but “practical merit” (AAOS); 500-1000 mg/day × 50 days; avoid in renal stone history TCAs (amitriptyline 25 tid or 50 qhs), CCBs (nifedipine 10-30 tid), clonidine patch NOT consistently effective: oral opioids, antidepressants per formal recs, oral muscle relaxants

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Treatment › Prognosis
text: 80% treated within 1st year improve < 50% treated after 1 year improve Cold skin temp = worse prognosis (more likely persistent > 1 yr) Early multidisciplinary management = best outcomes

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › SMP vs SIP
text: Sympathetically maintained pain (SMP) : responds to sympatholytic intervention (stellate block, phentolamine) Sympathetically independent pain (SIP) : does not respond Warm subtype (acute) vs cold subtype (chronic — worse prognosis)

title: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS)
heading: Treatment › Surgical
text: Nerve decompression if compression identified Release contracted joints, intrinsic releases, osteotomy for malunion Surgery in SMP can be safe with continuous sympatholytic protection Realistic goal: 50% improvement

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Layers (inside out): endoneurium (surrounds axon + Schwann cell basement membrane) → perineurium (blood-brain barrier extension; fascicles “pooch” when cut) → inner epineurium (cushion) → outer epineurium (vessels on surface = alignment landmarks) Fascicular topography: Sunderland described intraneural plexus with branching/interconnections; more recent work shows functional segregation even proximally — critical for nerve transfer design Blood supply: epineurial vessels → extensive internal network; nerve tolerates long-distance mobilization without ischemia (redundant supply reconstitutes in days) Wallerian degeneration : initiates 24-48 hrs post-injury; Schwann cells transdifferentiate, form Bands of Bungner (guidance channels); mediators include IL-4, IL-10, NGF, CNTF, GDNF Motor axons show slight preference for motor endoneurial tubes (limited specificity) 1% of functional potential lost per week of denervation ; after ~18 months, muscle irreversibly replaced by fibro-adipose tissue Regeneration rate: 1 mm/day (1 inch/month, 1.5 ft/year) Proximal injuries = worse prognosis (longer regeneration distance, axon “steal” by proximal muscles)

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: A patient sustains a closed humeral shaft fracture with complete radial nerve palsy. NCS/EMG at 3 weeks shows absent conduction distal to injury with no fibrillations. What does this suggest? — A: Too early to differentiate neurapraxia from axonotmesis; distal conduction may persist 3-11 days post-transection, and fibrillations take several weeks to develop. Repeat at 6 weeks. Q: What is the maximum gap length for which a synthetic conduit is generally reliable for digital nerve reconstruction? — A: < 2.5 cm (results decline significantly beyond 8-12 mm in some series). Q: A 30-year-old sustains a sharp laceration of the ulnar nerve at the wrist. Primary repair is performed. At what rate should you expect axon regeneration, and when might intrinsic function return? — A: 1 mm/day; ~8-10 months to hand intrinsics, though proximal ulnar injuries have a dismal intrinsic recovery prognosis regardless. Q: Intraoperative nerve conduction testing across a neuroma-in-continuity demonstrates an action potential. What is the recommended management? — A: Continued observation; presence of an action potential across the lesion is associated with a 90% chance of continued spontaneous recovery. Q: After 18 months of muscle denervation, why is nerve repair unlikely to restore meaningful motor function? — A: Schwann cell senescence, loss of endoneurial guidance channels, dispersion of ACh receptor clusters, satellite cell exhaustion, and irreversible fibro-adipose replacement of muscle.

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Classification
text: Sunderland (modified by MacKinnon) : I (neurapraxia) : myelin/local environment only; recovers minutes-months II (axonotmesis) : axons disrupted, endoneurial tubes intact; spontaneous recovery III : endoneurial tubes disrupted; variable recovery IV : perineurium disrupted; no spontaneous recovery V (neurotmesis) : complete rupture; requires surgery VI (MacKinnon) : mixed pattern across zone of injury — hardest to manage

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Digital nerve primary repair : mean static 2PD ~10.6 mm (normal contralateral 4.4 mm); 48-72% good/excellent; sharp > crush; age matters; children approach 100% normal sensation Digital nerve gaps ≤ 3 cm : autograft 70-100% S3+/S4; ANA 83-84% S3+/S4; conduits 50-89% Mixed/motor nerves : primary repair 72% ≥ grade 3 (ulnar), 85% (median/radial); early repair > delayed Autograft for mixed nerves : useful motor (M3+) in 63-81%; gaps > 4.5 cm (ulnar), 5 cm (median), 8 cm (radial) = worse ANA for mixed : 77-81% meaningful recovery (M3+); only 40-50% achieve M4+ Sural nerve harvest: persistent sensory loss in 93%; allodynia in 50% (few consider it a major problem) Neuroma management: reconstruction preferred when distal stump available; TMR (targeted muscle reinnervation) gaining enthusiasm; centro-central repair for digital stump neuromas

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Wait 2-3 weeks post-injury for meaningful NCS/EMG (Wallerian degeneration must progress) Neurapraxia: intact conduction distal to injury, no fibrillations Axonotmesis/neurotmesis: loss of distal conduction, fibrillations on EMG Cannot reliably distinguish Sunderland II from III/IV early 3-4 months : intraoperative nerve-to-nerve conduction across zone of injury; action potential present = 90% chance of continued recovery

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Serial exams (monthly): active ROM, isolated muscle strength, sensory testing, Tinel tracking Progressing Tinel = controversial but useful if documented with focal locations + measurements Neuroma pain (mechanical, triggered by direct stimulus/stretch) vs neuropathic pain (burning, tingling, nocturnal, cortical imprinting) — local block differentiates

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Treatment › Gap Bridging
text: Conduits : for digital/sensory nerves, gaps < 2.5 cm; collagen, PGA, polycaprolactone; fibrin clot scaffold unreliable > 15 mm Acellular nerve allograft (ANA) : 3D neural architecture advantage; digital/sensory up to 5-7 cm; growing use in mixed nerves; 84% S3+/S4 for short sensory gaps; autograft still gold standard for gaps > 7 cm Autograft : sural nerve = workhorse (30-40 cm per leg); cable graft technique for larger nerves; harvest 15-20% longer than defect; vascularized grafts theoretically better but not widely adopted Nerve transfers : sacrifice redundant nerve for critical function; especially useful for proximal injuries, long gaps, hostile tissue beds

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: US or MR neurography to identify complete ruptures (surgical indication) MRI advances may distinguish injury grades but clinical utility unproven

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Sunderland I-II with NCS/EMG confirmation or early clinical recovery: observation Passive ROM to prevent joint stiffness; strengthening once any recovery detected Gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline for neuropathic pain (minimize narcotics) Mirror therapy + desensitization for neuroma/neuropathic pain

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Indications : laceration with deficit, confirmed neurotmesis, closed injuries without recovery at 3-4 months Repair ASAP to minimize axotomy/denervation effects + stump retraction Avulsion/blast/GSW: wait 2-3 weeks for zone demarcation; acute repair of avulsed radial nerves = universal failure Tension > 8-15% = decreased perfusion, impaired Schwann cell function, stunted regeneration Coaptation tools : Suture (epineurial > fascicular in most situations) Fibrin glue (fast, equivalent in animal studies; risk of catastrophic failure; not FDA-approved for nerve) Connectors (entubulation improves alignment, protects repair site, may auto-correct malalignment)

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Neurapraxia vs axonotmesis cannot be distinguished in first 2-3 weeks — early EDX has minimal value Fascicles “pooch” from cut nerves due to perineurial pressure — inspect for this to confirm healthy fascicular pattern during resection Epineurial vessels = key alignment landmarks during repair Conduit gap > 15 mm for digital nerves = less predictable fibrin clot scaffold Radial nerve has best prognosis; ulnar nerve (especially proximal) has worst ANA vs autograft: unsettled debate; patient preference (cadaver tissue vs donor site morbidity) often decides

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Protective immobilization 3 weeks post-coaptation (60% burst strength at 8 wk in rodents, 77% at 4 wk in primates) Early motion OK after digital nerve repair (does not affect outcomes) Protected early ROM takes precedence if concurrent flexor tendon repair Emphasis on maintaining supple joints, pain control, nerve-modulating medications

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Incidence: ~0.6 per 100,000; 1.2% of trauma cases at level-1 centers; male:female 9:1; average age ~30 Mechanisms: traffic accidents, ATVs/snowmobiles, penetrating trauma, shoulder impact Upper plexus: traction separating arm from cervical spine or direct supraclavicular impact Lower plexus: sudden hyperabduction or anterior shoulder impact Most common patterns (descending): panplexus > C5-C8 > C5-C6 > C5-C7 True 5-level avulsion rare (2-5% of panplexus) Preganglionic (avulsion) : cell body in DRG intact → SNAP preserved despite sensory loss (hallmark EDX finding) Postganglionic (rupture) : Wallerian degeneration occurs; SNAP lost

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient with panplexus BPI has absent sensation in the C8-T1 distribution. NCS shows a normal ulnar SNAP. What is the diagnosis? — A: Preganglionic (root avulsion) injury of C8-T1; the DRG is intact so the sensory arc is preserved despite clinical sensory loss. Q: What is the preferred nerve transfer combination to restore both shoulder abduction and external rotation? — A: SAN-to-suprascapular nerve (ER/supraspinatus) + triceps branch-to-anterior branch of axillary nerve (deltoid abduction); the “double transfer” achieves 100% ≥ M3 in pooled data. Q: At what time point should surgical reconstruction proceed if serial exams show no recovery from a closed BPI? — A: 3 months if Tinel is stationary and no MUAPs on EMG; do not observe beyond 6 months without intervention. Q: Why does free functioning muscle transfer (FFMT) remain an option for patients presenting > 18 months after BPI? — A: FFMT brings its own muscle with it (gracilis), so it is not constrained by the 12-18 month window for native muscle denervation atrophy.

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Classification
text: Seddon : neurapraxia / axonotmesis / neurotmesis Sunderland : 1st-5th degree (ascending histologic damage) MacKinnon grade VI : mixed pattern across zone of injury

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Intraplexal transfers > nerve grafts for elbow flexion (83% vs 56% M4+) Double transfer for shoulder: 100% ≥ M3, 74% ≥ M4 (mean abduction 122°) vs single: 70% ≥ M3 Intercostal nerve harvest: 10% pleural breach rate; respiratory compromise usually transient FFMT flap loss rare but must monitor 5 days (hourly Doppler x 24h) 40% BPI patients do not return to work; ~80% satisfied with quality of life One-third of US patients undergo surgery > 1 year post-injury (suboptimal delays)

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Obtain at 4-6 weeks (allow Wallerian degeneration) Intact SNAP + clinical sensory loss = preganglionic injury (pathognomonic) MUAP characteristics indicate nascent reinnervation vs collateral sprouting If no MUAPs at 3 months → proceed with surgical reconstruction

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis) → likely C8-T1 avulsion Scapular winging → proximal upper trunk branch injury (long thoracic / dorsal scapular) Shoulder “ptosis” (sulcus below AC joint) → deltoid paralysis MRC grading 0-5; nearly all function within M4 — reliable serial testing critical Tinel sign : absent = preganglionic; stationary = non-recovering postganglionic (Sunderland IV/V); advancing distally = recovering (Sunderland II/III) Bouvier maneuver to assess intrinsic function Screen for concurrent rotator cuff injury (10% of BPI patients)

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Treatment › Free Functioning Muscle Transfer (FFMT)
text: Gracilis = workhorse; not constrained by denervation window Single-stage (Giuffre): clavicle anchor → FDP/FPL; intercostals for power, SAN for triceps Two-stage (Doi): stage 1 = elbow flexion + finger extension; stage 2 = finger flexion Vascular: thoracoacromial trunk (deltoid branch best size match) Obturator nerve innervation; tension set at 30° elbow flexion contracture at rest

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: XR: elevated hemidiaphragm (phrenic injury), clavicle/scapula fx, scapulothoracic dissociation CT myelogram : gold standard for pseudomeningoceles (85-95% sensitivity for avulsions) MRI : equivalent sensitivity (~93%), noninvasive, evaluates distal plexus + rotator cuff US: emerging tool for neuroma-in-continuity evaluation

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Treatment › Key Reconstruction Strategies
text: Function Preferred Transfer Alternative Shoulder abduction/ER SAN→SSN + triceps→axillary (double transfer) C5 graft to PDUT; intercostals Elbow flexion Double Oberlin (median→brachialis + ulnar→biceps) Intercostals, SAN+graft, FFMT Elbow extension Intercostals→long head triceps Thoracodorsal, ECRB fascicle Grasp FFMT (gracilis) Two-stage Doi procedure

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Treatment › Nerve Grafting
text: C5 graft to PDUT for shoulder; C6 graft to ADUT for elbow flexion Sural nerve = workhorse autograft (highest fascicular density; 30-40 cm per leg) Cable graft: lay on tongue depressor, fold back, fibrin glue ends, cut at folds Grafts < 12 cm preferred; > 12 cm = diminishing returns Intraoperative NAP + SSEP to assess root viability

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Suspected neurapraxia/mild axonotmesis with progressive recovery Passive ROM all joints (scapulothoracic to fingers), core/periscapular strengthening Pain management : gabapentin/pregabalin first-line; 75% report significant pain at long-term follow-up; involve pain management early Slings/orthotics to prevent contracture from muscle imbalance

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Timing : ideal referral 4-6 weeks; surgery by 3 months if no recovery; do not observe > 6 months Millesi algorithm : stationary Tinel + unchanged MMT + no MUAPs at 3 mo → operate; if Tinel advancing + MUAPs present but no clinical improvement → reassess at 6-week intervals Functional priorities (memorize this order): (1) elbow flexion, (2) shoulder abduction/ER, (3) protective hand sensation, (4) grasp/prehension, (5) elbow extension; intrinsic hand function is nearly impossible to restore in flail limb

title: Brachial Plexus Injuries
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Intact SNAP in area of sensory loss = preganglionic avulsion (cannot graft; must transfer) Always explore panplexus injuries — high likelihood of finding at least one graftable root (usually C5) Do not harvest phrenic + multiple intercostals simultaneously unless carefully weighing respiratory risk Contralateral C7 transfer = controversial; risk of permanent donor-side deficit Even modest reinnervation provides a “helper limb” — set realistic expectations early Psychological support is critical (depression prevalent, financial strain, prolonged recovery)

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › AIN Syndrome
text: Non-operative first : rest, immobilization, avoid provocative activities; onset of recovery 5.9 mo (range 3-12); full recovery 9.5 mo; age < 40 = better prognosis Operative (6 months without recovery + confirmed EDX + no other nerve lesions): same approach as pronator; consider interfascicular neurolysis for hourglass constrictions (Sneag: fascicular constrictions proximal to elbow in all 22 patients on MR neurography)

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Median nerve: C5-T1, formed by medial + lateral cords Crosses anterior to brachial artery at mid-humerus (lateral→medial) Ligament of Struthers : fibrous band from supracondylar process to medial epicondyle (1-4% of population); can compress median nerve ± brachial artery Compression sites (proximal → distal): ligament of Struthers → lacertus fibrosus → pronator teres (between heads) → FDS arch → carpal tunnel Martin-Gruber anastomosis (forearm median→ulnar motor crossover): 23% prevalence; bilateral in 19%; Type I (60%) and Type II (35%) most common AIN : largest muscular branch; arises 5-8 cm distal to medial epicondyle; innervates FPL, FDP (index/long), PQ; terminal sensory branch to volar wrist joint Gantzer’s muscle (accessory FPL head): present in up to 68% — a normal variant, not rare Carpal tunnel boundaries: carpal bones dorsally, TCL palmarly; narrowest at hook of hamate (20x10 mm) TCL : attaches pisiform/hamate (ulnar) to scaphoid/trapezium (radial); thickest at middle-distal third junction (up to 6 mm in CTS); division reduces carpal arch stiffness only 7% Recurrent motor branch: extraligamentous 46%, subligamentous 31%, transligamentous 23% (Lanz) Bifid median nerve : 2.8% prevalence; associated with persistent median artery in 79%

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient with forearm aching and numbness over the thenar eminence has a negative Phalen and Tinel at the wrist. What is the most likely diagnosis? — A: Pronator syndrome; palmar cutaneous branch involvement distinguishes it from CTS, and negative wrist provocative tests support proximal compression. Q: A 35-year-old presents with inability to make an “OK” sign after sudden severe shoulder pain 2 weeks ago. EMG shows denervation in FPL, FDP index, and brachioradialis. What is the diagnosis? — A: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy); brachioradialis involvement extends beyond isolated AIN territory, and the presentation with severe initial pain is classic. Q: What are the three variations of the recurrent motor branch course relative to the TCL? — A: Extraligamentous (46%), subligamentous (31%), transligamentous (23%) per the Lanz classification. Q: What is the most reliable MRI finding in AIN syndrome? — A: Edema within the pronator quadratus on T2-weighted fat-saturated images (Dunn); fascicular constrictions proximal to the elbow on MR neurography (Sneag). Q: After open carpal tunnel release, a patient reports persistent numbness. At revision, what is the most common finding? — A: Incomplete TCL release; also dense scar tissue with median nerve adherent to radial TCL leaflet. MABC neuroma found in 73% of failed cubital tunnels (analogous risk in CTR with cutaneous nerve injury).

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Pronator syndrome: incomplete decompression up to 55%; MABC neuroma risk AIN: incomplete correction most common; Park: 10/11 achieved M4 within 12 mo post-surgery CTS: pillar pain (12.7%), burning discomfort (18%), scar tenderness (7.3%); structural nerve/vessel/tendon injury rare with either approach Revision CTS: challenging; 41-91% persistent symptoms after revision; recurrent group improves most

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › CTS — Non-operative
text: Wrist neutral splint (especially nocturnal); neutral > 20° extension Steroid injection : benefits up to 6 months; 32% never need further treatment (Evers, 7.4 yr follow-up); diabetics 2.6x more likely to recur within 1 year Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo). CTS injection technique : enter ulnar to palmaris longus, just proximal to the distal wrist crease, angling 30-45 degrees

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › CTS — Operative
text: Indications : thenar atrophy, constant numbness, severe EDX changes, symptoms > 1 year, failed 6-week non-operative trial Open mini CTR (authors’ preferred): 3-cm incision from distal wrist crease in ring finger axis; divide TCL distal→proximal with 2-mm cuff on hook of hamate; release antebrachial fascia 2-3 cm proximal; inspect for anomalies; no routine tenosynovectomy or neurolysis Endoscopic (Agee single-portal) : 1-cm incision at wrist; divide TCL under direct visualization; faster return to work; higher nerve injury risk (mostly transient) No beneficial effect of post-op immobilization demonstrated (multiple studies) Outcomes: > 95% good/excellent; endoscopic preferred by 66% of patients (scar/pillar pain); revision rate 1-5%

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: CTS : prolonged median sensory peak latency > 4.0 ms at wrist; motor distal latency > 4.5 ms; median-ulnar difference > 0.5 ms (sensory) or > 1.5 ms (motor) Severity: mild (sensory only), moderate (sensory + motor), severe (absent sensory + abnormal motor), extreme (both absent) Pronator syndrome : often normal — NCS helps rule out other sites; normal wrist conduction + clinical findings → supports proximal compression AIN syndrome : acute denervation limited to AIN-innervated muscles; 60% have concomitant abnormalities in non-AIN distributions

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Pronator syndrome : tenderness over proximal PT, positive pronator compression test (30 sec), no Tinel at wrist, no Phalen/Durkan; resisted supination → bicipital aponeurosis; resisted long finger PIP flexion → FDS arch AIN syndrome : Kiloh-Nevin sign (cannot make “OK” sign — compensatory FPB/FDS flexion instead) CTS provocative tests : Phalen (sens 68%, spec 73%), Tinel (50%, 77%), Durkan (64%, 83%), combined Durkan+Phalen (80%, 92%) CTS-6 : numbness in median distribution, nocturnal numbness, thenar weakness/atrophy, Tinel, Phalen, loss of 2PD — probability score correlates with CTS diagnosis Barrera: CTS-6 score > 12 = positive for CTS. Sensory testing pearl : Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments test threshold (earlier finding); static 2PD tests innervation density (late finding) — use both for every suspected compression neuropathy

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › History
text: Pronator syndrome : vague forearm ache, daytime symptoms with pronation/supination, numbness in palmar cutaneous distribution (thenar eminence — distinguishes from CTS) AIN syndrome (Kiloh-Nevin) : sudden forearm pain → weakness/loss of FPL + index FDP + PQ; no sensory loss; overlap with Parsonage-Turner syndrome CTS : nocturnal paresthesias (hallmark), bimodal peaks (5th + 8th decades), female:male 3:1; > 500,000 releases/year in US

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Thenar eminence numbness = pronator syndrome (palmar cutaneous branch doesn’t traverse carpal tunnel) AIN syndrome and Parsonage-Turner overlap significantly — EDX + MRI help distinguish; PT has broader nerve involvement + severe initial pain CTS + pronator syndrome can coexist (double crush) — failed CTR should prompt proximal evaluation Incision for open CTR: ring finger axis, 5+ mm ulnar to interthenar depression to protect palmar cutaneous branch Kaplan’s cardinal line (parallel to abducted thumb ulnar border → hook of hamate) = distal TCL extent Recurrent motor branch exits 6.5 mm from distal TCL edge in ring finger axis — respect the fat pad

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Pronator Syndrome
text: Non-operative : activity modification, nerve glides, stretching, brief immobilization; Morris: 5/7 responded to intramuscular PT steroid injection Operative (> 3 months persistent symptoms): lazy-S incision from 5 cm above medial epicondyle across antecubital fossa extending distally 10 cm; release all compressive structures (lacertus, PT heads, FDS arch, ligament of Struthers if present); protect MABC nerves, median motor branches, radial artery Post-op: splint 7-10 days (elbow 90°, forearm 45° pronation, wrist slight flexion); ROM at 7-10 days; resistive exercises at 6-8 weeks Outcomes: complete relief 22%, improvement 63%, unchanged 9% (Hartz); minimally invasive approaches achieving 93% resolution (Zancolli)

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Revision CTS
text: Persistent (no relief) vs recurrent (relief then return after 6 mo) vs new symptoms (iatrogenic) Extended open approach; identify nerve proximal to scar in native tissue; external neurolysis Hypothenar fat pad flap (Strickland): well-vascularized coverage over scarred median nerve; ulnar-artery-based perforators

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: High median palsy (proximal to AIN): loss of FCR, FDS, FDP index (±long), FPL, PQ, thenar muscles, lumbricals 1-2 → index finger rests in full extension, thumb loses opposition + IP flexion Low median palsy (distal to AIN): thenar muscles + lumbricals 1-2 only → normal digital cascade, thenar wasting, lost opposition; clawing rare (interossei compensate) Wrist-level injury : primarily sensory (thumb through radial ring); palmar cutaneous branch spared; thenar wasting Long finger FDP often has dual ulnar + median innervation → may retain flexion Deep head FPB often dual innervated → some palmar abduction preserved even in median palsy

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient with high median nerve palsy has index and long fingers resting in extension while ring and small fingers maintain normal cascade. What muscles are denervated? — A: FDP to index (AIN), FDS to all digits (median), FPL (AIN), pronator teres, FCR, PQ, thenar muscles, lumbricals 1-2. Ring/small FDP are ulnar-innervated and preserved. Q: Which opponensplasty is preferred for a patient with combined median and ulnar nerve palsy? — A: EIP (Burkhalter) — it is radial nerve-innervated and does not require a pulley, making it reliable when both median and ulnar motors are unavailable. Q: What is the preferred nerve transfer to restore forearm pronation in an isolated pronator teres palsy? — A: ECRB branch to PT nerve — synergistic function (wrist extension + pronation occur together) facilitates intuitive motor re-education. Q: After a high median nerve injury, the long finger retains DIP flexion. Why? — A: Long finger FDP often has dual innervation from both the AIN (median) and ulnar nerve; the ulnar contribution preserves active DIP flexion.

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Nerve transfer outcomes: ECRB→AIN achieves M3-M4 finger/thumb flexion at 12-24 months; brachialis→AIN similar EIP opponensplasty: reliable but EDC subluxation if extensor hood not repaired; EIP absent in 4% FDS opponensplasty: adequate length and excursion; risk of swan neck and friction at pulley site Sural nerve harvest: persistent sensory loss in most (93%); allodynia in 50% but rarely clinically significant Sensory nerve transfer: risk of abnormal sensation, painful donor site, poor cortical reorientation FDP side-car: cannot achieve independent index flexion; transection prevents recovery if nerve regenerates

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Wait ≥ 3 weeks post-injury; NCS/EMG distinguishes neurapraxia from axonotmetic injury Cannot reliably differentiate Sunderland II from III/IV early Intraoperative NAP across neuroma-in-continuity: positive = 90% continued recovery

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Sensory: thumb, index, long, radial ring (volar + dorsal tips); palmar cutaneous branch → thenar eminence + radial palm (high vs low localization) Motor: test opposition (APB), FPL (thumb IP flexion), FDP index (DIP flexion), pronation Resting cascade : high palsy = index (±long) in full extension; low palsy = normal cascade + thenar wasting Resting cascade of a high median nerve palsy — the index and long fingers rest in extension with loss of flexor tone (FDP/FPL denervated), while the ulnar-innervated ring and small fingers keep a normal cascade; thenar wasting is also visible. (ASSH Handthology) Resting cascade of a high median nerve palsy — the index and long fingers rest in extension with loss of flexor tone (FDP/FPL denervated), while the ulnar-innervated ring and small fingers keep a normal cascade; thenar wasting is also visible. (ASSH Handthology) Thenar wasting — side-by-side comparison of the atrophic thenar eminence (patient) against normal thenar bulk (examiner), the hallmark of median motor loss. (ASSH Handthology) Thenar wasting — side-by-side comparison of the atrophic thenar eminence (patient) against normal thenar bulk (examiner), the hallmark of median motor loss. (ASSH Handthology)

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Repair
text: Same principles as NV-01: resect to healthy fascicles, tension-free, fascicular alignment, epineurial suture Avulsion/blast: wait 2-3 weeks for demarcation; cable graft for gaps Sural nerve = workhorse donor; 30-40 cm per leg; cable graft technique for larger nerves

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers for Motor
text: ECRB branch → AIN : restores extrinsic finger/thumb flexion (FDP index, FPL, PQ) Brachialis branch (musculocutaneous) → AIN or PT : for high injuries ECRB → PT nerve : restores pronation (simultaneous wrist extension + pronation = intuitive re-education) ADM ulnar motor branch → recurrent median motor branch : restores opposition (El-Haj) Nerve transfer technique pearl : check with anesthesia pre-op about avoiding long-acting paralytics — intraoperative stimulation required. At 0.5 mA the donor should fire strongly; at 2.0 mA the recipient target should have zero response. “Donor distal, recipient proximal” for tension-free coaptation.

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers for Sensation
text: Critical: restore sensation to radial index + ulnar thumb for precision pinch Ulnar 4th web space → median 1st web space (end-to-end, with reverse end-to-side for donor recovery) Dorsal cutaneous ulnar → median 1st/2nd web space fascicles (forearm level) Radial sensory branches → ulnar digital thumb + radial digital index (dorsal-to-palmar transfer) FDMA flap (innervated by dorsoradial sensory nerve) for thumb pulp resurfacing — sensate but donor morbidity limits use

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Neurapraxic/axonotmetic with evidence of recovery: observation + passive ROM Opponens splint (thumb in palmar abduction, slight pronation, slight MP flexion) Buddy straps for index/long finger flexion deficit Consider non-operative if minimal functional deficit or patient has adapted well (e.g., strong pulp-to-side pinch in quadriplegia)

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Index finger in full extension at rest = pathognomonic for high median palsy Thenar wasting + normal digital cascade = low median palsy EIP opponensplasty = best choice for combined median-ulnar injuries (radial nerve innervated) Camitz = abduction only, not true opposition — quick addition during open CTR in severe CTS with thenar atrophy Don’t forget to test deep head FPB (often ulnar innervated) — some palmar abduction may be preserved Full passive ROM at all joints required before any tendon transfer

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: All opponensplasties: thumb spica 4-6 weeks (thumb palmarly abducted, flexed, pronated, wrist neutral); therapy at 4-6 wk; strengthening at 8 wk FDP side-car: dorsal blocking splint (digits slightly flexed, wrist neutral) x 4-6 weeks Nerve transfers: motor re-education starts at 3 weeks (donor activation, mirror therapy, bilateral exercises)

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Tendon Transfers — Finger Flexion (High Palsy)
text: FDP “side-car” : paralyzed index (±long) FDP woven into functioning ring/small FDP; restores cascade + IP flexion; loses independent index flexion Alternative: ECRL → index FDP in combined median-ulnar palsy Side-car transfer for high median palsy — the paralyzed index (± long) FDP is sutured side-to-side to the working, ulnar-innervated ring and small FDP so all flex in unison; the dual-innervated long FDP need not be included. (ASSH Handthology) Side-car transfer for high median palsy — the paralyzed index (± long) FDP is sutured side-to-side to the working, ulnar-innervated ring and small FDP so all flex in unison; the dual-innervated long FDP need not be included. (ASSH Handthology)

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Tendon Transfers — Opposition
text: EIP Opponensplasty (Burkhalter) — preferred for trauma/combined median-ulnar palsy - EIP harvested at index MCP (ulnar side of sagittal band); rerouted dorsal-ulnar → palmar-radial around ulna; Pulvertaft weave into APB insertion - No pulley needed (ulna redirects); radial-nerve innervated (independent of median/ulnar) - Drawbacks: dorsal ulnar sensory nerve at risk; crosses over carpal tunnel scar EIP opponensplasty, step 1 — the EIP donor is identified at its insertion on the dorsal extensor hood, ulnar to the index EDC; repair the hood after harvest to prevent EDC subluxation. (ASSH Handthology) EIP opponensplasty, step 1 — the EIP donor is identified at its insertion on the dorsal extensor hood, ulnar to the index EDC; repair the hood after harvest to prevent EDC subluxation. (ASSH Handthology) EIP opponensplasty, step 2 — the EIP is withdrawn through a separate incision over the ulnar wrist, proximal to the extensor retinaculum, and the muscle is fully mobilized for palmar-ulnar redirection. (ASSH Handthology) EIP opponensplasty, step 2 — the EIP is withdrawn through a separate incision over the ulnar wrist, proximal to the extensor retinaculum, and the muscle is fully mobilized for palmar-ulnar redirection. title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Radial nerve enters the arm posteriorly via spiral groove at junction of middle/distal thirds of humerus Enters radial tunnel between brachialis (medial) and brachioradialis (proximal/lateral), ECRL (distal/lateral) Floor: anterior radiocapitellar capsule + deep supinator; roof: fibrous connection brachialis-brachioradialis Bifurcates at radial tunnel exit into SRN (sensory) and PIN (motor) PIN dives under arcade of Frohse (proximal edge of supinator) — common compression site Leash of Henry (radial recurrent artery branches) = most common compressor in radial tunnel SRN becomes subcutaneous 9 cm proximal to radial styloid between ECRL tendon and brachioradialis; bifurcates ~5 cm proximal to styloid Nerves stretched > 6% of length → detectable conduction block from altered perfusion

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient with lateral elbow pain has tenderness 3 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, pain with resisted middle finger extension, and normal grip strength. EDX is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis? — A: Radial tunnel syndrome; tenderness distal to the epicondyle + pain with resisted middle finger extension + normal EDX distinguishes it from lateral epicondylitis and PIN syndrome. Q: A patient with PIN palsy extends the wrist in radial deviation. Why? — A: ECRL is innervated by the radial nerve proximal to the PIN takeoff and is preserved; ECRB (mixed radial/PIN innervation) is weakened, leaving unopposed radial deviation. Q: What is the most common structure causing compression of the radial nerve within the radial tunnel? — A: Leash of Henry (branches of the radial recurrent artery). Q: A 55-year-old presents with progressive finger drop, EMG denervation of extensor muscles, and a palpable mass at the proximal forearm. What is the next step? — A: MRI to evaluate for space-occupying lesion (lipoma, ganglion, Schwannoma); if mass confirmed, surgical excision + PIN decompression.

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Classification
text: Saturday night palsy / crutch palsy / honeymoon palsy : proximal compression in spiral groove → neurapraxia; complete wrist/finger/thumb drop Radial tunnel syndrome : pain condition; radial nerve compressed within mobile wad PIN syndrome : motor compression at arcade of Frohse → finger/thumb extension weakness/palsy Wartenberg’s syndrome : SRN compression at brachioradialis exit → dorsoradial forearm/1st webspace numbness

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Saturday night palsy: excellent prognosis; less favorable with older age, EMG denervation, profound initial weakness Radial tunnel surgery: De Smet reported only 40% satisfaction; concurrent epicondylitis and workers’ comp = worse outcomes PIN decompression: 24/25 recovered motor function (Hashizume); avg 5.6 months to recovery; 1 patient required tendon transfer Wartenberg’s: most improve without surgery; surgical outcomes 75% success (Lanzetta)

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Saturday night palsy : decreased NCV + amplitude (conduction block); serial EMG — brachioradialis recovers first, EIP last Radial tunnel : typically normal (pain syndrome); dynamic testing may show conduction block with active supination PIN syndrome : motor NCV decreased across supinator; EMG shows denervation of extensor muscles; sensory radial nerve normal Wartenberg’s : variable — normal to complete SRN conduction block; no motor changes

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Saturday night palsy : complete wrist/finger/thumb extension palsy ± dorsal hand paresthesia; distinguish from PIN (BR + ECRL preserved in PIN) Radial tunnel : tenderness ≥ 2 cm distal to lateral epicondyle (vs epicondylitis = at epicondyle); pain with resisted middle finger extension + resisted supination; no weakness; Rule of Nine test (Loh) PIN syndrome : finger/thumb extension weakness; wrist extension in radial deviation (ECRL unopposed); SBRN sensation intact Wartenberg’s : Tinel over SRN; decreased 2PD in 1st webspace; symptoms with pronation + ulnar deviation; diagnostic lidocaine injection at brachioradialis exit

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › History
text: Saturday night palsy : acute wrist drop after prolonged arm compression (avg 180 min); worse with alcohol, opioids, DM, hypothyroidism, obesity Radial tunnel : aching mobile wad pain ≥ 2 cm distal to lateral epicondyle; worse with activity; no numbness or weakness; occupational risk = repetitive pronation/pinching PIN syndrome : finger/thumb weakness or extension lag; wrist deviates radially (ECRL intact, ECRB weakened); may have 25% traumatic etiology Wartenberg’s : numbness/paresthesia dorsoradial forearm and 1st webspace; onset with repetitive pronation; coexists with de Quervain’s in up to 50%

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: XR: fracture, malunion, osseous lesion (all syndromes) MRI for PIN: denervation edema/atrophy of supinator/extensors; identify lipomas, Schwannomas, synovitis

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Radial tunnel syndrome = a pain diagnosis; PIN syndrome = a motor diagnosis — exam distinguishes them BR + ECRL preserved → PIN palsy (not high radial); wrist extends with radial deviation Saturday night palsy almost always recovers — resist early surgery unless open fracture or penetrating injury Radial tunnel surgery without a confident diagnosis has high failure rates — exhaust non-operative care Wartenberg’s and de Quervain’s coexist in up to 50% — evaluate for both when either is suspected Reinnervation order after proximal radial injury: BR → ECRL → ECRB → EDC → ECU → EDQ → APL → EPL → EPB → EIP

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › PIN Syndrome
text: Non-operative if no EDX denervation: activity modification, therapy, serial EDX monitoring Operative if progressive weakness or EMG denervation: full PIN decompression through supinator including distal exit; release arcade of Frohse + distal fibrous edge 3-month rule : if no improvement at 3 months → proceed to decompression (85% good/excellent outcomes); ages > 50 do poorly — consider concomitant tendon transfer (Ochi) Spontaneous PIN recovery is rare; early intervention > conservative treatment

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Radial Tunnel Syndrome
text: Non-operative first : activity modification, elbow flexion + supination splinting, nerve glides, stretching; steroid injection (Sarhadi: 64% long-term relief) Operative (failed 3-6 months): extensile anterolateral approach; release radial nerve through radial tunnel, ligate Leash of Henry, release arcade of Frohse; do not over-dissect SRN beyond tunnel Outcomes: 67-92% success in systematic review; worse with concurrent lateral epicondylitis or workers’ comp Diagnostic pearl : localize tenderness precisely — epicondyle vs 2+ cm distal. A diagnostic lidocaine injection into the radial tunnel that relieves symptoms is the most helpful confirmatory test (warn the patient about transient finger/thumb drop)

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Saturday Night Palsy (Non-operative)
text: Observation: 89-94% spontaneous recovery (begins avg 2.4 weeks; complete by avg 3.4 months) Cock-up wrist splint + dynamic outriggers; maintain ROM with therapy/nerve gliding Surgery only if no clinical/EDX recovery by 12 weeks (atraumatic) or 3-6 months (traumatic) Open humeral shaft fractures with radial palsy → early nerve exploration (lower spontaneous recovery rate ~85%)

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Wartenberg’s Syndrome
text: Non-operative : desensitization therapy, nerve gliding, remove compressive straps/watches; NSAIDS, rest Operative (failed 3-6 months): longitudinal incision 6-8 cm proximal to radial styloid; release brachioradialis over SRN + overlying fascia; passive wrist manipulation to identify additional compression Outcomes: 71% improve non-operatively; surgical success ~75-86%

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Most common peripheral nerve injury with long-bone fractures — 11.8% of humeral shaft fractures Injury at junction of middle/distal thirds of humerus (least mobile segment) Holstein-Lewis (distal humeral shaft) fractures: up to 25% radial nerve palsy 71% of humeral shaft fracture radial palsies resolve with observation Reinnervation order (proximal→distal): BR → ECRL → ECRB → EDC → ECU → EDQ → APL → EPL → EPB → EIP Radial nerve has best recovery prognosis of the three major UE nerves: shorter distance to motor end plates, larger caliber, distinct fascicular organization, motor-predominant with similar target muscles

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient sustains a closed mid-shaft humerus fracture with complete wrist drop. At 6 weeks, EMG shows no MUPs in radial-innervated muscles. What is the management? — A: Continue observation to 3 months total; 71% of closed fracture radial palsies recover spontaneously. Splint with cock-up orthosis + maintain passive ROM. Q: In a FCR-based tendon transfer for radial nerve palsy, which tendon powers wrist extension, finger extension, and thumb extension? — A: PT → ECRB (wrist), FCR → EDC (fingers), PL → EPL (thumb). Q: What is the primary advantage of nerve transfer over tendon transfer for radial nerve palsy? — A: Nerve transfer restores independent finger extension, avoids sacrifice of wrist flexion strength, and avoids the radial deviation deformity seen with FCU-based tendon transfers. Q: What radial nerve graft gap length is associated with significantly worse outcomes? — A: > 8 cm (Petkovic); for median nerve > 5 cm, for ulnar nerve > 4.5 cm.

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Tendon transfer: reliable, time-proven; potential bowstringing (especially PL→EPL), radial deviation (FCU method), stiffness Nerve transfer: less dissection, no strength loss, independent finger extension; but 9-12 month wait Jain 2023 systematic review : TT clinical success 82% vs nerve transfer 59% vs nerve grafts Bertelli 2020 : nerve transfers better — TT group had wrist flexion limitation (9/13), permanent radial deviation (5/13), 50% needed wrist flexion for full finger extension

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Exam
text: High radial palsy : loss of BR, ECRL, ECRB, EDC, ECU, EIP, thumb extensors → no wrist/finger/thumb MCP extension + decreased 2PD dorsal hand Very proximal: also loses triceps + posterior arm sensation PIN palsy : BR + ECRL preserved → wrist extends with radial deviation; SBRN intact MRC grading; donor must be ≥ M4 (loses one grade with transfer)

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Repair/Reconstruction
text: Primary end-to-end : ideal; 91% ≥ M3 with primary suture (Murovic) Tension-free; resect to healthy fascicles; humeral shortening for 1-2 cm gaps Avulsions = universally failed with acute repair (inadequate debridement) Autograft : sural nerve or medial antebrachial cutaneous; Berger: 77% M4-M5 with interfascicular graft (avg 6.6 cm) Gaps > 8 cm = significantly worse outcomes (Petkovic) Open injuries, concomitant vascular injury, no recovery at 3 months → surgical exploration

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers (Median-to-Radial)
text: FDS branch → ECRB (wrist extension) FCR branch → PIN (finger + thumb extension) “Donor distal, recipient proximal” — curvilinear proximal forearm incision Ray & Mackinnon (19 pts) : 18/19 M4+ wrist extension at 20 mo; 12/19 M4+ finger/thumb extension Ideal window: 3-6 months from injury; reinnervation goal within 12-18 months Advantages: faster proximal-level recovery, avoids injured field, no graft, independent finger extension 9 patients also received concurrent PT→ECRB tendon transfer as dynamic internal splint Key teaching point : nerve transfers restore independent finger extension and don’t sacrifice wrist flexion power. The trade-off is 9-12 months waiting for reinnervation vs immediate function with tendon transfer.

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Mainstay for closed palsies; observe 3 months Cock-up wrist orthosis + dynamic outriggers; maintain passive ROM Radial nerve palsy alone is not an indication for surgical fixation of humeral fracture

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Tendon Transfers › Outcomes
text: Moussavi (41 pts) : all three methods successful; no ROM/DASH/RTW difference; 95% would repeat; mean RTW 4.5 months (FCR group) Ishida & Ikuta (21 pts, FCR-based, 11.3 yr) : avg wrist extension 54°, flexion 42°; MCP extension 5° with wrist at 30° extension; grip 63% contralateral; bowstringing in 12/21 (all PL→EPL)

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Radial nerve palsy with closed humeral fracture → observe 3 months; 71% recover spontaneously Open fractures + radial palsy → early exploration (lower spontaneous recovery) PT → ECRB is universal across all three transfer methods — start learning this one Don’t sacrifice FCU if you can avoid it — it’s the most powerful wrist flexor and critical for ulnar deviation PL absence (up to 20%) shifts you from FCR-based to FDS-based method Concurrent nerve transfer + tendon transfer (e.g., FDS→ECRB as “internal splint” while awaiting nerve transfer recovery) is an emerging strategy Full passive ROM mandatory before any tendon transfer

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Tendon Transfers › Principles (7 rules)
text: Donor must be expendable Adequate strength (loses 1 grade) Similar excursion/resting length One function per tendon Straight line of pull Synergistic (wrist flexion = finger extension; wrist extension = finger flexion) Full passive ROM at all joints before transfer
