title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Cubital tunnel borders : medial epicondyle (anterior), olecranon (posterior), Osborne’s ligament/FCU aponeurosis (roof), MCL posterior/transverse bands (floor) Cubital tunnel CSA decreases 40% at 135° elbow flexion; intraneural pressure increases 45% at 120° 5 compression sites at elbow: arcade of Struthers (5.7 cm proximal) → medial head triceps → Osborne’s ligament → between FCU heads → intermuscular ligament FCU-FDS Guyon’s canal : 3 zones (Gross & Gelberman 1985) Zone I : motor + sensory (ganglion, thrombosis, mass) Zone II : motor only (hook of hamate fracture, ganglion) Zone III : sensory only Nerve hypermobility at elbow: present in 37% of asymptomatic individuals — not automatic indication for transposition DCU branches 7 cm proximal to wrist → dorso-ulnar sensation affected at elbow level but spared with wrist-level compression

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient with ulnar neuropathy has numbness of the small finger and ulnar ring finger volarly but intact dorsoulnar hand sensation. Where is the compression? — A: Guyon’s canal (wrist level); the dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises 7 cm proximal to the wrist and is spared in wrist-level compression. Q: After cubital tunnel release, a patient has new pain along the medial forearm without ulnar distribution symptoms. What is the most likely cause? — A: MABC neuroma — the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve branches cross the surgical field and are injured in 73% of revision cases (Mackinnon). Q: A patient with cubital tunnel syndrome has a normal EDX study. Does this rule out the diagnosis? — A: No; 26% of patients with clinical cubital tunnel have no electrodiagnostic evidence (Kortlever). Up to 80% of the motor neuron pool can be lost before clinical detection due to compensatory motor unit enlargement. Q: What physical exam finding distinguishes a Zone II Guyon’s canal lesion from a Zone I lesion? — A: Zone II is motor-only — patient has intrinsic weakness/clawing but preserved sensation; Zone I involves both motor and sensory fibers. Q: Four RCTs comparing simple decompression vs anterior transposition for cubital tunnel syndrome showed what? — A: No significant difference in outcomes between techniques; simple decompression is preferred as the most cost-effective approach.

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Song (39 pts) : improved pinch (7.0→8.3), SWM, DASH (30.4→19.8), MHQ (55.5→70.7) at 12 mo Subjective scores plateau at 3 mo; objective improvement continues > 12 mo (Giladi) 4 RCTs : no difference between simple decompression and transposition Excellent results 45-57% regardless of technique; simple decompression most cost-effective Trend: transposition declining (67%→16%), in situ rising (~80%) Revision rate: 1.4-19%; predictors: trauma history (OR 7.1), McGowan I (OR 3.2), workers’ comp MABC neuroma in 73% of revision failures; perineural fibrosis in 68% McGowan I patients = OR 3.2 for failure (often other causes: cervical, polyneuropathy, TOS)

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: AAEM criteria; conduction velocity (demyelination) → CMAP amplitude reduction (axonal loss = later) Reduced CMAP at FDI predicts preoperative weakness (Power 2019) 26% with clinical cubital tunnel have no EDX evidence (Kortlever) — diagnosis can be clinical Up to 80% motor neuron pool can be lost with near-normal muscle function (single motor units enlarge 5x to compensate)

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Duchenne sign : ring/small clawing (weak lumbricals/interossei + unopposed extrinsic flexors) Wartenberg sign : small finger abduction (paralyzed 3rd volar interosseous + unopposed EDM) Froment sign : thumb IP flexion with lateral pinch (lost adductor pollicis → compensatory FPL) Nerve stability: “stable” (stays in groove) vs “perching” vs “dislocating” with flexion Elbow flexion-compression test (Novak): highly reliable Scratch collapse test : variable accuracy; ethyl chloride can unmask secondary sites 2PD: abnormal only in severe compression Barrera: For 2PD I always test in order: thumb, index, middle, ring, small. Compare ulnar to radial side of ring finger — that’s your median-ulnar watershed.

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Guyon’s Canal (Ulnar Neuropathy at Wrist)
text: Ganglion = most common cause ; also hook of hamate fracture (Zone II), ulnar artery thrombosis Spares dorsoulnar hand (DCU branches proximal to wrist) Allen test to evaluate ulnar artery patency Non-operative: activity modification, gel-padded gloves; no evidence for splinting/steroids Surgical: open Guyon canal, decompress deep motor branch around hook of hamate; release distal antebrachial fascia proximal to wrist crease

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Mild/early: activity modification, avoid prolonged flexion Night splinting: rigid orthosis or soft towel block in antecubital fossa x 3-4 weeks

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Operative — Endoscopic In Situ
text: 2-4 cm incision; endoscopic blade divides fascia 10 cm proximal + distal Check for subluxation after release Outcomes equivalent to open (Aldekhayel meta-analysis: 79.8% vs 81.8%)

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Operative — In Situ Decompression (Preferred for Most Cases)
text: 3-6 cm incision between olecranon and medial epicondyle Preserve MABC branches (neuroma in 73% of revision failures — Mackinnon) Release cubital tunnel retinaculum + deep brachial fascia (8 cm proximal) + FCU aponeurosis distally Do NOT dissect circumferentially → causes instability Check stability post-release: perching → evaluate triceps fascia; subluxation → stabilizing flap or transposition

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Operative — Transposition
text: Subcutaneous : excise medial intermuscular septum (proximal AND distal); sling/adipofascial flap to prevent fall-back; preserve FCU motor branches Submuscular : most protected, well-vascularized; often used for revision; Z-lengthen flexor-pronator origin Intramuscular: theoretically straighter; risk of scarring within muscle

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Incorrect diagnosis = critical complication — r/o C8-T1 radiculopathy, thoracic outlet, polyneuropathy before surgery McGowan grade I patients have highest failure rate — low threshold for additional workup Dorso-ulnar sensation affected → compression at elbow (not wrist) 37% nerve hypermobility is normal — don’t transpose for hypermobility alone; 79% do transpose for true subluxation Average 2.2 compression sites missed at revision (Gabel) — complete release from arcade of Struthers through FCU MABC injury during initial surgery → most common source of post-op pain; careful identification + preservation is essential Simple in situ decompression is now the dominant approach — supported by 4 RCTs showing no inferiority to transposition

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Supercharge AIN-to-Ulnar Motor (SETS)
text: Indication: severe compression, reduced CMAP, spontaneous activity on FDI/ADM EMG, normal PQ EMG Distal forearm incision; AIN harvested at PQ; epineurial window in ulnar motor fascicle ~9 cm proximal to wrist crease Doherty : 73% achieved M3 intrinsic strength Xie RCT : 13% greater pinch strength + lower DASH at 2 yr vs transposition alone Treatment algorithm : injections are not part of cubital tunnel management. Stepwise approach: activity modification → night splinting → surgical decompression. Default to simple in situ release unless nerve subluxes post-decompression.

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Origin: medial cord (C8-T1); pierces medial intermuscular septum ~8 cm above medial epicondyle Arcade of Struthers : aponeurotic band from medial intermuscular septum to medial head triceps (~5.7 cm proximal to epicondyle) Only major nerve on opposite side of axis of joint rotation → vulnerable to compression + traction with flexion FCU innervation: avg 3.4 branches (Tubbs); FDP ring/small: 3 cm distal to medial epicondyle DCU branches 7 cm proximal to wrist → key localizing feature At wrist: 2 fascicular bundles — sensory (volar/ulnar) and motor (dorsal/radial) Motor distribution: hypothenar (ADM, FDM, ODM, palmaris brevis), 3 palmar + 4 dorsal interossei, lumbricals 3-4, adductor pollicis, deep head FPB Most terminal motor branches are farthest from plexus of any terminal brachial plexus branch → high injuries have worst prognosis for intrinsic recovery Interconnections: Martin-Gruber (forearm, 17%), Riche-Cannieu (hand, 77%)

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient with a high ulnar nerve laceration has less clawing than expected. Why? — A: The “ulnar paradox” — FDP to ring and small fingers is also denervated in high lesions, so the extrinsic flexors cannot overpower the extensors at the IP joints, resulting in less apparent clawing. Q: A patient with ulnar claw hand has a positive Bouvier maneuver and full passive ROM. What is the simplest surgical option? — A: Zancolli FDS lasso (dynamic, modulates with wrist position) or MCP capsulodesis (static, simpler but stretches over time). Q: Which tendon transfer restores thumb adduction in ulnar nerve palsy? — A: Smith transfer — ECRB elongated with free graft, tunneled dorsal-to-volar between long and ring metacarpals, to the adductor pollicis insertion at the ulnar thumb MCP. Q: What nerve transfer provides “anti-clawing” by restoring intrinsic function after proximal ulnar nerve injury? — A: AIN-to-motor branch of ulnar nerve (end-to-end); the “supercharge” end-to-side variation can supplement recovery from proximal repair. Q: In a complex claw hand (negative Bouvier), why must the Stiles-Bunnell FDS 4-tail pass palmar to the deep transverse metacarpal ligament? — A: To maintain the volar axis relative to the MCP joint — this ensures the transfer flexes the MCP and extends the IPs (replicating intrinsic function) rather than just flexing the digit.

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Classification
text: Low ulnar palsy (at/distal to wrist): intrinsic motor + palmar ulnar sensory loss; FCU/FDP ring-small + dorsoulnar sensation PRESERVED High ulnar palsy (proximal to DCU): adds FCU/FDP ring-small weakness + dorsoulnar sensory loss Ulnar paradox : clawing is LESS pronounced in high palsy (FDP ring-small also weakened, so extrinsic flexors can’t hyperextend MCPs as effectively)

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Ulnar nerve: worst prognosis of 3 major UE nerves — Seddon: only 31% good sensory, 13% good motor recovery High repairs far worse than low (long regeneration to intrinsics) Children < 12: 87% complete recovery; adolescents 12-20: 67% (Chemnitz) Capsulodesis: stretches over time; only 47% satisfactory clawing resolution (Brown, 44 pts) FDS 4-tail + ECRL 4-tail both correct extensor lag equally; lag > 30° improves 45%; < 30° improves 75% Smith transfer: 50% contralateral lateral pinch strength; adding index abductorplasty → 75% pinch but unacceptable index posture AIN→ulnar motor: improved pinch + grip, decreased clawing, minimal donor morbidity (PT compensates for PQ)

heading: Treatment › Nerve Repair

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers
text: AIN → Ulnar Motor (End-to-End) - Indicated for high ulnar injury proximal to elbow - AIN harvested at PQ; coapt to proximally transected ulnar motor fascicle - Contraindications: late presentation (> 9-12 mo), concurrent median injury Supercharge End-to-Side (SETS) - Epineurial window in ulnar motor fascicle 8-10 cm proximal to wrist; AIN sutured end-to-side - Indicated for: severe cubital tunnel, axonotmetic elbow/forearm injury, Parsonage-Turner - Supplements, doesn’t replace, recovery from proximal repair Radial → Ulnar Motor - For combined median + ulnar injury: PIN branches (EDM + ECU) → ulnar motor (Tung) Bertelli Distal Transfer - Opponens pollicis branch → terminal deep branch ulnar nerve → reinnervates FDI + adductor pollicis for pinch Sensory Transfers - Palmar median branches → ulnar digital nerve of small finger - Combined median + ulnar palsy: PIN at wrist → DCU for ulnar border sensation

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Non-operative

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Ulnar paradox: less clawing with high palsy (seems counterintuitive) — because FDP ring/small is also denervated Bouvier maneuver is the key decision point: positive → static/lasso; negative → 4-tail transfer Don’t use Stiles-Bunnell in a patient with positive Bouvier — creates iatrogenic swan neck Lumbrical bar splinting early prevents progression from simple → complex claw Riche-Cannieu anastomosis (77%) can mask ulnar motor deficits — intrinsic function may be partially preserved via median crossover Anterior transposition reduces gap by ~4 cm — consider before defaulting to graft Late presentation, failed repair, long gaps → tendon transfers; outcomes limited by scar, line-of-pull challenges

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Thumb Adduction — Smith Transfer (ECRB)
text: ECRB harvested from long MC base → elongated with free graft Tunneled superficial to extensor retinaculum → dorsal-to-volar between long + ring MCs → ulnar thumb MCP at adductor pollicis insertion Tenodesis: wrist extension → thumb abducts; wrist flexion → thumb adducts Results: 50% contralateral lateral pinch, 63% adduction force Smith adductorplasty — the ECRB is harvested from the long-finger metacarpal base and withdrawn through a counter-incision proximal to the extensor retinaculum. Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Radiography = initial modality of choice for suspected bony pathology (trauma, arthritis, congenital) Minimum 2 orthogonal views; beam centered on capitate (wrist PA) or 3rd MC head (hand PA) Adequate lateral wrist confirmed when pisiform volar surface lies midway between volar capitate and distal scaphoid pole

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: What is the most sensitive and specific location for measuring median nerve CSA on ultrasound in suspected CTS? — A: Carpal tunnel inlet at the level of the pisiform. Q: A lateral wrist radiograph shows a scapholunate angle of 75°. What does this indicate? — A: DISI pattern (dorsal intercalated segment instability); normal SL angle is 30-60°. Q: Gilula’s arc II is disrupted on a PA wrist radiograph after a fall. What pathology should be suspected? — A: Carpal instability — perilunate dislocation or intercarpal ligament disruption. Q: What is the PPV of CT for scaphoid fracture union? — A: 99%.

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Image-Guided Intervention
text: US-guided arthrocentesis > blind, especially small hand joints US-guided radiocarpal injection: 100% accuracy vs 76% palpation-guided (better DASH/Mayo/VAS) Glenohumeral US-guided injection: 93% accuracy vs 73% landmark US-guided barbotage for calcific tendinitis: minimal benefit vs subacromial steroid alone Percutaneous sclerotherapy efficacious for low-flow vascular malformations Ultrasound in experienced hands can replace MRI for many tendon and nerve pathologies — real-time, inexpensive, and no scheduling required

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Imaging — CT
text: Superior osseous detail; multiplanar reconstruction for complex fracture patterns Scaphoid union: PPV 99% ; reformat along scaphoid long axis for humpback deformity Radiographs over/underestimate articular step-off in 30% of intra-articular DRFs Gold standard for fracture healing when radiographs indeterminate Radiation doses: 0.03 mSv (hand) to 2.06 mSv (shoulder) — well below 3 mSv annual background CT arthrography more accurate than MRI/MR arthrography for partial SLIL and LTIL tears For occult scaphoid fracture, CT confirms cortical injury but MRI is preferred — it directly evaluates marrow edema and associated soft tissue injury

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Imaging — MRI
text: 3.0T = current standard of care (2x SNR vs 1.5T) Superb contrast resolution for soft tissue, marrow, ligaments Scaphoid AVN (13-50% incidence, predominantly proximal fifth): diffusely decreased T1 in proximal pole ≤ skeletal muscle signal = high specificity; dynamic gadolinium MRI is not superior to unenhanced MR arthrography : gold standard for shoulder labroligamentous pathology; superior to conventional MRI for joint pathology (shoulder, elbow, wrist) MR neurography (3.0T): better anatomic localization than EMG; abnormal nerve = focal enlargement, T2 hyperintensity, fascicular abnormality, course deviation Titanium hardware preferred over stainless steel for MRI compatibility Specialized positions: ABER (anteroinferior labrum), FABS (distal biceps), supination/pronation axial (ECU subsheath)

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Imaging — Other
text: Bone scintigraphy : highly sensitive, low specificity; high NPV; positive results need MR/CT characterization SPECT-CT : hybrid imaging increases accuracy over scintigraphy alone Digital tomosynthesis : viable alternative for radiographically occult scaphoid fractures

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Imaging — Radiography
text: Standard Views PA hand/wrist, lateral, oblique (30° pronated for dorsal/ulnar wrist; 30° supinated for pisotriquetral) Shoulder requires true orthogonal: 40° posterior oblique AP + axillary lateral + scapular Y Special Views Scaphoid view : PA with 30° ulnar deviation — elongates scaphoid, improves sensitivity for nondisplaced fractures Carpal tunnel view : supinated wrist dorsiflexed 30-35°, beam along 3rd MC axis Stress views : Wolf thumb CMC stress view, clenched fist PA (SL widening) Key Measurements Scapholunate angle (lateral): normal 30-60° Radiolunate angle : ~10° flexion normal (range: 15° flexion to 20° extension) Lunocapitate angle : abnormal if > 15° Gilula’s arcs (PA): Arc I = proximal row convexity, Arc II = distal proximal row concavity, Arc III = capitate/hamate convexity; disruption = joint integrity loss Carpal height ratio : 0.54 ± 0.03 Ulnar variance : measure in neutral rotation (pronation lengthens, supination shortens); power grip PA uncovers dynamic positive variance Elbow AP + lateral + radial head view; lateral in flexion shows fat pads Sail sign = elevated anterior fat pad = effusion Posterior fat pad visible = effusion (normally hidden in olecranon fossa) Raised fat pads + trauma + no visible fracture = suspect occult intra-articular fracture

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Imaging — Ultrasound
text: Flexor tendon laceration : 90% accuracy Displaced thumb UCL tear : 100% accuracy RC full-thickness tear : 88% accuracy (MRI 95%) — no statistically significant difference; meta-analysis: both > 90% CTS : median nerve CSA at carpal tunnel inlet (pisiform level) = most sensitive/specific location; more accurate and cost-effective than NCS Cubital tunnel: CSA cutoff 10 mm² → sensitivity 93%, specificity 98% De Quervain’s EPB separate subcompartment reliably detected — risk factor for nonoperative failure Sonoelastography: quantifies tissue stiffness; healthy tendons stiffer, diseased tendons softer

title: Imaging of the Hand, Wrist, and Upper Extremity
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Radiography first for bony injury; occult scaphoid fracture rate after negative initial XR = 9-33% CT > MRI for cortical injury, but MRI best overall for occult fractures (marrow edema + soft tissue) Ulnar variance must be measured in neutral rotation — pronation falsely lengthens the ulna Negative imaging does not rule out the clinical diagnosis; positive imaging does not always correlate clinically MRI is method of choice for arthritic joints (especially inflammatory) — early erosions, synovitis, marrow edema Elbow MR arthrography is gold standard for the throwing athlete CT arthrography is a valid alternative when MRI is contraindicated or has failed

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Workup › Allergic Reactions
text: Very rare; most from ester subtype (PABA metabolite) or methylparaben preservative True lidocaine allergy essentially non-existent (< 20 case reports in 20 years)

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Classification › Amide vs Ester
text: Amides (have “i” before “-caine”): lidocaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine — metabolized by liver Esters : cocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, procaine — hydrolyzed by plasma pseudocholinesterase

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Treatment › Anesthesia in Pregnancy
text: Nonurgent surgery: second trimester preferred Local anesthetics not known teratogenic → WALANT/regional without sedation preferred in first trimester Emergent: proceed as indicated WALANT eliminates the need for an anesthesia team, recovery room, or overnight stay. For flexor tendon repairs and tendon transfers, intraoperative active motion verification sets tension and reduces rupture risk.

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient develops circumoral paresthesias and metallic taste during a WALANT CTR. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment? — A: LAST (local anesthetic systemic toxicity); IV lipid emulsion bolus then infusion. Q: Which local anesthetic is most cardiotoxic and why? — A: Bupivacaine — it has high avidity for cardiac Na+ channels, causing refractory arrhythmias. Q: Which brachial plexus block always causes ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy? — A: Interscalene block. Q: A patient’s fingertip is white and without capillary refill 2 hours after a digital block with lidocaine + epinephrine. What is the antidote? — A: Phentolamine (1.5 mg in 1 mL 2% plain lidocaine, inject subcutaneously). Q: What is the most common cause of fingertip tissue loss after a digital block with epinephrine? — A: Patient accidentally burning the fingertip with hot water while trying to restore sensation.

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Workup › Epinephrine Toxicity
text: Antidote: phentolamine — 1.5 mg diluted in 1 mL 2% plain lidocaine, inject subcutaneously until site pinks up

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Local Anesthetic Mechanism
text: Reversibly block voltage-gated Na+ channels → prevent depolarization Differential blockade by fiber size/myelination: pain → cold → heat → touch → deep pressure → motor

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Workup › Methemoglobinemia
text: Primarily prilocaine (metabolite ortho-toluidine); rare with lidocaine; no reported cases with WALANT MetHb > 3-5 mg/dL → cyanosis, chocolate-colored blood Treatment: O2 + IV methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg over 5 min (repeat q60min, max 7 mg/kg)

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Nerve Physiology
text: Resting potential -70 mV; threshold -55 mV triggers voltage-gated Na+ channel opening → depolarization Repolarization via K+ efflux to -95 mV; Na/K ATPase restores gradient Myelinated nerves: saltatory conduction (nodes of Ranvier) — faster Conduction rate proportional to axon cross-sectional area

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Amides have “i” before “-caine” — lidocaine, bupivacaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine LAST is progressive — circumoral paresthesias and metallic taste are early warning signs before seizures Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local; avoid for WALANT (also has 30 hr numbness) Phentolamine is the specific antidote for both epinephrine-related ischemia and LAST-related vasoconstriction Always inject proximal to distal for WALANT — anesthetize the nerve before the operative field Big nerves (median at wrist) may take up to 100 min for full anesthesia without US guidance — tumesce epineurium early

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Classification › Pharmacology
text: ↑ Lipid solubility → faster onset ↑ Protein binding → longer duration pKa determines onset: lower pKa = more uncharged base = faster diffusion (lidocaine pKa 7.9 = rapid; bupivacaine pKa 8.1 = slower) NaHCO3 buffering raises extracellular pH → more uncharged base → faster onset + less pain All locals except cocaine are vasodilators → epinephrine added for hemostasis, prolonged effect, decreased systemic absorption Max dose: 7 mg/kg lidocaine with epinephrine

text: Brachial Plexus Blocks Block Coverage Key note Interscalene Shoulder Always blocks phrenic nerve Supraclavicular Any UE incl. shoulder Less phrenic block; pneumothorax < 0.04% with US Infraclavicular Elbow and below Reliably blocks musculocutaneous Axillary Forearm + hand Often misses musculocutaneous (needs separate block) All UE blocks need separate intercostal brachial nerve block for tourniquet tolerance Bier block : not recommended given WALANT/nerve block advances (limited by tourniquet pain + systemic toxicity risk) Peripheral Blocks Median at wrist : between FCR and PL, 2-3 cm proximal to crease Ulnar at elbow : 3-5 cm proximal to elbow (avoid subcutaneous position behind medial epicondyle — neuritis risk) Radial at wrist : field block 5-7 cm proximal to radial styloid, lateral to radial artery

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Workup › Toxicity — LAST (Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity)
text: Progression : lightheadedness → circumoral paresthesias/metallic taste → tinnitus/slurred speech → nystagmus/tremors → seizures → coma/arrest Treatment : ABCs + IV lipid emulsion (bolus then infusion) + seizure management Bupivacaine particularly cardiotoxic (avid for cardiac Na+ channels) — bradyarrhythmias, wide QRS, negative inotropy, cardiac collapse

title: Local Anesthesia + WALANT
heading: Treatment › WALANT — Wide Awake Local Anesthesia No Tourniquet
text: Tumescent local anesthesia floods surgical field; no tourniquet, no sedation Wait ≥ 30 min for optimal vasoconstriction — inject 2-3 patients ahead Even 0.25% lidocaine with 1:400,000 epinephrine provides adequate analgesia and hemostasis Fingers: max 2 mL volar/dorsal at P1 and P2; < 1 mL at P3 Always inject proximal to distal (anesthetize nerves first) Key Advantages No preop testing, fasting, IV, or medication changes Safer than sedation for ASA 4 patients No need to discontinue anticoagulation Intraoperative active motion verification — reduces flexor tendon rupture, sets tendon transfer tension No tourniquet let-down bleeding; often no cautery needed Simple procedures (CTR, K-wires) can move to clinic without increased infection WALANT sequence: local injection → 30-min wait → prep/drape → operate Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lidocaine (never Depo-Medrol) — separate from the WALANT local. title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Amyloidosis
text: Misfolded transthyretin (TTR) deposition in carpal tenosynovium + TCL Consider tenosynovial biopsy with Congo red staining during CTR for: men ≥ 50, women ≥ 60, bilateral CTS, history of spinal stenosis or biceps tendon rupture, atrial fibrillation, CHF, family history

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Anticoagulation
text: Most hand/wrist procedures have minimal muscle dissection → low bleeding risk Recommend continuing warfarin perioperatively unless high risk for hematoma necrosis or compartment syndrome Continued antiplatelets distal to DR metaphysis: rare bleeding complications ASA discontinuation for secondary coronary prevention: up to 3x increased cardiac complications ; thrombotic events average 11 days post-cessation Rebound prothrombotic state with acute withdrawal of antiplatelets or warfarin VKA stoppage (when indicated): stop 5 days preop, resume 12-24h postop Bridging anticoagulation: yes for high VTE risk, no for low risk; meta-analysis shows bridging increases bleeding without reducing VTE NOACs : low bleeding risk surgery = no interruption (ASRA: ≥ 12h last dose to surgery); no bridging if interruption < 96h NOAC reversal: idarucizumab (dabigatran-specific); activated charcoal within 2h for dabigatran/apixaban; hemodialysis decreases dabigatran

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient on warfarin for atrial fibrillation needs open CTR. Should warfarin be held? — A: No. Hand/wrist procedures are low bleeding risk; continuing warfarin is recommended to avoid thromboembolic complications. Q: An insulin-dependent diabetic has bilateral trigger fingers involving 3 digits. CSI has failed once per digit. What is the next step? — A: Surgical release. Insulin-dependent DM has higher CSI failure rates and multi-digit involvement predicts poor injection response. Q: A 55-year-old man with bilateral CTS, spinal stenosis, and atrial fibrillation undergoes CTR. What additional step should be considered? — A: Tenosynovial biopsy with Congo red staining to rule out ATTR amyloidosis. Q: What preoperative evaluation is essential before GA in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis? — A: Flexion-extension cervical spine radiographs — 43-86% have cervical involvement, and up to 50% are asymptomatic. Q: A pregnant patient in the third trimester presents with bilateral CTS. What is the recommended management? — A: Night splinting (> 80% relief); surgery is generally avoided as > 90% resolve within 2 weeks of delivery.

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › CKD
text: 14% of US adults; CKD = risk factor for postop AKI, MI, heart failure, stroke Platelet dysfunction → bleeding tendency; also prothrombotic Dialysis day before surgery preferred; emergent = same day without heparin Pain management: avoid NSAIDs (nephrotoxic if CrCl < 30), avoid morphine + codeine; prefer tramadol, fentanyl

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Diabetes Mellitus
text: “Diabetic hand” : limited joint mobility, Dupuytren’s (2-8x more common), trigger finger (up to 20% prevalence), CTS (up to 15%) Trigger finger in DM: more likely bilateral, multidigit, fail CSI → require surgery; insulin-dependent = higher failure rate Blood glucose elevation post-CSI lasts up to 5 days — counsel diabetic patients CTS in DM: more advanced nerve pathology on NCS but no clinical outcome difference after OCTR vs non-diabetic Ideal HbA1c < 7.5% preop, optimal ≤ 7.0% Counsel diabetic patients that steroid injections are less likely to work and blood glucose will spike for up to 5 days. For trigger finger in insulin-dependent diabetics with multiple digits involved, consider early surgical release rather than repeated injections. Perioperative DM Medication Management Hold day of surgery : sulfonylureas, alpha-glucose inhibitors, short/rapid-acting insulin Hold day before + day of : SGLT-2 inhibitors Continue : metformin (hold for IV contrast), thiazolidinediones, DPP-4 inhibitors Insulin adjustments : intermediate-acting = 50% morning dose day of; long-acting = 75% morning dose; pump = sick day/sleep basal rate

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Hepatic Disease
text: Risk assessment: Child-Pugh + MELD score Elective surgery contraindicated in acute hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, acute liver failure, decompensated cirrhosis Acetaminophen safe and first-line for pain; avoid NSAIDs Opioids: avoid controlled-release; co-prescribe laxatives (prevent constipation + encephalopathy)

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › NSAIDs and Bone Healing
text: Short-term use (< 3-4 weeks): no impact on bone healing Long-term (> 3-4 weeks): association with nonunion and delayed union COX-2 inhibition decreases PGE2 required for BMP-induced osteogenesis

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Default to continuing anticoagulation for hand/wrist surgery — the bleeding risk is almost always lower than the thromboembolic risk of stopping No DVT has been reported after elbow/wrist/hand surgery — do not over-prophylax RA patients need cervical spine imaging before intubation even if asymptomatic — up to 50% have silent disease Continue DMARDs perioperatively; hold biologics and schedule surgery at end of dosing cycle Counsel smokers that vaping is not safer — equivalent complication rate STOP-BANG: undiagnosed OSA is more dangerous than diagnosed OSA perioperatively Short-course NSAIDs (< 3-4 weeks) do not impair fracture healing

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Pregnancy
text: Imaging: maximize US + MRI; minimize ionizing radiation gestational weeks 3-8 (organogenesis) 1st/2nd gen cephalosporins: Category B (relatively safe); aminoglycosides + vancomycin: Category C Warfarin contraindicated in pregnancy Ibuprofen/ketorolac: Category D in 3rd trimester CTS in pregnancy: prevalence 1-62%, often bilateral, 3rd trimester; > 90% resolve within 2 weeks of delivery ; night splinting gives > 80% relief; surgery generally avoided CTS in pregnancy is driven by fluid retention, not structural compression — reassure patients that the vast majority resolve after delivery. Night splinting is first-line; surgery is rarely indicated.

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Rheumatoid Arthritis
text: Preop cervical spine evaluation essential: 43-86% have cervical involvement; up to 50% with radiographic disease are asymptomatic Recommend flexion-extension cervical XR minimum + communicate with anesthesia Atlantoaxial instability, cranial settling, subaxial subluxation → affects intubation DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, HCQ): generally safe to continue perioperatively Biologics (etanercept, infliximab, abatacept): stop, schedule surgery at end of dosing cycle, resume ≥ 14 days postop if no wound issues Decreasing rate of rheumatoid hand surgery with modern DMARDs/biologics

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Sleep Apnea
text: 80-90% undiagnosed; STOP-BANG screening tool S noring, T ired, O bserved apnea, blood P ressure, B MI > 35, A ge > 50, N eck circumference (M ≥ 17”, F ≥ 16”), G ender male Low: 0-2; Intermediate: 3-4; High: 5-8 Suspected/undiagnosed OSA → worse outcomes than preop diagnosis (↑ respiratory complications, ICU admission, 30-day mortality) WALANT ideal for OSA — patient protects own airway Restart CPAP at outpatient settings ASAP post-extubation; minimize postop opioids

title: Perioperative Medical Conditions in Hand Surgery
heading: Treatment › Smoking
text: Independent predictor of unplanned readmission after outpatient hand/elbow surgery Increased infection after trigger digit release and open CTR Increased CTS development + more severe preop symptoms + persistent symptoms after OCTR Cessation ≥ 4 weeks preop for best outcomes E-cigarettes have equivalent complication rate and microcirculation impact

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Patient’s thoughts, emotions, beliefs, behaviors, and circumstances may matter more than pathophysiology in determining symptom intensity and disability Mind uses pattern-based shortcuts (heuristics, automatic thoughts) — adaptive for danger, maladaptive for benign pain Negative affect amplifies symptoms; positive affect buffers Depression should be treated as a distinct pathology, not a consequence of pain

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient with bilateral hand pain out of proportion to exam, normal imaging, and high PHQ-9 score asks for MRI and surgery consultation. What is the most appropriate next step? — A: Address depression as a primary condition (CBT referral, consider pharmacotherapy); additional imaging and surgical consultation are unlikely to help and may reinforce illness behavior. Q: What validated instrument specifically measures catastrophizing and predicts poor hand surgery outcomes? — A: Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS) — measures magnification, helplessness, and rumination. Q: A patient presents with recurrent dorsal hand swelling and fibrosis without a clear mechanism. What factitious condition should be suspected? — A: Secretan syndrome (repetitive self-striking of the hand dorsum). Q: What is the difference between secondary gain and malingering? — A: Secondary gain is unconscious environmental reinforcement (e.g., doting spouse, escape from stressful job); malingering is a conscious plan for objective material gain. They exist on a spectrum.

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Depression + anxiety predict: more pain, more limitations, difficult-to-treat diagnoses, poor treatment response High psychological distress predicts onset of forearm pain (prospective data) CRPS + phantom limb pain may be conceptualized as disproportionate pain syndromes Nonspecific arm pain (crossing anatomical areas, disproportionately disabling) strongly associated with catastrophizing + depression + heightened illness concern

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Classification › Coping Constructs
text: Self-efficacy : belief in one’s ability to cope — strongest protective factor reducing symptoms Catastrophizing (Pain Catastrophizing Scale): magnification, helplessness, rumination → greater symptoms, delayed RTW, larger pain diagrams Heightened illness concern (Illness Anxiety Disorder): conviction of serious illness despite normal workup + reassurance; > 6 months with anxiety

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Classification › DSM-5-TR Conditions in Hand Patients
text: Condition Key features Somatic Symptom Disorder Unexplained symptoms beyond pain (pruritus, numbness); sensory amplification; denial of psychological issues Illness Anxiety Disorder Misinterpretation of benign symptoms as serious disease; persists despite reassurance Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (conversion) Motor/sensory deficit not explained by pathophysiology; not intentionally feigned Factitious Disorder Deliberately produces/feigns symptoms for attention (not conscious material gain)

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Symptoms disproportionate to pathology — the core red flag Clenched fist/posturing : functional neurological symptom disorder; DDx UMN lesion Factitious lymphedema : surreptitious tourniquet → “broken windowpane” collateral pattern; cast immobilization resolves it Secretan syndrome : repetitive self-striking of hand dorsum → swelling → peritendinous fibrosis

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Workup › History
text: Screen for depression, anxiety, life stressors, financial/legal context Ask about prior surgeries for nonspecific pain (Munchausen pattern: many illnesses, many surgeries, migrates between centers) Secondary gain (unconscious environmental reinforcement) vs malingering (conscious plan for objective gain) — a spectrum, not categorical

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Workup › Measurement Tools
text: PHQ-2/PHQ-9 , CES-D, Beck Depression Inventory — depression Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS) — magnification, helplessness, rumination PROMIS Depression CAT + PROMIS-Pain Interference CAT — recommended validated instruments Health Anxiety Inventory, Whitley Index — illness concern When symptoms are wildly disproportionate to pathology, resist the urge to order more tests or offer surgery. The trap is stress contagion — the patient’s distress drives the physician to act, and acting (imaging, injections, procedures) reinforces illness behavior without improving health.

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: CBT consistently effective in trials for disproportionate pain, catastrophizing, illness constructs Pathophysiology-targeted treatments for illness constructions (repetitive strain injury, whiplash) often ineffective or harmful Build self-efficacy: acceptance, adaptation, resiliency Treat comorbid depression and anxiety as primary conditions Biomedical labels help avoid stigma but risk iatrogenic harm, medicalization of normal symptoms, and missed opportunities for self-management

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Treatment › Operative — Pitfalls
text: Operative treatment is not associated with more relief of depression than nonoperative management (Crijns et al.) Unnecessary surgery reinforced by placebo effect, regression to mean, self-limited natural history Multiple CTRs or surgeries for nonspecific pain → suspect factitious disorder

title: Psychological Aspects of Arm Illness
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Symptoms disproportionate to pathology = think psychosocial, not “harder workup” Catastrophizing (PCS) is the single strongest psychological predictor of poor surgical outcomes Treat depression directly — it is not just a reaction to pain Self-efficacy is the most powerful protective factor; help patients build it Surgery does not treat depression; operating on somatizers causes harm Secondary gain is unconscious; malingering is conscious — most patients are on the secondary gain end “Illness constructions” (RSI, whiplash, cumulative trauma disorder) imply known pathophysiology where none exists — CBT works, pathology-targeted treatments do not Stress contagion is the physician’s trap: the patient’s distress drives you to act when watchful support is the right answer
