text: Work stepwise: malformation vs deformation vs dysplasia 20.5% of patients need multiple OMT codes Substantial to almost perfect inter/intraobserver reliability

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A child is born with only a radius and thumb on the affected limb. Which signaling molecule is most likely absent? — A: Sonic hedgehog (Shh) from the ZPA; its absence eliminates ulnar-sided structures while preserving radial structures. Q: What syndrome results from haploinsufficiency of Lmx1b? — A: Nail-patella syndrome (dorsal-ventral axis defect). Q: In the OMT classification, a child with syndactyly and camptodactyly is classified under which main category and subcategory? — A: Category I (Malformation), subcategory B (hand plate), axis 4 (unspecified). Q: Which transcription factor initiates chondrogenesis in the developing limb? — A: Sox9.

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Classification

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › High-Yield Molecular Details
text: Fgf10 → Wnt3 → Fgf8 loop drives proximal-distal outgrowth; three segments: stylopod (arm), zeugopod (forearm), autopod (hand) Shh from ZPA generates posterior-to-anterior gradient; Gli3 is the key mediator; loss of Shh → only radius and thumb form Wnt7a → Lmx1b : dorsalizes bone, muscle, tendons, skin appendages (nails). Haploinsufficiency of Lmx1b → Nail-patella syndrome En1 in ventral ectoderm determines dorsal-ventral boundary Thumb is Shh-independent but requires Gli3r for patterning; digit 4 forms first, digit 1 last

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Limb Development Timeline
text: Limb buds appear end of week 4 (day 26, Carnegie stage 12) Y-shaped anlagen (humerus, radius, ulna) by day 35 (Carnegie stage 15) Arm/forearm muscles evident by day 41 (Carnegie stage 17) Proportional human extremity by week 8; sensory fibers reach fingertips by Carnegie stage 23

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Classification › OMT Classification (Oberg-Manske-Tonkin, 2020)
text: Adopted by IFSSH 2014; based on molecular biology of limb development. Replaced Swanson’s morphology-based system. I. Malformations — abnormal formation - A. Abnormal axis formation — entire limb - Proximal-distal (symbrachydactyly, transverse deficiency) - Radial-ulnar (RLD/thumb hypoplasia, ULD, radioulnar synostosis) - Dorsal-ventral (absent extensors/flexors) - Unspecified (arthrogryposis) - B. Abnormal axis formation — hand plate - Proximal-distal (brachydactyly) - Radial-ulnar (radial/ulnar polydactyly, triphalangeal thumb) - Unspecified (syndactyly, camptodactyly, clinodactyly, cleft hand, Apert) II. Deformations — altered limb with presumed normal initial development - Constriction ring sequence, trigger digits III. Dysplasias — abnormal cell size/shape - Hypertrophy (macrodactyly, hemihypertrophy) - Tumorous conditions IV. Syndromes — 44 named syndromes

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: AER disruption → transverse deficiency; ZPA disruption → radial-ulnar patterning defects Shh absence with Gli3r present → only radius and thumb form (board favorite) Nail-patella syndrome = Lmx1b haploinsufficiency (dorsal-ventral axis) OMT replaced Swanson — know both for boards but OMT is the current standard Symbrachydactyly vs transverse deficiency classification remains challenging even with OMT Digit 4 forms first, digit 1 (thumb) forms last — counterintuitive but high-yield Board-prep mnemonic — three axes + signaling centers: AER → Fgf → proximal-distal , ZPA → Shh → radial-ulnar , dorsal ectoderm → Wnt7a/Lmx1b → dorsal-ventral

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: References
text: Oberg KC, Manske PR, Tonkin MA. OMT Classification of Congenital Anomalies. IFSSH, 2020. Swanson AB. Classification of limb malformations. J Hand Surg Am. 1964. Limb development molecular biology — ASSH Handthology synthesis

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Skeleton Formation
text: Sox9 initiates chondrogenesis; Runx2 drives osteoblast differentiation Metacarpals and digits have only one secondary ossification center → unidirectional growth Gdf5 orchestrates joint formation; loss → progressive joint deformity

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Three Axes of Limb Development
text: Axis Direction Organizing center Key signal Proximal-distal Shoulder → finger AER (apical ectodermal ridge) Fgf8/Fgf10 reciprocal loop Anteroposterior Radial → ulnar ZPA (zone of polarizing activity) Shh (Sonic hedgehog) Dorsal-ventral Dorsal → volar Dorsal ectoderm Wnt7a → Lmx1b

title: Embryology and Classification of Congenital Hand Differences
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Tissue Differentiation Origins
text: Lateral plate mesoderm → cartilage, dermis, connective tissue, ligaments, tendons Ectoderm → epidermis, nail structures Somites → muscle (myocytes migrate to limb guided by tendon precursors) Spinal cord → motor neurons (FoxP1 = limb-specific; Lhx1 = dorsal/extensor; Isl2 = ventral/flexor)

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A neonate has bilateral absent radii with intact thumbs and thrombocytopenia. What is the diagnosis? — A: TAR syndrome (thumbs are always present, distinguishing it from RLD type 4). Q: A child has Blauth grade IIIB thumb hypoplasia. What is the recommended surgical treatment? — A: Ablation and index finger pollicization — the unstable/absent CMC joint precludes reconstruction. Q: What genetic test must be performed in all patients with radial longitudinal deficiency? — A: Chromosomal breakage studies to evaluate for Fanconi anemia. Q: During pollicization, what is the critical skin landmark that determines thumb appearance? — A: The volar transverse limb must be placed just proximal to the PIP crease; too proximal makes the thumb look too long.

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Treatment › Central Deficiency
text: Close cleft (draw MCs together), create first web (Snow-Littler transposes cleft skin radially) Extraperiosteal excision of transverse bones to prevent regrowth Thumb hypoplasia teaching point: CMC stability determines reconstruction vs pollicization — stable CMC → reconstruct; absent or unstable CMC → pollicize Parents often resist ablation of a vestigial thumb; connecting them with families post-pollicization helps the conversation — don’t rush the decision

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Classification › Central Deficiency — Manske Classification
text: I: Normal first web; II (A/B): Narrowed first web; III: Syndactylized first web; IV: Cleft merged with first web Thumb/first web status prognosticates outcomes

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Pollicization: outcomes affected by whether isolated thumb hypoplasia vs RLD; RLD patients have stiffer fingers and weaker grip Centralization: average 36° radial deviation, ~50% forearm length, ~20% grip/pinch strength at 20-year follow-up; DASH scores variable MCP instability is most common complication of thumb reconstruction (20/22 in one series regardless of technique)

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Epidemiology
text: RLD: 1:30,000 (most common absent/hypoplastic), often bilateral ULD: 1:100,000, usually unilateral Central deficiency (cleft hand): 1:90,000 Transverse deficiency: 3:100,000 Phocomelia: < 1:1,000,000

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Treatment › Index Finger Pollicization (Grades IIIB-V)
text: After 18 months; good prognosis if index pronates to pinch against long finger Critical skin point : volar transverse limb just proximal to PIP crease MC head = new CMC; PIP = new MCP; DIP = new IP Digit positioned in 20° radial abduction, 40° palmar abduction , 90-150° pronation MC head fully flexed to prevent CMC hyperextension Preserve physeal artery to prevent growth arrest (decreased to 7% with technique adjustment) Digit loss < 1%; revision rate ~25% (most commonly for opponensplasty)

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Always screen for VACTERL, Fanconi, TAR, Holt-Oram in RLD — systemic conditions can be lethal Fanconi anemia requires chromosomal breakage studies (not just CBC) TAR: thumbs always present despite bilateral absent radii — distinguish from RLD type 4 Don’t pollicize if elbow has extension contracture (wrist flexion/radial deviation brings hand to face) Ulnar prehension is a contraindication to pollicization (would preclude hand-forearm grasp)

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: References
text: Blauth W, Manske PR, McCarroll HR. Thumb hypoplasia classification and reconstruction. Bayne LG, Klug MS, Goldfarb CA. RLD classification and outcomes. Buck-Gramcko D. Pollicization technique and refinements. Manske PR. Central deficiency classification.

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Workup › RLD Associated Conditions (Must Screen)
text: VACTERL : ≥ 3 of vertebral, anal, cardiac, TE fistula, renal, limb anomalies (16:100,000) Fanconi anemia : autosomal recessive, progressive bone marrow failure by age 5 (1:40,000) — chromosomal breakage studies mandatory TAR syndrome : autosomal recessive, bilateral absent radii but thumbs always present , thrombocytopenia resolves Holt-Oram syndrome : autosomal dominant, TBX-5 mutation, cardiac anomalies, higher prevalence of type 1 RLD Workup: echo, renal US, spine XR, CBC, chromosomal breakage studies

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Classification › RLD — Modified Bayne-Klug (Goldfarb)
text: Type Description N Isolated thumb hypoplasia/absence 0 Type N + radial carpal anomaly 1 Shortened distal radius (> 2mm shorter than ulna) 2 Hypoplastic radius (miniature) 3 Partial absence of radius 4 Total absence of radius (most common, 27%) 5 Total absence + proximal humeral/glenoid deficiency

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Treatment › RLD — Wrist Treatment
text: Treat wrist before thumb — radially deviated wrist limits thumb function Passive stretching 5-10 min, 4x/day; night splint when arm is large enough Centralization : carpus balanced on ulna, long finger aligned with ulna; K-wire fixation, ECU advancement Soft tissue centralization : extra-capsular, avoids ulnar physeal injury — similar recurrence but better ulnar growth Distraction lengthening : when stretching insufficient; 0.5-1 mm/day; complications in ≥ 50% Vilkki procedure : vascularized 2nd MTP transfer — technically demanding, high complication rate

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Classification › Thumb Hypoplasia — Modified Blauth (Manske-McCarroll)
text: Grade Features Treatment I Small but stable joints, adequate soft tissue Observation IIA MCP UCL instability (uniaxial) Reconstruction (soft tissue) IIB MCP multiaxial instability Chondrodesis consideration IIIA Extrinsic tendon anomalies, stable CMC Reconstruction IIIB Extrinsic anomalies, unstable/absent CMC Pollicization IV Pouce flottant (vestigial digit) Pollicization V Absent thumb Pollicization CMC stability is the watershed — stable CMC = reconstruct; unstable/absent = pollicize Tapered proximal MC base on XR = unstable CMC; flared base = some stability FPL function inferred from well-developed IP joint crease Pollex abductus (aberrant FPL-extensor connection) in 63% of type IIIA thumbs

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Treatment › Thumb Reconstruction (Grades II-IIIA)
text: Surgery ideally after 18 months (lower anesthesia risk, hand doubles in size by 2.5 years) First web deepening : four-flap z-plasty (most common); flap configuration CADB Opponensplasty : ADM (Huber) — bulkier, better thenar contour; FDS — extra length for UCL reconstruction UCL reconstruction : capsule-ligament-adductor flap advanced distally; FDS opponensplasty provides tendon for collateral augmentation Extrinsic tendon reconstruction : FDS ring finger for FPL; EIP for EPL (if needed, second stage)

title: Absence and Hypoplastic Disorders
heading: Classification › ULD — Modified Bayne Classification
text: Type 0-5; Type 0 = normal ulna with ulnar hand anomalies; Type 4 = absent ulna with radiohumeral synostosis

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Treatment › Amniotic Constriction Band (Patterson Classification)
text: Type 1: simple band; Type 2: distal atrophy/lymphedema; Type 3: acrosyndactyly; Type 4: amputation Deep bands with distal ischemia = emergency Upton technique for band reconstruction

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Syndactyly: 1 in 2,500 live births; M > F; unilateral = bilateral Third web most commonly affected, then fourth, second, first Symbrachydactyly: ~0.6/10,000; primarily males, usually unilateral (left), central digits most hypoplastic/absent Symbrachydactyly: mesoderm primarily affected with ectodermal preservation (nail plate, distal phalanges)

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Treatment › Apert Hand
text: Upton Type I (Spade): free thumb, complex syndactyly index-ring Upton Type III (Rosebud): all digits fused — most severe First web deepening + delta phalanx osteotomy for thumb clinodactyly

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A child with syndactyly of the ring and small fingers also has a prolonged QT interval on EKG. What syndrome should be suspected? — A: Timothy syndrome — border digit syndactyly with long QT, requiring cardiac management before any surgery. Q: During syndactyly release, why should both sides of a single digit never be released simultaneously? — A: Risk of devascularization and digital necrosis from compromising both digital arteries. Q: What distinguishes symbrachydactyly from transverse deficiency? — A: Symbrachydactyly preserves ectodermal structures (nail plates, distal phalanges) because mesoderm is primarily affected. Q: A 10-month-old has complete thumb-index syndactyly. When should release be performed? — A: Around 6 months for border digits to prevent tethering deformity — this child should be booked promptly.

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Web creep: 4.2% (Barabas-Pickford); higher in complex syndactyly (up to 1/3 reoperation) Groin graft hair growth in 17/24 web spaces (Lumenta) Nonvascularized toe phalanx: considerable donor site morbidity increasing with growth, early epiphyseal closure (24%), phalanx resorption

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Never release both sides of the same digit at once — risk of digital necrosis Border digits (thumb-index, ring-small) released first and earlier (6 months) to prevent angular deformity Timothy syndrome (border digit syndactyly + long QT): mandatory EKG screening before any GA Symbrachydactyly preserves ectodermal structures (nails) — distinguishes from transverse deficiency Graftless techniques decrease morbidity but web creep risk is similar

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: References
text: Tentamy SA, McKusick VA. Syndactyly subtypes and genetics. Upton J. Apert hand classification and treatment. Blauth W, Gekeler J, Foucher G. Symbrachydactyly classification. Barabas AG, Pickford MA. Web creep after syndactyly release.

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Classification › Symbrachydactyly — Blauth-Gekeler (Modified Foucher)
text: Type Features I All bones present, brachydactyly + syndactyly IIA ≥ 2 fingers, normal thumb, hypoplastic fingers IIB Functional border digits, central nubbins IIIA Monodactyly, normal thumb IIIB Monodactyly, hypoplastic/unstable thumb IVA/B Peromelic (± wrist mobility) Etiology: subclavian artery supply disruption sequence (Bavinck-Weaver) May be associated with Poland syndrome

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Treatment › Symbrachydactyly Treatment
text: Most unilateral children function almost normally Nonvascularized toe phalanx transfer (Goldberg): extraperiosteal harvest of entire proximal phalanx of 3rd/4th toe; best at 6-18 months; relies on intact periosteum for growth Free vascularized toe-to-hand transfer : for absent thumb or all fingers absent; average 2PD = 5 mm Distraction osteogenesis: high complication rate (43-75%), rarely indicated Timothy syndrome is the rare-but-fatal association: any child with border-digit syndactyly needs a preoperative EKG to rule out long QT, which can trigger fatal arrhythmia under general anesthesia

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Classification › Syndactyly
text: Feature Type Soft tissue only Simple Bony fusion Complex Accessory/abnormal bones Complicated Extends to fingertip/nailbed Complete Connection ends proximal to tip Incomplete Tentamy-McKusick subtypes : Type 1 (long-ring, most common, AD) → Type 5 (MC fusion) Key syndrome associations : - Poland syndrome : ipsilateral chest wall + syndactyly - Apert syndrome : FGFR2 mutation, craniosynostosis + complex syndactyly (Upton Types I-III) - Timothy syndrome : border digit syndactyly + long QT — requires EKG before GA

title: Syndactyly and Symbrachydactyly
heading: Treatment › Syndactyly Release
text: Surgery at 12-24 months ; 6 months for border digits (prevent tethering) Never release both sides of one digit simultaneously (vascular risk) Staging: thumb-index + long-ring first; index-long + ring-small second Technique Normal web: volar extent at midpoint of proximal phalanx, 45° slope proximal-dorsal to distal-volar, hourglass shape Dorsal commissural flap: 2/3 distance MCP to PIP Zigzag incisions on remaining syndactyly Buck-Gramcko flaps for lateral nail folds in complete syndactyly FTSG for defects (inguinal crease lateral to femoral artery, antecubital fossa, volar wrist, hypothenar) Long-arm mitten cast with supracondylar mold for 4 weeks Graftless technique : V-Y dorsal metacarpal island flap for commissure; defatting distal flaps allows primary closure

title: Polydactyly
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Most common congenital hand difference: 23.4 per 10,000 live births Ulnar polydactyly in African Americans : up to 1 in 143 (autosomal dominant, variable penetrance) Radial polydactyly in Caucasians/Asians : 1 in 3,000 (usually unilateral, spontaneous) Triphalangeal thumb: higher hereditary predisposition (chromosome 7q36) Central polydactyly: may be linked to HOXD13 mutation (chromosome 2) Ulnar polydactyly in Caucasians may indicate syndrome (Ellis-van Creveld, Bardet-Biedl, Pallister-Hall)

title: Polydactyly
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: What is the most common type of radial polydactyly in the Wassel classification? — A: Type IV (duplication at the level of the proximal phalanx). Q: A Caucasian infant presents with bilateral ulnar polydactyly. What should be done beyond surgical planning? — A: Evaluate for associated syndromes (Ellis-van Creveld, Bardet-Biedl, Pallister-Hall) — ulnar polydactyly in Caucasians may indicate an underlying syndrome. Q: After radial polydactyly reconstruction, residual angular deformity of 25° is noted. What is the appropriate intervention? — A: Closing wedge osteotomy — angular deformity > 20° will not correct with soft tissue rebalancing alone. Q: What is the most common complication at long-term follow-up after radial polydactyly reconstruction? — A: Angular deformity (46% at 36-year follow-up), though most patients are pain-free.

title: Polydactyly
heading: Classification › Central Polydactyly
text: Buck-Gramcko classification (level of duplication) Wall radiographic classification for synpolydactyly: excellent reliability (kappa 0.87-0.97)

title: Polydactyly
heading: Treatment › Central Polydactyly
text: Challenging; ray resection with web space and transverse MC ligament reconstruction Corrective osteotomies commonly required Functional and aesthetic results often inferior to radial/ulnar polydactyly Ulnar polydactyly type B in a Black child is most often autosomal dominant and benign — office excision with local is appropriate Ulnar polydactyly in a Caucasian child should prompt syndromic workup (family history + screen for other anomalies) before assuming isolated

title: Polydactyly
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Reconstructed thumb will be smaller in length and girth than unaffected thumb even at skeletal maturity 36-year follow-up (Gholson): no difference in pinch/grip strength vs unaffected; 46% angular deformity but no pain; 15% IP joint arthritis 10-year follow-up (Stutz): lateral/tripod/tip pinch 96/86/92% of unaffected; 19% reoperation (mostly IP arthrodesis) Satisfaction decreases significantly with joint angulation Type B ligation may leave small (~2 mm) residual bump

title: Polydactyly
heading: Treatment › General Principles
text: Prefer term “split thumb” over “duplicated thumb” — retained thumb will always be smaller Surgery typically at ~1 year (before pinch development, lower anesthesia risk) Ablate nonfunctional parts but retain any usable component for stability, motion, function Maximize skeletal length and joint stability Keep periosteal sleeve for intrinsic muscles and collateral ligaments Closing wedge osteotomies heal faster than opening wedge 20° angular deformity requires closing wedge osteotomy (soft tissue rebalancing alone insufficient)

title: Polydactyly
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Wassel Type IV is most common radial polydactyly — know this for boards Ulnar polydactyly in Caucasians = think syndromes; in African Americans = usually isolated AD Angular deformity > 20° needs osteotomy, not just soft tissue work Don’t use extensor mechanism for collateral reconstruction (creates checkrein effect) Central polydactyly has the worst outcomes of all three types

title: Polydactyly
heading: Treatment › Radial Polydactyly Techniques
text: Simple excision : no bony connection, dominant thumb adequate; traction neurectomy to avoid neuroma Excision and reconstruction : preserve collateral from minor thumb via periosteal sleeve; contour widened bone; K-wire protection; tendon realignment for pollex abductus Bilhaut-Cloquet : combine outer portions of two similarly hypoplastic thumbs; modified to preserve one articular surface On-top plasty : proximal of one + distal of other; preserve NV bundle

title: Polydactyly
heading: Classification › Radial Polydactyly — Wassel (Flatt)
text: Based on level of bone/joint involvement Type IV most common (29-43%); Type I least common Interobserver reliability kappa = 0.65 Rotterdam classification : expanded to include triphalangeal variants; 40% of Wassel-unclassifiable cases captured

title: Polydactyly
heading: References
text: Wassel HD. Radial polydactyly classification. Clin Orthop. 1969. Gholson JJ et al. 36-year follow-up of radial polydactyly reconstruction. Stelling RD, Turek SL. Ulnar polydactyly classification. Stults AP, Peljovich AE. Office excision of type B ulnar polydactyly.

title: Polydactyly
heading: Treatment › Ulnar Polydactyly
text: Type B : suture ligation, surgical clip, or formal office excision with local anesthesia + traction neurectomy (high satisfaction) Type A : formal surgical excision and reconstruction as for radial polydactyly

title: Polydactyly
heading: Classification › Ulnar Polydactyly — Stelling-Turek / Temtany-McKusick
text: System Types Stelling-Turek I: skin bridge; II: articulates with bifid MC head; III: entire ray duplicated Temtany-McKusick A: well-developed, bony; B: rudimentary, pedunculated Type B is 10x more frequent in African descent , bilateral in 70%

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A 2-year-old presents with the thumb locked in IP flexion and a palpable nodule at the MCP crease. What percentage will resolve with observation? — A: ~76% at 49 months (Baek); 92% with nighttime splinting (Koh). Q: A child has progressive small finger angulation from a trapezoidal middle phalanx on radiograph. What is the underlying pathology? — A: Delta phalanx (longitudinal epiphyseal bracket) causing asymmetric growth. Q: What is the most common type of macrodactyly? — A: Type I — lipofibromatosis (“true” macrodactyly). Q: What is the preferred tendon donor for tendon transfer in congenital clasped thumb? — A: EIP (extensor indicis proprius).

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Camptodactyly
text: Nonsurgical mainstay : Hori protocol — splinting 24 hr/day until full extension, then 8 hr/day until skeletal maturity Passive stretching effective in children < 3 years (Rhee: 20° → 1° in mild, 75° → 28° in severe) Surgery: stepwise — volar skin z-plasty → FDS release → NV assessment → volar plate release → collateral release → K-wire

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Classification › Camptodactyly Types
text: Type I (Infantile) : birth, M = F, very responsive to splinting Type II (Adolescent) : preadolescent growth spurt, F > M, less responsive Type III (Syndromic) : infants with other conditions, often severe

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › CBS
text: Simple rings: excision with z-plasty or modified w-plasty; Upton technique (excise all scar to fascia, mobilize fat) Acrosyndactyly: early release by 6 months for mild cases Thumb + 2 digits allows chuck pinch, precision/power pinch, hook grip, power grasp

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Clasped Thumb
text: Full-time extension splinting initially; surgery if no functional extension by age 2 EIP is preferred donor for tendon transfer; palmaris longus alternative First web augmented with Ezaki-Oishi index rotation flap

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Classification › Clinodactyly
text: Radioulnar (coronal) plane angulation, most common in small finger (ulnar deviation) Delta phalanx (longitudinal epiphyseal bracket) limits growth on affected side → progressive angulation Clinically relevant: > 10°; present in > 1% of normal children

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Clinodactyly
text: Observation for most small finger clinodactyly (splinting provides no benefit) Physiolysis (Vickers procedure) : open physes, < 6 years; resect bracketed epiphysis + fat graft; mean 82% correction Closing wedge osteotomy : severe deformity; mean correction 33° → 9°

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Classification › Congenital Clasped Thumb — Tsuyuguchi
text: Type I: passively extendable; Type II: not passively extendable; Type III: arthrogryposis-associated Due to hypoplasia/absence of EPB and/or EPL

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Classification › Constriction Band Syndrome (CBS)
text: 1:2,000 to 1:15,000; no hereditary pattern; amnion adhesion theory Patterson : I = simple ring; II = distal atrophy/lymphedema; III = acrosyndactyly (IIIa-c by web depth); IV = intrauterine amputation

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Bunnell test (camptodactyly): PIP flexion less with MCP extended = intrinsic tightness Notta’s nodule (trigger thumb): palpable at MCP volar crease; thumb locked in IP flexion

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Macrodactyly
text: Amputation favored : isolated digital, progressive, very stiff/angulated Retention favored : thumb involvement, static type, willing family Debulking : mid-lateral, one side at a time; can excise hypertrophied nerves preserving vessels Epiphysiodesis : most dependable method to stop longitudinal growth; performed when digit matches same-sex parent’s length; percutaneous drill at all 3 phalangeal physes

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Classification › Macrodactyly — Flatt Classification
text: Type Pathology I Lipofibromatosis (most common, “true” macrodactyly) II Neurofibromatosis III Hyperostosis IV Hemihypertrophy PIK3CA mosaicism / PI3K-AKT pathway implicated Radial side of hand most commonly affected

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Pediatric trigger thumb: most resolve with observation/splinting — don’t rush to surgery Camptodactyly: splinting is the mainstay; surgery risks creating extension contracture (FDS-to-extensor transfers) Delta phalanx = longitudinal epiphyseal bracket; splinting does nothing for clinodactyly Macrodactyly: epiphysiodesis timing = when digit matches parent’s size (most predictable method) CBS: acrosyndactyly release by 6 months; deep bands with ischemia are emergencies

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: References
text: Patterson TJS. Constriction band syndrome classification. Flatt AE. Macrodactyly classification. Baek GH et al. Natural history of pediatric trigger thumb; symphalangism classification. Hori M et al. Camptodactyly splinting protocol.

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Symphalangism
text: Majority = observation; compensatory hyperflexion at adjacent joints Early joint release (18-24 months) for Flatt type I fibrous/cartilaginous; average 40° improvement

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Classification › Symphalangism — Flatt / Baek Classifications
text: Absence of IP joint motion (PIP most common); NOG gene mutation Baek : fibrous (10-20° passive motion) → cartilaginous (minimal) → bony (none)

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Trigger Finger (Pediatric)
text: 10x less common than trigger thumb; long finger most commonly affected Often associated with MPS, JRA, Ehlers-Danlos, Down syndrome May require FDS slip resection, A3 release, partial A2 release Recurrence 9% with A1 excision + FDS slip resection Pediatric trigger thumb is acquired (not congenital) and distinct from adult trigger finger; most resolve spontaneously, with reported splinting resolution rates around 92% — splint first, operate later

title: Finger and Thumb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Trigger Thumb
text: Presents age 1-4; incidence 1-3 per 1,000; believed acquired, not congenital 76% spontaneous resolution at 49 months (Baek); 92% with nighttime splinting at 22 months (Koh) US practice: open A1 pulley release; transverse incision at volar MCP crease FPL runs from center of thumb pulp toward hook of hamate Avoid complete division of oblique pulley (bowstringing)

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Arthrogryposis (Amyoplasia)
text: 1 in 10,000; no definite genetic basis; normal intelligence Characteristic position: shoulder IR, elbow extension, wrist flexion/UD, thumb-in-palm Bilateral symmetric findings mandatory — asymmetry requires further investigation

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Arthrogryposis — Key Procedures
text: Elbow release/tricepsplasty : W-plasty or VY-plasty in triceps + posterior capsulotomy → ≥ 90° flexion; 22/23 children able to self-feed (Van Heest) Dorsal carpal wedge osteotomy : biplanar opening; ECU to ECRB transfer; goal neutral to +10° extension; 55° flexion → 11° at 5.7 years, 9.1/10 parent satisfaction (Foy) Thumb release : Ezaki-Oishi flap, thenar release, MCP chondrodesis if unstable, EIP/EDQ to EPL transfer Long head triceps transfer : requires good passive flexion ≥ 90° and adequate lateral head on MRI; fascia lata graft extension DHO (distal humeral external rotation osteotomy): for cross-over grasp; ~90° external rotation; never combine with elbow release (severe flexion contracture risk) Three adaptive hand-to-mouth mechanisms without active elbow flexion: table push, trunk thrust, cervical bend Most kids with radioulnar synostosis adapt without surgery; operative candidates are typically those with ≥ 60° fixed pronation who can’t supinate enough for ADLs Ezaki-Oishi technique creates a periosteum-tube pseudarthrosis with morsellized bone to prevent re-synostosis — overnight admission warranted (compartment syndrome is the high-stakes complication)

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: What ligament must be released during surgical treatment of Madelung’s deformity? — A: The Vickers ligament (abnormal tether from lunate/TFCC to volar-ulnar radius metaphysis). Q: A child with bilateral symmetric elbow extension contractures, wrist flexion, and thumb-in-palm deformity is evaluated. What is the most likely diagnosis? — A: Arthrogryposis (amyoplasia) — bilateral symmetric positioning is characteristic. Q: A 14-year-old with MHE develops new pain at a forearm osteochondroma. MRI shows a 2.5-cm cartilage cap. What is the concern? — A: Malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma — cartilage cap > 2 cm after skeletal maturity is suspicious. Q: What is the most feared complication of derotation osteotomy for proximal radioulnar synostosis? — A: Acute compartment syndrome. Q: What genetic mutation causes Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis and is associated with Madelung’s deformity? — A: SHOX gene haploinsufficiency (pseudoautosomal region of sex chromosomes).

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Workup › Madelung’s
text: Presentation: shortened forearm, volar sag, dorsally prominent ulna, ulnar-sided wrist pain McCarroll diagnostic thresholds: ulnar tilt ≥ 33°, lunate subsidence ≥ 4 mm, lunate fossa angle ≥ 40°, palmar carpal displacement ≥ 20 mm Whole forearm radiographs mandatory — some patients have radial head subluxation/dislocation

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Madelung’s
text: Observation : many asymptomatic patients with minimal deformity; 6-12 month XR follow-up Physiolysis + Vickers ligament release : skeletally immature with growth remaining; volar approach, divide Vickers ligament, physiolysis with burr until normal cartilage, fat interposition Dome osteotomy : most commonly used; 3D correction; volar approach, crescent osteotomy proximal to sigmoid notch, translate distal fragment dorsally/radially, K-wire fixation; lasting correction at 11 years Ulnar shortening osteotomy : minimal radial deformity + prominent ulna; volar plate decreases hardware irritation

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Madelung’s Deformity
text: Premature physeal arrest of volar-ulnar distal radius; 4x more common in girls; clinically evident in adolescence Vickers ligament : abnormal tether from lunate/TFCC to volar-ulnar radius metaphysis Most commonly idiopathic; Madelung-like deformity from trauma, infection, Ollier, MHE, Turner Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis : autosomal dominant, SHOX gene haploinsufficiency → mesomelic dwarfism + Madelung’s

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › MHE
text: Intervene for: pain, maintaining radiocapitellar joint, improving forearm rotation, aesthetics Simple excision : painful tumors or those limiting rotation; substantial radial bow remodeling in young children Ulnar tether release + osteochondroma excision : correct ulnar wrist deviation Ulnar lengthening : for older patients with limited growth remaining Radial head dislocation: reduction rarely indicated (recurs); symptomatic patients do well with radial head excision

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Classification › MHE Forearm — Jo (Modified Masada)
text: Type I: isolated distal ulna osteochondroma Type II: distal ulna + radial head dislocation (IIA with, IIB without proximal radial tumor) Type III: isolated distal radius osteochondroma Type IV: both distal ulnar and radial (IVA no, IVB with radial head dislocation)

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › MHE (Multiple Hereditary Exostosis)
text: Autosomal dominant, 1:50,000; EXT1 or EXT2 loss-of-function mutations EXT1 mutations more common and more severe phenotype Forearm deformities in 30-60%: shortened ulna, radial bowing, ulnar wrist deviation, radial head dislocation Malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma in up to 2% — cartilage cap > 2 cm on CT/MRI raises concern

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Madelung’s: get whole forearm films — don’t miss proximal radial head pathology Vickers ligament is the tether causing Madelung’s deformity — release it during physiolysis SHOX haploinsufficiency → Leri-Weill → mesomelic dwarfism + Madelung’s MHE: any osteochondroma with pain/rapid growth after skeletal maturity → rule out chondrosarcoma (cap > 2 cm) Arthrogryposis: bilateral symmetry is mandatory — if asymmetric, reconsider diagnosis Never combine DHO with elbow release in arthrogryposis (risk of severe flexion contracture)

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Proximal Radioulnar Synostosis
text: Failure of segmentation of radius and ulna; fixed in neutral to full pronation Bilateral (asymmetric) in 60-80%; 1.5x more common in males

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Treatment › Radioulnar Synostosis
text: Most patients do NOT need surgery — shoulder and wrist compensate Surgery for functional limitations (typically ≥ 60° fixed pronation) Ezaki-Oishi technique : osteotomies of both radius (distal to PT insertion) and ulna (mid-distal 1/3); 1-2 cm segment removed, morsellized, replaced in intact periosteal sleeve; target neutral to slight pronation Most feared complication: acute compartment syndrome — mitigate with fasciotomies, shortening, staged correction; admit overnight Outcomes: average correction 74-78° with high satisfaction

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: Classification › Radioulnar Synostosis — Cleary and Omer
text: Type Description I Radiocapitellar joint reduced, no bony synostosis II Reduced, bony synostosis III Bony synostosis + posterior radial head dislocation IV Bony synostosis + anterior radial head dislocation

title: Wrist and Upper Limb Anomalies
heading: References
text: Vickers D. Madelung’s deformity: physiolysis and ligament release. Cleary JE, Omer GE. Radioulnar synostosis classification. Jo AR et al. Modified Masada classification for MHE forearm. Foy CA et al. Dorsal carpal wedge osteotomy outcomes in arthrogryposis. Van Heest AE et al. Elbow release outcomes in arthrogryposis.

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Brachial plexus: C5-T1 ventral rami; variations with C4 (prefixed, more common) or T2 (postfixed) in up to 50% Components: roots → trunks → divisions → cords → branches Erb’s point : C5 + C6 converge to form upper trunk; just lateral/superior to SCM insertion on clavicle Phrenic nerve on anterior surface of anterior scalene → key surgical landmark guiding to C5 root Posterior cord absent in up to 20% of patients (anatomic variation)

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A 6-month-old with BPBI cannot flex the elbow against gravity. What is the recommended next step? — A: Microsurgical brachial plexus reconstruction (neuroma excision + nerve grafting or nerve transfer). Q: A neonate with a flail arm has ipsilateral ptosis and miosis. What does this indicate about the injury? — A: Pre-ganglionic nerve root avulsions (Horner syndrome from sympathetic chain involvement) — Narakas group 4 with the worst prognosis. Q: What nerve serves as the intraoperative landmark to locate the C5 root during brachial plexus exploration? — A: The phrenic nerve, on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene muscle. Q: In the Oberlin transfer, what is the donor nerve and what function is restored? — A: A fascicle of the ulnar nerve is transferred to the biceps branch of the musculocutaneous nerve, restoring elbow flexion. Q: A child with BPBI has passive shoulder external rotation of 40°. What evaluation is needed? — A: Imaging (US or MRI) to assess glenohumeral congruency and glenoid version for dysplasia.

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Epidemiology
text: ~1.5 per 1,000 live births; right > left (left occiput anterior presentation) 50% isolated C5-C6; 30% C5-C7; 20% C5-T1 (global) Risk factors: shoulder dystocia ( OR = 138.7 ), prior BPBI, macrosomia > 4,000 g, instrumented delivery Up to 50% have no known risk factors Spontaneous recovery in 66-82%; ~30% have persistent deficits

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Classification › Glenohumeral Dysplasia — Waters Classification
text: Type I-VII, from < 5° retroversion difference (I) to proximal humeral growth arrest (VII)

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: XR: clavicle/humerus fractures, chest for hemidiaphragm US/MRI: glenohumeral congruency, glenoid version, humeral head deformity EMG/NCS: less reliable in BPBI (underestimates injury, overestimates recovery)

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Workup › Infant Evaluation
text: Detailed birth history: dystocia, instrumentation, birth weight DDx: clavicle/humerus fracture, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, cerebral palsy, arthrogryposis Examine: torticollis, Horner’s, asymmetric chest wall motion (phrenic), scapular winging, limb posture Active Movement Scale (AMS) : 15 motions, 8-point scale Toronto Test : elbow flex + elbow/wrist/finger/thumb extension; < 3.5 at 3 months → may indicate surgery Passive shoulder ER ≤ 60° → prompt radiographic evaluation (glenohumeral dysplasia)

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Treatment › Microsurgical Reconstruction — Nerve Grafting
text: Supraclavicular transverse approach; identify phrenic → C5 → trace to Erb’s neuroma Sural nerve cable grafts at 110% defect length; 9-0 or 10-0 nylon + fibrin glue C5-C6: prioritize shoulder ER/abd, elbow flexion, wrist extension Global: prioritize hand function first , then elbow flexion, then shoulder

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Classification › Narakas Classification
text: Group Roots Presentation Prognosis 1 (Erb’s) C5-C6 Absent shoulder abd/elbow flex, weak wrist ext, hand OK Best 2 (Extended Erb’s) C5-C7 “Waiter’s tip”: shoulder IR, elbow ext, forearm pronation, wrist drop 2A: early wrist recovery; 2B: late/absent 3 (Global) C5-T1 Flail limb Poor 4 (Global + Horner) C5-T1 Flail + ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis Worst — often avulsions

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Classification › Nerve Injury Severity (Seddon/Sunderland)
text: Neurapraxia (I) : demyelination only → full spontaneous recovery Axonotmesis (II-IV) : variable recovery depending on endoneurium/perineurium/epineurium injury Neurotmesis (V) : complete disruption → no spontaneous recovery, requires surgery

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers
text: Transfer Restores SAN → suprascapular Shoulder ER/abd Oberlin (ulnar → biceps MC) Elbow flexion Radial (triceps branch) → axillary Shoulder abd Median → brachialis Elbow flexion Intercostal → musculocutaneous Elbow flexion (global palsies) Advantage over grafting: avoids scar dissection, closer to motor endplates Evidence favors SAN → suprascapular nerve transfer

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Treatment › Nonsurgical
text: All infants start with nonsurgical care: stretching and ROM (emphasis on glenohumeral abduction/ER with scapular stabilization)

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Treatment › Operative Indications
text: Age Indication 3 months Flail + Horner; Toronto < 3.5 6 months No antigravity elbow flexion (AMS < 5); Toronto not improving 9 months Failure of “cookie test”

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Treatment › Other Sequelae
text: Elbow flexion contracture (~50%): nighttime splinting for 20-40°; serial casting for ≥ 40° Forearm supination contracture (7%): biceps rerouting if passively correctable; osteotomy if fixed BPBI surgical decision tree pivots on antigravity elbow flexion: absent by 6 months → microsurgical reconstruction indicated Horner’s syndrome at birth with a flail limb implies avulsions — proceed early (at ~3 months) rather than waiting

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Antigravity elbow flexion by 3 months = excellent prognosis; absent by 6 months = surgery indicated Horner’s syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) = pre-ganglionic avulsion, worst prognosis → early surgery at 3 months Phrenic nerve on anterior scalene = the surgical landmark to C5 EMG/NCS unreliable in infants — serial clinical exam is the gold standard Global palsy reconstruction: prioritize hand function over shoulder Passive shoulder ER ≤ 60° → image the glenohumeral joint for dysplasia External rotation osteotomy: fear overcorrection (iatrogenic ER contracture, loss of midline function)

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Classification › Pre- vs Post-Ganglionic
text: Pre-ganglionic (avulsion) : poor prognosis; clinical signs = Horner’s, elevated hemidiaphragm (phrenic), scapular winging (long thoracic), weak rhomboids (dorsal scapular) Post-ganglionic: better potential for spontaneous recovery

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: References
text: Narakas AO. BPBI classification. Waters PM. Glenohumeral dysplasia classification and secondary reconstruction. Oberlin C et al. Ulnar nerve transfer for elbow flexion. Van Heest AE et al. Outcomes of brachial plexus reconstruction.

title: Brachial Plexus Birth Injury
heading: Treatment › Secondary Shoulder Reconstruction
text: Internal rotation contracture in 8-29% of infants; glenohumeral dysplasia in 30% of older children Mild dysplasia : anterior musculotendinous lengthening + lat dorsi/teres major transfer to rotator cuff (90° abd, 60-80° ER) Moderate dysplasia : add open glenohumeral reduction + capsulorraphy Severe dysplasia : external rotation humeral osteotomy (deltopectoral, 45-70° rotation; most feared complication = overcorrection with loss of midline function)

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Nonprogressive disturbance of the developing fetal brain → motor disorder Upper motor neuron injury → spasticity of agonists + weakness of antagonists Primary problem (CNS) → secondary (peripheral muscle imbalance, joint malpositioning) → tertiary (fixed deformities, contractures) Primary problem generally not remediable; secondary/tertiary are targets for intervention

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Assessment Tools
text: House Functional Use Scale : 0 (does not use) to 8 (spontaneous use) MACS (Manual Abilities Classification System): Levels I-V GMFCS (Gross Motor Function Classification System): Levels I-V AHA (Assistive Hand Assessment): bimanual activity Dynamic EMG : distinguishes spastic vs phasic muscle control → guides transfer decisions

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A 10-year-old with hemiplegic CP has wrist flexion contracture > 45° and dynamic EMG shows spastic FCU with phasic ECRB. What is the recommended procedure? — A: FCU to ECRB tendon transfer — the FCU is spastic (removing the deforming force) and the ECRB is phasic (can accept a transfer for wrist extension). Q: What is the most common finger deformity in cerebral palsy? — A: Swan neck deformity (from intrinsic spasticity and extrinsic extensor overactivity). Q: A child with CP has a type 3 thumb-in-palm deformity with MCP hyperextension. Why should EPB augmentation be avoided? — A: The MCP hyperextension is secondary to chronic adduction, not EPB weakness — augmenting EPB worsens the hyperextension deformity. Q: What tone pattern is a contraindication to tendon transfer in CP? — A: Dystonic or athetoid tone — these patterns are unpredictable and poor candidates for lengthening or transfer.

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Tendon transfer > botulinum toxin or ongoing therapy at 12 months Average improvement: 2.6 House functional levels Cosmesis dramatically improved; patient satisfaction most highly correlated with cosmetic results Hyperselective neurectomy (2/3 to 3/4 fascicles): for elbow flexor spasticity in patients with near-full passive ROM + volitional control + true spasticity

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Distribution Patterns
text: Monoplegia, hemiplegia, diplegia, triplegia, quadriplegia/tetraplegia

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Evaluation
text: Hand dominance before 18-24 months → suspect neurologic pathology Volkmann’s angle : maximum wrist extension with fingers extended = quantifies finger flexor contracture Stereognosis : impaired in up to 97% of children

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Key Procedures
text: Elbow : Z-lengthening biceps + fascial lengthening brachialis; < 45° rarely needs surgery; > 90° approach cautiously (contracted NV bundle) Forearm : PT release vs rerouting (dynamic EMG determines: spastic → release; phasic → transfer); FCU around ulnar border produces greatest supination (cadaveric); fixed supination more problematic than pronation in modern society Wrist — FCU to ECRB Transfer : Harvest FCU at pisiform, mobilize distal 2/3 origin, subcutaneous tunnel dorsally, Pulvertaft weave to ECRB; tension so wrist rests in neutral against gravity Wrist fusion : skeletally mature + severe contracture + little digital control; with PRC; test finger/thumb contractures pre/intra/postop Fingers : Swan neck most common finger deformity (intrinsic spasticity + extrinsic extensor overactivity); Tonkin lateral band rerouting for locking > 40°; FDS tenodesis Thumb-in-Palm — Four Types : - Type 1: adductor spasticity → 1st MC adduction - Type 2: + FPB → MCP flexion - Type 3: chronic adduction → secondary MCP hyperextension ( do NOT augment EPB ) - Type 4: + FPL → IP flexion Matev release : release transverse head of adductor off 3rd MC; protect radial digital NV of long finger EPL rerouting (Manske) : EPL transected over MCP, retracted through 3rd compartment, rerouted through 1st compartment to achieve abduction Dynamic EMG before surgery is invaluable — it tells you whether the pronator teres is truly spastic (release it) or has phasic control (transfer it); operating on a pha

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: OT: splints, stretching, strengthening, functional use activities Nighttime splinting for contractures; daytime for pre-positioning Constraint therapy : higher-functioning children (forces affected hand use) Tone management : diazepam, baclofen (oral/intrathecal pump), botulinum toxin, phenol, selective dorsal rhizotomy, selective neurectomy

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Hand dominance before 18 months = red flag for neurologic diagnosis Volkmann’s angle quantifies flexor contracture — essential for surgical planning Dystonic/athetoid patients are poor surgical candidates — spasticity is the treatable pattern Swan neck is the most common finger deformity in CP (not boutonniere) Type 3 thumb-in-palm: do NOT augment EPB (MCP hyperextension is secondary to chronic adduction) FCU to ECRB tension: wrist should rest in neutral against gravity — overtensioning creates extension contracture Cosmesis drives satisfaction more than function in CP surgery

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Postoperative Protocol
text: Multiple simultaneous procedures common Cast at 30° elbow flexion, maximum supination, slight wrist extension, thumb out of palm Cast 4 weeks → custom splints + active ROM 3-5x/day → strengthening at 8 weeks

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: References
text: House JH. Functional use scale for the upper extremity in CP. Manske PR. EPL rerouting technique for thumb-in-palm. Tonkin MA. Lateral band rerouting for swan neck. Van Heest AE et al. Outcomes of tendon transfer surgery in CP.

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Surgical Contraindications
text: Severe medical comorbidities Dystonic or athetoid tone (poor candidates for lengthening/transfer) Fixed joint contracture (contraindication to transfer alone) Continuously spastic muscle (relative contraindication — may create opposite deformity)

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Surgical Indications
text: Failed nonsurgical management with loss of ROM / developing contractures Thresholds: elbow flexion contracture > 45°, pronation prevents supination past neutral, wrist flexion > 45°, fixed thumb adduction/MCP flexion Ideal transfer candidate: ≥ 7 years old, full passive ROM, limited active ROM

title: Cerebral Palsy — Upper Extremity
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Typical UE Posture
text: Joint Spastic (overpull) Weak Elbow Biceps, brachialis → flexion Triceps Forearm PT, PQ → pronation Supinator Wrist FCU, FCR → flexion/UD ECRL/B, ECU Fingers FDS, FDP → clenched fist EDC, EIP/EDQ Thumb Adductor, FPB → in-palm EPL, EPB, APL

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Distal radius fractures: most common pediatric fractures (31% of all), 1.5x more common in boys Physis is biomechanically weaker than ligaments → physeal injuries more common than ligamentous in children Thicker periosteum = more inherently stable shaft fractures; greater remodeling potential Remodeling occurs in the plane of motion; coronal and rotational deformities will NOT remodel 5-10° of rotational malunion causes visible digital scissoring

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A child’s nail plate is malaligned and swollen at the base after a crush injury. XR shows a SH I fracture of the distal phalanx. What is the diagnosis and management? — A: Seymour fracture (open physeal fracture with entrapped eponychium); requires open debridement, nail bed repair, and fracture stabilization. Q: A 7-year-old has a boxer’s fracture with 60° of flexion angulation. What is the recommended treatment? — A: Soft wrapping alone — up to 75° of angulation is acceptable with no loss of function or grip strength in children. Q: A distal radius fracture in a 12-year-old shows bayonet apposition on XR. The child is 9 years old. What management is appropriate? — A: Non-operative management (short arm cast); bayonet apposition in children < 10 remodels over 6-9 months. Q: A phalangeal neck fracture in a child appears minimally displaced on initial XR. What follow-up is recommended? — A: Weekly radiographic follow-up — phalangeal neck fractures are inherently unstable and remodel very slowly; early pinning if displacement develops. Q: What is the most common distribution of scaphoid fractures in children with open physes? — A: Waist (67.9%), followed by distal pole (26.5%) and proximal pole (5.9%).

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Seymour fracture: high osteomyelitis rate if missed (initially appears as simple mallet) Phalangeal condyle fractures: AVN risk with late open osteotomy → condylar advancement osteotomy for severe malunion Distal radius physeal arrest: 1-7%; risk factors = forceful/late manipulation, SH III/IV, compression

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Classification › Distal Phalanx Injuries
text: Seymour fracture : open SH I/II physeal injury; eponychium avulsed and entrapped in fracture → high osteomyelitis risk if missed; requires open debridement + nail bed repair + fixation Mallet finger : extensor avulsion at distal phalanx epiphysis (tendon or SH III/IV bony); most managed with extension splinting 6 weeks regardless of fragment size Jersey finger : zone I FPL avulsion; diagnose clinically; US useful

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Treatment › Distal Radius Fractures
text: Type Management Buckle (torus) Removable brace/wrap (superior to cast per RCTs); 3-4 weeks Greenstick Well-molded cast ± closed reduction; weekly XR Complete Weekly XR monitoring × 3 weeks; percutaneous pinning for instability Bayonet apposition Children < 10: manage without formal reduction; remodels 6-9 months

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Treatment › Galeazzi / DRUJ
text: 0.3-3% of pediatric forearm fractures; Galeazzi-equivalent = distal ulnar physeal injury Anatomic radius reduction usually realigns ulna Dorsal dislocation: immobilize in supination; volar: in pronation

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Scaphoid fracture series: PA with maximal ulnar deviation; 81% occult fractures detected by MRI (NPV 100%) Scaphoid fat pad sign may be present Buckle fractures: repeat XR unnecessary (clinical healing assessment sufficient)

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Classification › MCP Joint Injuries
text: Dorsal dislocation : irreducible “noose” — volar plate trapped between accessory collateral ligaments, flexors, lumbricals, natatory ligament; reduce via hyperextension then push base over MC head; dorsal open approach if irreducible UCL avulsion (Skier’s thumb) : high Stener lesion incidence → complete injuries best treated operatively; in children = SH III/IV pattern; fragment size often underestimated on XR

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Classification › Metacarpal Injuries
text: Boxer’s fracture : unimpaired function with no grip strength loss even up to 75° flexion; soft wrapping alone similar to closed reduction and casting Shaft fractures: malrotation will not remodel Thumb MC base: tolerates up to 30° angulation

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Seymour fracture is the most commonly missed pediatric hand injury — look for nail plate malalignment + eponychial swelling Coronal and rotational deformity does NOT remodel — only sagittal plane remodeling occurs Buckle fractures: removable brace, no repeat XR needed, clinical follow-up only Boxer’s fractures in kids: up to 75° acceptable — don’t reduce, don’t cast Phalangeal neck fractures: look benign but remodel poorly — pin if displaced Unicondylar phalanx fractures: follow weekly even if nondisplaced — inherently unstable Limit reduction attempts to 1-2 gentle manipulations; no reductions after 10 days

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Treatment › Physeal Fractures (Distal Radius)
text: Most common: SH I/II; fracture through zone of provisional calcification Gentle closed reduction — forceful or multiple attempts increase physeal arrest risk No reductions after 10 days (increases arrest risk) SH III/IV with > 2 mm articular displacement → surgery Physeal arrest: 1-7% of all distal radius physeal injuries Peterson type I (Mercedes fracture) : metaphyseal fracture with vertical physeal component — not in Salter-Harris system

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Classification › Proximal Phalanx Injuries
text: Unicondylar/bicondylar : inherently unstable even nondisplaced — follow weekly ; limited blood supply through collateral origin; late osteotomy risks AVN Subcapital (neck) : distal fragment dorsally displaced blocking PIP flexion; remodeling very slow (years), only in plane of motion; closed reduction + percutaneous pinning: 92% good-excellent ; percutaneous osteoclasis successful up to 36 days Extra-octave fracture (base SH II): closed reduction with MCP flexion + buddy taping; broad fracture surface + physeal proximity = substantial remodeling

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: References
text: Seymour N. Juxta-epiphyseal fracture of the terminal phalanx. Ploegmakers JJ et al. Acceptable alignment guidelines by age and sex. Pediatric scaphoid fracture management — ASSH Handthology synthesis. Galeazzi-equivalent injuries in children.

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Treatment › Scaphoid Fractures
text: Most common pediatric carpal fracture; peak age ~15; 28-37% may present as nonunions Distribution (open physes): waist 67.9%, distal pole 26.5%, proximal pole 5.9% Cast times: distal 4-8 weeks, waist 7-16 weeks, proximal ~15 weeks Healing rates 90-99% when promptly diagnosed and treated Displaced: retrograde headless screw (volar approach) for waist/distal; antegrade (dorsal) for proximal AVN of proximal pole rare in pediatric patients (vs adults)

title: Pediatric Hand and Wrist Fractures
heading: Treatment › TFCC Injuries
text: Usually associated with distal radius fractures; most heal with long arm cast 4-6 weeks Persistent ulnar pain → MRI, arthroscopic repair/debridement Pediatric boxer’s fractures tolerate up to ~75° flexion with unimpaired function and no grip strength loss; soft wrap is non-inferior to casting — don’t overtreat Phalangeal neck fractures look benign on x-ray but are inherently unstable and remodel slowly — pin if displaced

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Blood Supply
text: Epiphyseal arteries (through resting zone) Nutrient artery (diaphysis → metaphysis capillary loops) Perichondrial arteries (Ring of LaCroix, Groove of Ranvier)

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: What percentage of upper extremity physeal fractures are Salter-Harris type II? — A: ~75%. Q: A child’s distal radius fracture was reduced at 14 days post-injury. Six months later, there is asymmetric growth arrest. What is the likely cause? — A: Iatrogenic physeal arrest from late reduction (reductions after 10-14 days increase arrest risk). Q: An adolescent gymnast has chronic wrist pain. XR shows asymmetric physeal widening of the distal radius with sclerosis. What is the diagnosis and management? — A: Gymnast wrist (distal radial epiphysitis); cessation of weight-bearing for minimum 6 weeks with serial radiographs. Q: In the CRITOE mnemonic, which ossification center is last to fuse? — A: The medial (internal) epicondyle apophysis, fusing at age 15-20. Q: What is the imaging study of choice for mapping a physeal bar before surgical resection? — A: CT (for size and location) complemented by MRI (for non-ossified bars and 3D mapping).

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Treatment › Corrective Osteotomy
text: For angular deformity from partial arrest Closing wedge, opening wedge (tricortical iliac crest autograft), or dome Addresses sagittal and coronal malalignment

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Workup › Distal Radius Physeal Arrest
text: Occurs in 1-7% of distal radius fractures (most common UE location for arrest) Risk factors: forceful/late manipulation (> 10 days), SH III/IV, compression, infection, irradiation, repetitive stress (gymnasts) Presentation: prominent ulnar head, radial deviation, decreased rotation, DRUJ instability CT : size and location of physeal bar for surgical planning MRI : assess non-ossified bars, edema, 3D bar mapping

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Treatment › Epiphysiodesis
text: Percutaneous cannulated drill technique; predictable results Short arm cast 10-14 days; XR at 8-12 weeks for bridge formation Can be applied to radius and/or ulna as indicated

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Growth Plate Zones (Proximal to Distal)
text: Zone Function Resting Adjacent to epiphysis; supplies proliferative zone Proliferative Longitudinal columns; increases bone length Hypertrophic Cells enlarge 5-7x; provisional calcification Primary spongiosa Metaphyseal bone synthesis via osteoblasts Groove of Ranvier : proliferative cells for bone diameter increase Ring of LaCroix : structural support around the growth plate Most fractures occur through the zone of provisional calcification (hypertrophic zone)

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Specific Overuse Injuries › Gymnast Wrist (Distal Radial Epiphysitis)
text: 70% of adolescent gymnasts have wrist pain; repetitive loading → stress injury to physis XR: asymmetric widening of distal radial physis + sclerosis (compare contralateral) Treatment: cessation of weight-bearing minimum 6 weeks (casting for compliance); serial XR at 6 and 12 weeks Premature arrest → ulnar shortening + distal ulnar epiphysiodesis

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Specific Overuse Injuries › Little League Pitch Count Rules
text: Age Pitches/day 7-8 50 9-10 75 11-12 85 13-16 95 Curveball not recommended before age 14; slider/splitter not before 16 Prevention is paramount: limit reduction attempts to one or two gentle tries; every forceful manipulation increases arrest risk No reductions after ~10 days — the physis is already healing; further manipulation does more damage than good Follow at-risk fractures for at least 6 months to confirm continued growth

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Specific Overuse Injuries › Little League Shoulder
text: Repetitive microtrauma to proximal humerus physis; male pitchers age 11-14 GIRD (glenohumeral internal rotation deficit) on exam; XR may show physeal widening, sclerosis, periosteal reaction Treatment: rest + PT (sleeper stretches, periscapular strengthening); no throwing until symptoms resolve (6-12 weeks); gradual return per protocol 21/23 returned to baseball without pain at 3 months (Carson-Gasser)

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Ossification Timing — High-Yield
text: Elbow (CRITOE) : Capitellum (< 1 yr), Radial head (4-5), Internal epicondyle (6-7), Trochlea (8-10), Olecranon (10), External epicondyle (11). Medial epicondyle apophysis is last to fuse (15-20 yr) Distal radius : epiphysis appears 0.4-2.3 yr; 75-80% of radius/ulna growth from distal physis ; fusion 16.5 (F) to 17.5 (M) yr Proximal humerus : 80% of humeral length; fusion begins 14, ends 17 yr Hand : thumb physis at base of MC; digits 2-5 at distal MC end; close distal to proximal

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: SH II is by far the most common UE physeal fracture (~75%) — the Thurston-Holland fragment is pathognomonic SH V is invisible on initial XR — diagnosed retrospectively when arrest appears at 6-9 months Forceful or repeated reductions are the leading iatrogenic cause of physeal arrest 75-80% of radius/ulna growth is from the distal physis — arrest here is consequential CRITOE mnemonic for elbow ossification: the medial epicondyle is last to fuse and most commonly avulsed Gymnast wrist: rest is the treatment — minimum 6 weeks cessation; casting ensures compliance Pitch counts are preventive medicine — curveballs before 14 are a risk factor for Little League shoulder

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Treatment › Physeal Bar Resection and Interposition
text: Reserved for young children with substantial growth remaining + small/peripheral bar Remove bar without destroying healthy physis; fat interposition (local or upper lateral thigh) CT/MRI mapping essential for planning

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Treatment › Physeal Fractures
text: Stable SH I/II : cast/splint 4 weeks; gentle closed reduction under adequate anesthesia SH III/IV with > 2 mm articular displacement : surgical fixation Limit reduction attempts to 1-2 ; no reductions after 10-14 days Extra-octave fracture (proximal phalanx SH II): closed reduction + buddy taping; open reduction rarely needed (entrapped flexor/soft tissue)

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: References
text: Salter RB, Harris WR. Physeal injury classification. JBJS. 1963. Peterson HA. Physeal fracture types and Peterson type I description. Carson WG, Gasser SI. Little League shoulder outcomes. Waters PM et al. Distal radius physeal arrest: outcomes of 30 patients.

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Classification › Salter-Harris
text: Type Description Key point I Through physis only May be radiographically occult II Through physis + exits metaphysis ( Thurston-Holland fragment ) ~75% of all UE physeal fractures III Through physis + into epiphysis/articular surface Articular involvement IV Across all zones (metaphysis → physis → epiphysis) Highest arrest risk V Axial crush injury Not visible initially ; arrest apparent 6-9 months later

title: Physeal Injury (Traumatic and Acquired)
heading: Treatment › Ulnar Shortening Osteotomy
text: For ulna positive variance with impaction symptoms Between FCU and ECU, as distal as possible; volar plate decreases hardware irritation

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What is the most common cervical level of spinal cord injury? A: C5 (15.2%). Q: In ICSHT classification, what does the group number represent? A: The number of muscles available at grade 4 strength as potential tendon transfer donors. Q: What is the priority order for surgical reconstruction in tetraplegia? A: Elbow extension → wrist extension → lateral pinch/release → palmar grasp/release. Q: What nerve transfer restores finger and thumb extension in tetraplegia? A: Supinator branch to posterior interosseous nerve (PIN). Q: What percentage of candidates for upper limb reconstruction actually undergo surgery? A: Only 12-14%.

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Classification — ICSHT (International Classification for Surgery of the Hand in Tetraplegia)
text: Group Grade 4 Muscle Key Implication 0 None No tendon transfers; FES research 1 BR Elbow ext + wrist ext + tenodesis pinch 2 ECRL Elbow ext + active lateral pinch 3 ECRB + Palmar grasp possible 4 PT Lateral pinch + palmar grasp 5 FCR May not need elbow ext 6 EDC Same as above 7 EPL Single stage; intrinsic restoration 8+ Finger flexors Individualized T+/T- Triceps grade 4 ICSHT number = potential donor muscles

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Coaptation
text: Modified side-to-side (Brown) — stronger, lower profile, allows early mobilization vs Pulvertaft weave Tendon transfer loses one grade of strength — a grade 4 donor becomes grade 3 at best (antigravity only). Donors at grade 3 are not candidates.

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Contracture Management
text: Forearm supination contracture → radial pronation osteotomy (transverse midshaft, rotate 10-20° pronation, locking plate) Elbow contractures: serial casting first; surgical for > 50° (triceps strong) or > 25° (no triceps) Intrinsic tightness: selective ulnar-sided intrinsic release before any reconstruction

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Elbow Extension
text: Posterior Deltoid to Triceps Posterior 1/3 deltoid + central 1/3 triceps turn-up graft Long-arm cast 20° flex × 3-4 wk → hinged orthosis, progressive flexion 15°/wk Average MMT 3 achieved Biceps to Triceps (Kuz/Revol) Brachialis = primary elbow flexor; biceps can be spared Route medially under ulnar nerve, weave into triceps + olecranon bone tunnel Re-educate via forearm supination (synergy) Rupture rate up to 14% (early mobilization + fluoroquinolones) ~47% flexion strength loss but acceptable

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Epidemiology
text: ~54/million annual incidence (~17,500/yr US); 285,000 Americans with SCI C5 = most common level (15.2%); C4 + C6 next 54.2% tetraplegic (most incomplete) Hand function = greatest functional loss cited by 76% of patients First-year cost $780K; lifetime $3.5M (low-level tetraplegia, young patient) Only 12-14% of candidates undergo upper limb reconstruction

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Lateral Pinch — 4 Components
text: Thumb IP stabilization — split FPL transfer (radial half FPL → EPL) CMC stabilization — arthrodesis (40° palmar abd, 25° ext, 10° pronation) or adductor-opponensplasty FPL activation — BR → FPL (workhorse); set tension: pinch at 0-10° wrist extension Extensor tenodesis if needed (EPL/APL lasso at retinaculum)

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Nerve Transfers
text: Alternative to tendon transfer; single donor → multiple muscles Supinator branch → PIN (finger + thumb extension) — most common Fox study: 73% achieve M4+ recovery; minimal donor deficit Advantages: no immobilization, less intensive therapy Disadvantages: 6 mo-2 yr for strength; failure 10-40% (vs near 0% for tendon transfer rupture) Time-sensitive: ~18-21 mo window before chronic denervation

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Joint suppleness, contracture prevention Spasmolytics (oral, intrathecal, botulinum toxin) TES (transcutaneous electrical stimulation): converts type II glycolytic → slow oxidative fibers (fatigue resistant) Splinting matched to level (C1-C4 resting hand → C6 wrist-drive flexor hinge → C7 MCP block)

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Operative — Goal Priority Order
text: Elbow extension — workspace + stabilizes distal transfers Wrist extension — foundation for tenodesis pinch/grasp Lateral pinch + release — most-used grasp pattern Palmar grasp + release — larger objects

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Outcomes
text: 80-83% good-excellent functional gains at 7+ yr (Lamb/Chan) 75% gain self-catheterization after pinch reconstruction 81-90% would have surgery again FES: 87% general satisfaction, 88% life improvement

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Palmar Grasp
text: ECRL → synchronized FDP (“reverse cascade”) for finger flexion Set tension: fingers flex with wrist 30-45° extended Intrinsic reconstruction: Zancolli FDS lasso (FDS → A1 pulley, MCP flexion with wrist extension) or House lateral band graft

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Hand function is the #1 priority for tetraplegic patients — yet only 12-14% get reconstruction ICSHT classification drives surgical planning — know donor muscles by group Elbow extension first, then wrist, then pinch — proximal stability before distal finesse Never sacrifice ECRB unless 2+ wrist extensors are strong BR = workhorse donor; mobilize fully for 78 mm excursion (native only 42 mm) Biceps-to-triceps: counsel about 14% rupture rate and 47% flexion loss Nerve transfers offer an alternative but have higher failure rates and longer recovery

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Treatment › Tendon Transfer Principles
text: Supple joints with functional passive ROM Donor MMT ≥ 4 (loses 1 grade with transfer) Comparable excursion + force; synergy facilitates re-education Straight line of pull; minimal donor morbidity Never sacrifice ECRB unless 2+ wrist extensors strong ECRL preferred donor when 2 wrist extensors available

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › UMN vs LMN
text: Feature UMN LMN Pattern Myotome groups Individual muscles Atrophy Mild (disuse) Pronounced (70-80%) Tone Spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski Flaccid, hypotonia, decreased reflexes Fasciculations Absent May be present EMG/NCS Normal NCS, no denervation Abnormal NCS, denervation

title: Tetraplegia and Stroke
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Zone of Injury (Coulet)
text: Three-dimensional zone centered on but not confined to cord level Above zone: normal; below zone: UMN (hyperreflexia); within zone: mixed UMN/LMN Nerve-root avulsion or anterior horn cell injury → pure LMN Larger zones → more contractures + worse forearm/hand posturing Forearm supination contracture risk correlates with C5-segment zone size

title: Upper Limb Amputation, TMR, and Prosthetics
Upper Limb Amputation, TMR, and Prosthetics
heading: Targeted Muscle Reinnervation (TMR) › Acute TMR
text: Single operation at initial amputation: prevents neuroma + phantom pain, faster prosthetic control TMR at the time of initial amputation is the standard of care when feasible — zero reported neuromas in TMR-treated nerves, less phantom pain, and faster prosthetic fitting

title: Upper Limb Amputation, TMR, and Prosthetics
heading: Basic Science
text: 1.6M Americans with major amputation (doubling by 2050); >500K upper extremity 50-90% of UE amputations are trauma-related (vs LE = peripheral vascular disease) Any nerve transection = neuroma unless prevented Do not suture flexors to extensors over bone end (quadrigia) Myodesis (muscle to bone) vs myoplasty (agonist-antagonist sutured) — physiologic tension critical for myoelectric drive

title: Upper Limb Amputation, TMR, and Prosthetics
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What percentage of total hand function does the thumb represent? A: 40-50%. Q: What is the “golden period” for upper limb prosthetic fitting? A: < 1 month after amputation. Q: What is TMR and what is its primary advantage for neuroma prevention? A: Targeted muscle reinnervation redirects severed nerves to expendable motor branches — zero reported neuromas in treated nerves. Q: What is the Starfish procedure? A: Dorsal interossei transfer to dorsal MC periosteum at transmetacarpal amputation — enables immediate independent myoelectric finger control. Q: What is the grip strength difference between myoelectric and body-powered prostheses? A: Myoelectric up to 30 lbs vs body-powered 6-8 lbs.
