title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone I-II — Mallet Deformity
text: Doyle Classification: I = closed ± avulsion; II = open laceration; III = open + tissue loss; IVa = pediatric physeal; IVb = 20-50% articular; IVc = > 50% + volar subluxation Closed (Type I): - DIP extension splint 24/7 × 6-8 weeks + gradual daytime weaning; leave PIP free - Even large bony fragments respond to splinting alone - Outcomes: 7.6° extensor lag, 12.8% complication rate Bony mallet with DIP subluxation: - Extension block pinning (Ishiguro) : 0.045 K-wire 45° to P2 head as block + second retrograde K-wire across DIP; remove 4-6 weeks Open (Type II/III): 5-0 monofilament tendon repair + K-wire DIP pinning Chronic mallet → swan neck: Fowler tenotomy (divide central extensor at PIP); wait ≥ 6 months; SORL reconstruction or FDS volar PIP tenodesis for fixed deformity

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone III — Central Slip / Boutonniere
text: Initial presentation may be subtle — lateral bands can extend PIP early Modified Elson test : PIP fully flexed against resistance; rigid DIP extension = positive (central slip injury) Acute closed: PIP extension splint 6-8 weeks continuous + active DIP flexion hourly; then part-time 4-6 weeks Acute open: < 50% → wound care + early motion; complete → ORIF with 4-0/5-0 + PIP pinning in extension × 5-6 weeks Chronic boutonniere: - Boyes test : passive DIP flexion harder with PIP extended (vs pseudoboutonniere) - Conservative first — serial casting/splinting → relative motion flexion splint × 3 months - Surgical outcomes unpredictable; worse with PIP fixed flexion, age > 45, prior surgery - Curtis stepwise approach : TRL release → tenolysis → central slip reinforcement

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone V — Sagittal Band Injuries
text: Closed sagittal band rupture: radial side middle/ring most common Acute (< 3 wk): relative motion extension splint × 6 weeks — 95% success (Peelman) 3 wk delay: only ~50% succeed with splinting → surgical repair Fight bite : always evaluate for MCP joint penetration; aggressive I&D + IV antibiotics + delayed closure

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone VI (Dorsum of Hand)
text: Thicker tendons; 3-0 core suture; > 80% good/excellent regardless of postop protocol Loss of MCP flexion = most frequent complication

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone VII-VIII
text: EPL rupture after non-displaced DRF → EIP-to-EPL transfer (optimal) Zone VIII: don’t wait > 4 weeks — muscle contracture becomes permanent Relative motion splinting is increasingly preferred for zones V-VI — leverages the quadriga concept, keeping the injured tendon in relative extension while permitting near-normal hand function and therapy

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Reciprocal concave saddle joint ; lacks bony congruity → ligament-dependent stability 16 ligaments; 7 primary stabilizers Current view: DRL + POL = primary stabilizers (not the AOL/“beak ligament” as historically taught) DRL (dorsoradial ligament) : thickest, strongest, shortest; restrains dorsal migration in flexion-adduction POL = posterior oblique AOL histology = loose passive tissue; DRL histology = dense organized active tissue AOL degeneration = secondary, not causative Joint compression force at TMC = 12× tip pinch force (Cooney + Chao) Degeneration starts volar → progresses dorsally ; dorsal joint spared even in advanced disease

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: Which ligament is the primary stabilizer of the thumb CMC joint per current evidence? A: The dorsoradial ligament (DRL), with contribution from the POL — NOT the anterior oblique (AOL/“beak”) despite historic teaching. Q: What does the Eaton-Littler stage IV designation indicate? A: Pantrapezial arthritis — both CMC AND STT joints involved. Q: Per RCT data, what is the efficacy of corticosteroid injection for CMC OA? A: No difference vs saline placebo. Q: Which is the workhorse procedure for advanced CMC arthritis and what are its long-term outcomes? A: LRTI (Burton-Pellegrini); 9.4-yr outcomes include 92.5% grip improvement, 95% excellent pain relief, 11-13% arthroplasty space loss. Q: What is the ideal position for thumb CMC arthrodesis? A: 30-40° abduction, 15-20° extension, ~10° pronation (distal phalanx rests on middle phalanx of clenched fist).

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Classification — Eaton + Littler
text: Stage Findings I Normal/widened joint (synovitis); subluxation on stress II Narrowing; osteophytes < 2 mm III Further narrowing + subchondral sclerosis; osteophytes > 2 mm; STT NORMAL IV Pantrapezial (CMC + STT) Poor correlation clinical:radiographic — treat by symptoms, not film

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Workup › Clinical
text: Postmenopausal female with radial-sided thumb/hand pain, no trauma Pain with pinching, grasping, keys, writing, sewing CTS coexists in 26-29% (up to 46-80% in women, diabetics, workers’ comp)

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Epidemiology
text: 1 in 4 women / 1 in 12 men develop radiographic disease F:M = 10:1 Higher in Caucasian > Asian (flatter Asian hand surface) ↑ prevalence with age

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Advanced: adduction contracture + dorsal subluxation; CMC prominence (synovitis + osteophytes) Palpate CMC dorsal to APL insertion (vs STT — palmar over scaphoid tuberosity) Rule out de Quervain’s (Finkelstein), FCR tendonitis (palmar trapezial ridge), trigger thumb Trapezial dysplasia in young females: instability without arthritis from increased trapezial articular slope

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Robert’s view (hyperpronated AP, dorsal thumb on plate) — visualizes all 4 trapezial facets CMC view, lateral, oblique Stress views (Wolf — thumbs together with nails parallel)

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Complications & Outcomes › Implant
text: De Quervain’s, cup loosening, dislocation; revision < 10%

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Complications & Outcomes › MCP Hyperextension
text: ≤ 30° painless → no treatment 30° or painful → palmar capsulodesis (volar plate imbrication) + EPB transfer + K-wire 3-6 wk , OR fusion if collateral instability + arthritis

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Nonoperative
text: Activity modification + thumb proprioception/strengthening = effective Splinting: hand-based opponens, IP free Marotta meta-analysis : long custom splint best for pain; short custom best for function Initial near-full-time × 3-4 wk → wear during exacerbations NSAIDs: insufficient evidence Steroid injection: NO DIFFERENCE vs saline HA, PRP, autologous fat: insufficient evidence Counsel patients before any CSI: RCT evidence shows no difference vs saline; many patients still report symptomatic relief Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo).

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Stage I — Ligament Reconstruction Indication: instability + minimal erosion Rule out trapezial dysplasia first (soft tissue alone insufficient → bony reconstruction needed) Eaton-Littler Volar incision; protect sensory branches + radial artery Drill hole through MC base perpendicular to thumbnail ½ FCR harvested at wrist (radial half = ulnar half in forearm due to rotation) Pass through hole, suture to dorsal MC periosteum under tension; pronate + abduct + palmarly reduce MC base Pass remainder under APL → under other half of FCR → loop back, suture to itself 4 wk thumb spica DRL Imbrication Dorsal approach; identify thickened DRL 2.5 mm suture anchor OR bone tunnel → advance DRL Reduce thumb in extension + palmar abduction Stages II-IV — Trapeziectomy Family Many procedures with ~90-95% good-to-excellent results — no single technique clearly superior Trapeziectomy Alone (Gervis) Risk: proximal migration → weakness + instability Pain relief comparable to complex procedures in recent series LRTI (Burton + Pellegrini 1986) Trapeziectomy + FCR through MC drill hole reconstructs beak + interposes 9.4-yr outcomes : grip ↑ 92.5%, pinch ↑ 50%, 95% excellent pain relief, 11-13% arthroplasty space loss Thompson APL Suspensionplasty Trapeziectomy + APL dorsal slip → MC tunnel → 2nd MC tunnel → ECRL weave Weilby Suspensionplasty ½ FCR woven between APL + remaining FCR; grip 80% normal, durable Suture Suspensionplasty (DelSignore-Accardi) No graft needed; 91% satisfaction Suture Button (

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: DRL + POL = primary stabilizers (NOT AOL despite traditional teaching) Steroid injection = no better than saline (counsel pre-injection) Treat by symptoms, not radiograph (poor correlation) LRTI = 90-95% good-to-excellent at 9-yr; long-term gold standard Implants promising but more complications — long-term data still developing Always check for coexisting CTS, de Quervain’s, trigger thumb Rule out trapezial dysplasia before soft tissue-only reconstruction Robert’s view = essential first film Hemi-hamate CPT for PIP and stem fixation CPT for CMC are distinct — coding accuracy matters

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Complications & Outcomes › Persistent Pain (most common)
text: Typical 3-6 mo resolution Hypertrophic scar / cutaneous neuroma → desensitization CRPS → pain management consult Proximal migration after LRTI difficult to revise

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: LRTI: thumb spica 4 wk → IP ROM immediate, MCP/CMC at 1 mo, strengthening 3 mo, full activity 3 mo TMC arthroplasty (implant): immediate ROM, full activity 6 wk Continued improvement up to 1 yr

title: Thumb CMC (Basal Joint) Arthritis
heading: Workup › Provocative Tests
text: Crank test : axial load + passive flex/ext of MC → pain + crepitus Grind test : axial load + rotation of MC through flexed MCP → pain + crepitus Adduction-extension test (Gelberman) : specific for OA — pain with adduction to plane of index MC OR extension to plane of palm Laxity exam: compare bidirectional translation to contralateral

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: PIP + DIP similar; differ in dimensions + DIP mobility Unlike MCP, osseous shape plays major role in PIP/DIP stability Not a perfect hinge — small abduction/adduction + rotation Instantaneous rotational axis (not fixed) Radial PIP (index, middle) : more stability needed for thumb pinch Ulnar PIP (ring, small) : more mobility for grasp Anatomical implants cannot fully replicate this complexity

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: DIP Joint › Arthrodesis (First Choice for Painful DIP OA)
text: Screw fixation (preferred), K-wires, tension band, endomedullary staples Screw Technique Headless or 2.0 mm AO (1.5 mm for small finger if mismatched) Length ~30 mm (allow future PIP arthroplasty without removal) Dorsal transverse incision, transverse tenotomy of extensor CRITICAL: protect germinal nail matrix (few mm distal to joint line) — violation = permanent nail deformity Bone prep: precision saw proximal (minimal); rongeur distal Fusion angle: 5-10° flexion Screw aim: middle phalanx side → dorsal recess of PIP (slight flexion); distal phalanx side → subungual Distal phalanx over-drilled (lag); screw flush with subungual bone Splint 4-6 wk K-wire Insert proximal-dorsal → distal-volar (avoid fingertip) 2 crossed K-wires for rotation Higher infection rate

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What are the recommended fusion angles for PIP arthrodesis? A: Radial digits 15-20° flexion; ulnar digits 25-40° flexion. Q: What is the 10-year survival rate for silicone PIP arthroplasty? A: ~90%. Q: Why is DIP arthroplasty contraindicated for the index finger? A: Lateral pinch loads cause ulnar deviation and instability. Q: Per Kulkarni systematic review, what is the reoperation rate for surface PIP arthroplasty? A: 21% reoperation, 11% revision. Q: What is the fusion angle for DIP arthrodesis? A: 5-10° flexion (functional + cosmetic).

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Classification — Kellgren-Lawrence
text: Doubtful narrowing, possible osteophytic lipping Definite osteophytes + narrowing Moderate osteophytes, narrowing, sclerosis ± deformity Large osteophytes, marked narrowing, severe sclerosis, definite deformity

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Complications & Outcomes › DIP Arthrodesis
text: High fusion rates; complications dependent on technique Permanent nail deformity if germinal matrix violated

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: DIP Joint › DIP Arthroplasty
text: Alternative for selected ulnar fingers NOT for index (pinch loads → ulnar deviation) Swanson 00 implant typical Dorsal approach + transverse tenotomy NO passive motion testing (extensor disruption risk) Immobilize 3-4 wk Expected ROM: 30-40°

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Complications & Outcomes › DIP Arthroplasty
text: Limited publications Extension deficit common (cosmetic limit)

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Treatment › Nonoperative
text: NSAIDs, activity modification, splinting Treating affected joints doesn’t alter progression in unaffected joints Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo).

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Index = stability priority (arthrodesis or modified arthroplasty rehab) Ulnar fingers = mobility priority (arthroplasty) Lateral deformity > 30° → arthrodesis Silicone = gold standard PIP; 10-yr survival 90% Always check rotation by lifting hand off table Fusion angles : PIP radial 15-20°, ulnar 25-40°, DIP 5-10° DIP nail matrix protection mandatory Painful DIP OA = fusion is first choice Fixed swan neck/boutonniere with PIP arthritis = fusion, not arthroplasty Failed arthroplasty → fusion with structural bone graft

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: PIP Joint › PIP Arthrodesis
text: Indications Severe instability + deformity Difficult bone (post-infection, post-trauma) Revision after failed arthroplasty Lateral deformity > 30° in radial digits Fusion Angles Radial digits: 15-20° flexion Ulnar digits: 25-40° flexion Techniques Tension band wiring : active compression with motion; cost-effective; risk pin protrusion Plate fixation Herbert screw : immediate strong fixation, low complication Technique Pearls Dorsal curvilinear, central slip midline split Remove osteophytes, release collaterals Osteotomy: desired angle on proximal phalanx; perpendicular on middle phalanx Lift hand off table to check 3D rotation Avoid malrotation — disabling Suture extensor over hardware

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: PIP Joint › PIP Arthroplasty
text: Indications OA, post-traumatic Intact tendons + at least some residual stability Contraindications Insufficient bone stock Missing/dysfunctional tendons Severe tendon imbalance (contracted boutonniere, swan neck) Severe instability or deformity > 30° Implants Silicone (Swanson 1968 — gold standard) - Joint spacer concept - ROM 40-60° active flex/ext - 10-30% fracture at long-term (less than MCP rate) - 90% survival at 10 yr - Good pain relief - Less silicone synovitis than at MCP Surface Replacement (2-component) - Chrome-cobalt/poly, ceramic/ceramic, pyrocarbon/pyrocarbon - CapFlex: short-stem subchondral fixation - Pyrocarbon: excellent biocompatibility but squeaking + osteointegration issues - Kulkarni systematic review (1324 joints, 54 mo): - VAS pain ↓ 4.5; ROM ↑ 10.5°; DASH ↑ 18 - Reoperation 21%, revision 11% Approaches Dorsal (most common): - Longitudinal incision, preserve dorsal veins + sensory branch - Midline central slip split (preferred) OR Chamay V-shaped flap (calcification + hyperextension risk) - Release dorsal collaterals - Cannot correct deformity intraoperatively — even with rehab Volar (Herren) : - Tendons NOT violated - Bruner incision, radial flap; protect NV bundles - Open A3 pulley, release accessory collaterals - Immediate passive motion (no extensor protection) - Technically demanding, less space Lateral (least common): - Bain modification: split collateral + side-to-side repair → less instability + early ROM Surgical Approach Selection (Burton-Pel

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Complications & Outcomes › PIP Arthroplasty
text: Silicone: 10-30% fracture long-term ; doesn’t always need revision Forster meta-analysis: Silicone: 11% complications, 1% reoperation Pyrocarbon: 14% complications, 7% reoperation Metal-poly: 10% complications, 10% reoperation Revision 4% all types Helder registry: surface 20% complications vs silicone 11% Literature revision rate 2-13% Preexisting deformity recurs (silicone esp); ROM rarely improved Newer pyrocarbon/ceramic/resurfacing: dislocation + squeaking RA patients fare worse

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Complications & Outcomes › PIP Fusion
text: Nonunion (biological or technical) Malunion (malrotation, lateral deviation) = disabling Hardware irritation → removal Rotation check intraoperatively essential

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: PIP fusion: stable construct → buddy tape + early adjacent joint motion PIP arthroplasty (dorsal): protected motion 6 wk; index = later mobilization + prolonged splinting PIP arthroplasty (volar): immediate passive motion OK DIP fusion: splint 4-6 wk; radiographic union confirm DIP arthroplasty: 3-4 wk immobilization For fixed swan neck or boutonniere with PIP arthritis → primary fusion (not arthroplasty); arthroplasty cannot correct already-fixed deformity

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: PIP Joint › Surgical Decision Framework
text: Index + middle (pinching partners with thumb) → prioritize stability (often arthrodesis or modified arthroplasty rehab) Ring + small (grasp) → prioritize mobility (arthroplasty) Lateral deformity > 30° → arthrodesis in radial digits Woodworth: simulated PIP fusion 40° on all 4 fingers → significant ADL impairment (precision tasks)

title: Finger Arthritis (PIP and DIP)
heading: Workup
text: Clinical + radiographs sufficient Fusiform swelling, tender joints, stiffness Mucoid cysts ± nail deformity at DIP CT only for post-traumatic PIP considering joint-preserving osteotomy

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Systemic fibroproliferative disorder → palmar nodules → cords → flexion contractures Most common inherited connective tissue disorder Myofibroblast = characteristic cell; TGF-beta, EGF, PDGF, CTGF drive fibrosis Luck’s 3 stages : proliferative (hypercellular nodules) → involutional (aligned cords) → residual (hypocellular fibrotic) Type III collagen elevated in early stages, normalizes but never reaches baseline

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: Which cord displaces the neurovascular bundle and makes it vulnerable during surgery? A: The spiral cord — displaces the NV bundle midline and superficial (“spiral nerve”). Q: What is the recurrence rate of CCH at 5 years (CORDLESS)? A: 47%. Q: What defines Hueston diathesis? A: Family history, bilateral disease, knuckle pads (Garrod), Ledderhose (plantar fibromatosis) — predicts early recurrence. Q: What is Luck’s characteristic cell of active Dupuytren disease? A: The myofibroblast. Q: Why are revision fasciectomies higher risk? A: 10x arterial injury and 5x nerve injury compared to primary, due to scarring and distorted anatomy.

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Collagenase Injection (CCH)
text: FDA 2010; inject day 0, manipulate day 1-7 Two cords same session OK (Gaston RCT) Degrades collagen I + III; rare tendon/pulley rupture, CRPS, anaphylaxis Recovery: light activities < 1 wk, RTW 1-2d

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Cord-Contracture Map
text: Cord Contracture NV Bundle Risk Central MCP Safe (bundles lateral) Spiral PIP HIGH — displaces NV midline + superficial Retrovascular DIP Deep to NV bundle Natatory Webspace Low Spiral cord = key surgical hazard: NV bundle spirals dorsal-to-volar around cord Suspect spiral cord when subdermal cord passes beneath a soft compressible mass + tender on tensioning PIP contracture > 45° often involves retrovascular cord + multiple cords Digital cords may involve Grayson’s OR Cleland’s ligaments (contrary to older teaching)

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Dermofasciectomy
text: Fasciectomy + skin excision + FTSG — lowest recurrence in diathesis patients Tendon exposure up to 1 cm: skin graft on vascularized bed OK Recovery: light activities 4 wk, RTW 9 wk

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Epidemiology
text: Caucasian 3-6%; Hispanic 1/3, African American 1/5, Asian American 1/10 M:F ratio decreases with age: 30:1 at < 40 yo → 1:1 at 85 Ring + small fingers most affected (50-60%); thumb + index least (5-7%) Risk factors: diabetes, smoking, heavy ETOH, hyperlipidemia, psoriasis, manual labor RA and obesity are protective

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Diagnosis is clinical — no imaging needed Modified Tubiana stages (0/N/1/2/3/4) — total extension deficit per ray (MCP + PIP + DIP) Measure MCP extension with PIP flexed; PIP extension with MCP flexed Hueston table-top test — cannot place palm flat on table Document neuro + digital Allen test pre-procedure (especially in previously treated hands)

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Fasciectomy
text: Regional (all visibly diseased) — US standard; radical abandoned (high complications, no benefit) Incisions: Bruner zigzag, Watson V-Y, transverse (McCash open palm — less pain/hematoma) Dissection: magnification, known to unknown , do NOT skeletonize NV bundle Loose closure; sutures left 2-3 wk (abnormal wound healing biology) Recovery: light activities 2 wk, RTW 5 wk, full unrestricted 2 mo

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Fasciectomy Complications (Denkler)
text: Major: CRPS 6% , digital nerve 3%, infection 2%, hematoma 2%, arterial injury 2% Minor: wound healing 23% Revision = 10x artery injury, 5x nerve injury vs primary More complications with PIP > 60°

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Epidemiology › Hueston Diathesis (Predicts Early Recurrence)
text: Family history, bilateral disease, knuckle pads (Garrod), Ledderhose (plantar fibromatosis) Onset < 50, Peyronie, > 2 digits, male, Caucasian, thumb involvement

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Non-operative — Nodules
text: Do not excise isolated nodules — triggers inflammation + progression Intralesional corticosteroid for tender/itchy nodules Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo). Reserve intralesional steroid for symptomatic nodules without contracted cords

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Operative Indications (Hueston Table-Top Test)
text: MCP contracture ≥ 30° PIP contracture > 15° Adduction contracture Worse correction outcomes : MCP > 50°, PIP > 40°, composite > 90°

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Outcomes
text: MCP: 80-90% success (< 5° from full extension) — all methods comparable PIP: 25-50% success — all methods; small finger worst Fasciectomy > PNF/CCH for severe contractures CORDLESS 5-yr : 47% recurrence after CCH

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Spiral cord displaces the NV bundle superficially — palpate before any procedure PNF + CCH best for MCP; fasciectomy for PIP or severe contractures Nodule excision worsens disease — inject instead Revision surgery carries 10x vascular and 5x nerve injury risk PIP > 60° = suspect pseudo-boutonniere with central slip attenuation Anticoagulants safe for PNF Dermofasciectomy for young diathesis patients — lowest recurrence

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Treatment › Percutaneous Needle Fasciotomy (PNF)
text: Hypodermic needle under local; cords tight, tendons loose on passive extension Work distal → proximal to preserve patient feedback (paresthesias) Complications: skin tears 8%, dysesthesia 3%, tendon rupture 0.2% Anticoagulants do NOT need to be held Recovery: light activities < 1d, RTW 1-2d

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Outcomes › Recurrence Rates (Per Year)
text: Method Rate Dermofasciectomy < 2%/yr Fasciectomy ~5%/yr CCH/PNF MCP ~10%/yr CCH/PNF PIP ~20%/yr “Recurrence is an inevitable consequence if the patient lives long enough” (Bulstrode)

heading: References

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Secondary Deformities
text: Pseudo-boutonniere : PIP > 60° → central slip attenuation, lateral band subluxation, DIP hyperextension Secondary swan neck : chronic MCP contracture → PIP volar plate stretch

title: Dupuytren Disease
heading: Severe / Recurrent PIP Contracture
text: Routine open joint release NOT recommended (gains lost, flexion decreases) Two-stage for severe : external fixator (Digit Widget) for progressive lengthening → fasciectomy/dermofasciectomy Dorsal closing wedge osteotomy = ineffective Salvage: amputation, arthrodesis, middle phalangectomy

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › AIN Syndrome
text: Non-operative first : rest, immobilization, avoid provocative activities; onset of recovery 5.9 mo (range 3-12); full recovery 9.5 mo; age < 40 = better prognosis Operative (6 months without recovery + confirmed EDX + no other nerve lesions): same approach as pronator; consider interfascicular neurolysis for hourglass constrictions (Sneag: fascicular constrictions proximal to elbow in all 22 patients on MR neurography)

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Median nerve: C5-T1, formed by medial + lateral cords Crosses anterior to brachial artery at mid-humerus (lateral→medial) Ligament of Struthers : fibrous band from supracondylar process to medial epicondyle (1-4% of population); can compress median nerve ± brachial artery Compression sites (proximal → distal): ligament of Struthers → lacertus fibrosus → pronator teres (between heads) → FDS arch → carpal tunnel Martin-Gruber anastomosis (forearm median→ulnar motor crossover): 23% prevalence; bilateral in 19%; Type I (60%) and Type II (35%) most common AIN : largest muscular branch; arises 5-8 cm distal to medial epicondyle; innervates FPL, FDP (index/long), PQ; terminal sensory branch to volar wrist joint Gantzer’s muscle (accessory FPL head): present in up to 68% — a normal variant, not rare Carpal tunnel boundaries: carpal bones dorsally, TCL palmarly; narrowest at hook of hamate (20x10 mm) TCL : attaches pisiform/hamate (ulnar) to scaphoid/trapezium (radial); thickest at middle-distal third junction (up to 6 mm in CTS); division reduces carpal arch stiffness only 7% Recurrent motor branch: extraligamentous 46%, subligamentous 31%, transligamentous 23% (Lanz) Bifid median nerve : 2.8% prevalence; associated with persistent median artery in 79%

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient with forearm aching and numbness over the thenar eminence has a negative Phalen and Tinel at the wrist. What is the most likely diagnosis? — A: Pronator syndrome; palmar cutaneous branch involvement distinguishes it from CTS, and negative wrist provocative tests support proximal compression. Q: A 35-year-old presents with inability to make an “OK” sign after sudden severe shoulder pain 2 weeks ago. EMG shows denervation in FPL, FDP index, and brachioradialis. What is the diagnosis? — A: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy); brachioradialis involvement extends beyond isolated AIN territory, and the presentation with severe initial pain is classic. Q: What are the three variations of the recurrent motor branch course relative to the TCL? — A: Extraligamentous (46%), subligamentous (31%), transligamentous (23%) per the Lanz classification. Q: What is the most reliable MRI finding in AIN syndrome? — A: Edema within the pronator quadratus on T2-weighted fat-saturated images (Dunn); fascicular constrictions proximal to the elbow on MR neurography (Sneag). Q: After open carpal tunnel release, a patient reports persistent numbness. At revision, what is the most common finding? — A: Incomplete TCL release; also dense scar tissue with median nerve adherent to radial TCL leaflet. MABC neuroma found in 73% of failed cubital tunnels (analogous risk in CTR with cutaneous nerve injury).

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Pronator syndrome: incomplete decompression up to 55%; MABC neuroma risk AIN: incomplete correction most common; Park: 10/11 achieved M4 within 12 mo post-surgery CTS: pillar pain (12.7%), burning discomfort (18%), scar tenderness (7.3%); structural nerve/vessel/tendon injury rare with either approach Revision CTS: challenging; 41-91% persistent symptoms after revision; recurrent group improves most

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › CTS — Non-operative
text: Wrist neutral splint (especially nocturnal); neutral > 20° extension Steroid injection : benefits up to 6 months; 32% never need further treatment (Evers, 7.4 yr follow-up); diabetics 2.6x more likely to recur within 1 year Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo). CTS injection technique : enter ulnar to palmaris longus, just proximal to the distal wrist crease, angling 30-45 degrees

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › CTS — Operative
text: Indications : thenar atrophy, constant numbness, severe EDX changes, symptoms > 1 year, failed 6-week non-operative trial Open mini CTR (authors’ preferred): 3-cm incision from distal wrist crease in ring finger axis; divide TCL distal→proximal with 2-mm cuff on hook of hamate; release antebrachial fascia 2-3 cm proximal; inspect for anomalies; no routine tenosynovectomy or neurolysis Endoscopic (Agee single-portal) : 1-cm incision at wrist; divide TCL under direct visualization; faster return to work; higher nerve injury risk (mostly transient) No beneficial effect of post-op immobilization demonstrated (multiple studies) Outcomes: > 95% good/excellent; endoscopic preferred by 66% of patients (scar/pillar pain); revision rate 1-5%

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: CTS : prolonged median sensory peak latency > 4.0 ms at wrist; motor distal latency > 4.5 ms; median-ulnar difference > 0.5 ms (sensory) or > 1.5 ms (motor) Severity: mild (sensory only), moderate (sensory + motor), severe (absent sensory + abnormal motor), extreme (both absent) Pronator syndrome : often normal — NCS helps rule out other sites; normal wrist conduction + clinical findings → supports proximal compression AIN syndrome : acute denervation limited to AIN-innervated muscles; 60% have concomitant abnormalities in non-AIN distributions

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Pronator syndrome : tenderness over proximal PT, positive pronator compression test (30 sec), no Tinel at wrist, no Phalen/Durkan; resisted supination → bicipital aponeurosis; resisted long finger PIP flexion → FDS arch AIN syndrome : Kiloh-Nevin sign (cannot make “OK” sign — compensatory FPB/FDS flexion instead) CTS provocative tests : Phalen (sens 68%, spec 73%), Tinel (50%, 77%), Durkan (64%, 83%), combined Durkan+Phalen (80%, 92%) CTS-6 : numbness in median distribution, nocturnal numbness, thenar weakness/atrophy, Tinel, Phalen, loss of 2PD — probability score correlates with CTS diagnosis Barrera: CTS-6 score > 12 = positive for CTS. Sensory testing pearl : Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments test threshold (earlier finding); static 2PD tests innervation density (late finding) — use both for every suspected compression neuropathy

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › History
text: Pronator syndrome : vague forearm ache, daytime symptoms with pronation/supination, numbness in palmar cutaneous distribution (thenar eminence — distinguishes from CTS) AIN syndrome (Kiloh-Nevin) : sudden forearm pain → weakness/loss of FPL + index FDP + PQ; no sensory loss; overlap with Parsonage-Turner syndrome CTS : nocturnal paresthesias (hallmark), bimodal peaks (5th + 8th decades), female:male 3:1; > 500,000 releases/year in US

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Thenar eminence numbness = pronator syndrome (palmar cutaneous branch doesn’t traverse carpal tunnel) AIN syndrome and Parsonage-Turner overlap significantly — EDX + MRI help distinguish; PT has broader nerve involvement + severe initial pain CTS + pronator syndrome can coexist (double crush) — failed CTR should prompt proximal evaluation Incision for open CTR: ring finger axis, 5+ mm ulnar to interthenar depression to protect palmar cutaneous branch Kaplan’s cardinal line (parallel to abducted thumb ulnar border → hook of hamate) = distal TCL extent Recurrent motor branch exits 6.5 mm from distal TCL edge in ring finger axis — respect the fat pad

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Pronator Syndrome
text: Non-operative : activity modification, nerve glides, stretching, brief immobilization; Morris: 5/7 responded to intramuscular PT steroid injection Operative (> 3 months persistent symptoms): lazy-S incision from 5 cm above medial epicondyle across antecubital fossa extending distally 10 cm; release all compressive structures (lacertus, PT heads, FDS arch, ligament of Struthers if present); protect MABC nerves, median motor branches, radial artery Post-op: splint 7-10 days (elbow 90°, forearm 45° pronation, wrist slight flexion); ROM at 7-10 days; resistive exercises at 6-8 weeks Outcomes: complete relief 22%, improvement 63%, unchanged 9% (Hartz); minimally invasive approaches achieving 93% resolution (Zancolli)

title: Median Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Revision CTS
text: Persistent (no relief) vs recurrent (relief then return after 6 mo) vs new symptoms (iatrogenic) Extended open approach; identify nerve proximal to scar in native tissue; external neurolysis Hypothenar fat pad flap (Strickland): well-vascularized coverage over scarred median nerve; ulnar-artery-based perforators

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Radial nerve enters the arm posteriorly via spiral groove at junction of middle/distal thirds of humerus Enters radial tunnel between brachialis (medial) and brachioradialis (proximal/lateral), ECRL (distal/lateral) Floor: anterior radiocapitellar capsule + deep supinator; roof: fibrous connection brachialis-brachioradialis Bifurcates at radial tunnel exit into SRN (sensory) and PIN (motor) PIN dives under arcade of Frohse (proximal edge of supinator) — common compression site Leash of Henry (radial recurrent artery branches) = most common compressor in radial tunnel SRN becomes subcutaneous 9 cm proximal to radial styloid between ECRL tendon and brachioradialis; bifurcates ~5 cm proximal to styloid Nerves stretched > 6% of length → detectable conduction block from altered perfusion

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient with lateral elbow pain has tenderness 3 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, pain with resisted middle finger extension, and normal grip strength. EDX is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis? — A: Radial tunnel syndrome; tenderness distal to the epicondyle + pain with resisted middle finger extension + normal EDX distinguishes it from lateral epicondylitis and PIN syndrome. Q: A patient with PIN palsy extends the wrist in radial deviation. Why? — A: ECRL is innervated by the radial nerve proximal to the PIN takeoff and is preserved; ECRB (mixed radial/PIN innervation) is weakened, leaving unopposed radial deviation. Q: What is the most common structure causing compression of the radial nerve within the radial tunnel? — A: Leash of Henry (branches of the radial recurrent artery). Q: A 55-year-old presents with progressive finger drop, EMG denervation of extensor muscles, and a palpable mass at the proximal forearm. What is the next step? — A: MRI to evaluate for space-occupying lesion (lipoma, ganglion, Schwannoma); if mass confirmed, surgical excision + PIN decompression.

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Classification
text: Saturday night palsy / crutch palsy / honeymoon palsy : proximal compression in spiral groove → neurapraxia; complete wrist/finger/thumb drop Radial tunnel syndrome : pain condition; radial nerve compressed within mobile wad PIN syndrome : motor compression at arcade of Frohse → finger/thumb extension weakness/palsy Wartenberg’s syndrome : SRN compression at brachioradialis exit → dorsoradial forearm/1st webspace numbness

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Saturday night palsy: excellent prognosis; less favorable with older age, EMG denervation, profound initial weakness Radial tunnel surgery: De Smet reported only 40% satisfaction; concurrent epicondylitis and workers’ comp = worse outcomes PIN decompression: 24/25 recovered motor function (Hashizume); avg 5.6 months to recovery; 1 patient required tendon transfer Wartenberg’s: most improve without surgery; surgical outcomes 75% success (Lanzetta)

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Saturday night palsy : decreased NCV + amplitude (conduction block); serial EMG — brachioradialis recovers first, EIP last Radial tunnel : typically normal (pain syndrome); dynamic testing may show conduction block with active supination PIN syndrome : motor NCV decreased across supinator; EMG shows denervation of extensor muscles; sensory radial nerve normal Wartenberg’s : variable — normal to complete SRN conduction block; no motor changes

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Saturday night palsy : complete wrist/finger/thumb extension palsy ± dorsal hand paresthesia; distinguish from PIN (BR + ECRL preserved in PIN) Radial tunnel : tenderness ≥ 2 cm distal to lateral epicondyle (vs epicondylitis = at epicondyle); pain with resisted middle finger extension + resisted supination; no weakness; Rule of Nine test (Loh) PIN syndrome : finger/thumb extension weakness; wrist extension in radial deviation (ECRL unopposed); SBRN sensation intact Wartenberg’s : Tinel over SRN; decreased 2PD in 1st webspace; symptoms with pronation + ulnar deviation; diagnostic lidocaine injection at brachioradialis exit

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › History
text: Saturday night palsy : acute wrist drop after prolonged arm compression (avg 180 min); worse with alcohol, opioids, DM, hypothyroidism, obesity Radial tunnel : aching mobile wad pain ≥ 2 cm distal to lateral epicondyle; worse with activity; no numbness or weakness; occupational risk = repetitive pronation/pinching PIN syndrome : finger/thumb weakness or extension lag; wrist deviates radially (ECRL intact, ECRB weakened); may have 25% traumatic etiology Wartenberg’s : numbness/paresthesia dorsoradial forearm and 1st webspace; onset with repetitive pronation; coexists with de Quervain’s in up to 50%

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: XR: fracture, malunion, osseous lesion (all syndromes) MRI for PIN: denervation edema/atrophy of supinator/extensors; identify lipomas, Schwannomas, synovitis

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Radial tunnel syndrome = a pain diagnosis; PIN syndrome = a motor diagnosis — exam distinguishes them BR + ECRL preserved → PIN palsy (not high radial); wrist extends with radial deviation Saturday night palsy almost always recovers — resist early surgery unless open fracture or penetrating injury Radial tunnel surgery without a confident diagnosis has high failure rates — exhaust non-operative care Wartenberg’s and de Quervain’s coexist in up to 50% — evaluate for both when either is suspected Reinnervation order after proximal radial injury: BR → ECRL → ECRB → EDC → ECU → EDQ → APL → EPL → EPB → EIP

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › PIN Syndrome
text: Non-operative if no EDX denervation: activity modification, therapy, serial EDX monitoring Operative if progressive weakness or EMG denervation: full PIN decompression through supinator including distal exit; release arcade of Frohse + distal fibrous edge 3-month rule : if no improvement at 3 months → proceed to decompression (85% good/excellent outcomes); ages > 50 do poorly — consider concomitant tendon transfer (Ochi) Spontaneous PIN recovery is rare; early intervention > conservative treatment

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Radial Tunnel Syndrome
text: Non-operative first : activity modification, elbow flexion + supination splinting, nerve glides, stretching; steroid injection (Sarhadi: 64% long-term relief) Operative (failed 3-6 months): extensile anterolateral approach; release radial nerve through radial tunnel, ligate Leash of Henry, release arcade of Frohse; do not over-dissect SRN beyond tunnel Outcomes: 67-92% success in systematic review; worse with concurrent lateral epicondylitis or workers’ comp Diagnostic pearl : localize tenderness precisely — epicondyle vs 2+ cm distal. A diagnostic lidocaine injection into the radial tunnel that relieves symptoms is the most helpful confirmatory test (warn the patient about transient finger/thumb drop)

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: References
text: Arnold WD, et al. Prognosis of acute compressive radial neuropathy. Muscle Nerve. 2012;45:893-895. Wolf JM, et al. Radial tunnel syndrome: review and best evidence. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2023;31(15):813-819. Hashizume H, et al. Non-traumatic paralysis of the posterior interosseous nerve. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 1996;78:771-776. Lanzetta M, Foucher G. Entrapment of the SRN (Wartenberg’s syndrome). Int Orthop. 1993;17(6):342-345.

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Saturday Night Palsy (Non-operative)
text: Observation: 89-94% spontaneous recovery (begins avg 2.4 weeks; complete by avg 3.4 months) Cock-up wrist splint + dynamic outriggers; maintain ROM with therapy/nerve gliding Surgery only if no clinical/EDX recovery by 12 weeks (atraumatic) or 3-6 months (traumatic) Open humeral shaft fractures with radial palsy → early nerve exploration (lower spontaneous recovery rate ~85%)

title: Radial Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Wartenberg’s Syndrome
text: Non-operative : desensitization therapy, nerve gliding, remove compressive straps/watches; NSAIDS, rest Operative (failed 3-6 months): longitudinal incision 6-8 cm proximal to radial styloid; release brachioradialis over SRN + overlying fascia; passive wrist manipulation to identify additional compression Outcomes: 71% improve non-operatively; surgical success ~75-86%

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Cubital tunnel borders : medial epicondyle (anterior), olecranon (posterior), Osborne’s ligament/FCU aponeurosis (roof), MCL posterior/transverse bands (floor) Cubital tunnel CSA decreases 40% at 135° elbow flexion; intraneural pressure increases 45% at 120° 5 compression sites at elbow: arcade of Struthers (5.7 cm proximal) → medial head triceps → Osborne’s ligament → between FCU heads → intermuscular ligament FCU-FDS Guyon’s canal : 3 zones (Gross & Gelberman 1985) Zone I : motor + sensory (ganglion, thrombosis, mass) Zone II : motor only (hook of hamate fracture, ganglion) Zone III : sensory only Nerve hypermobility at elbow: present in 37% of asymptomatic individuals — not automatic indication for transposition DCU branches 7 cm proximal to wrist → dorso-ulnar sensation affected at elbow level but spared with wrist-level compression

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient with ulnar neuropathy has numbness of the small finger and ulnar ring finger volarly but intact dorsoulnar hand sensation. Where is the compression? — A: Guyon’s canal (wrist level); the dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises 7 cm proximal to the wrist and is spared in wrist-level compression. Q: After cubital tunnel release, a patient has new pain along the medial forearm without ulnar distribution symptoms. What is the most likely cause? — A: MABC neuroma — the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve branches cross the surgical field and are injured in 73% of revision cases (Mackinnon). Q: A patient with cubital tunnel syndrome has a normal EDX study. Does this rule out the diagnosis? — A: No; 26% of patients with clinical cubital tunnel have no electrodiagnostic evidence (Kortlever). Up to 80% of the motor neuron pool can be lost before clinical detection due to compensatory motor unit enlargement. Q: What physical exam finding distinguishes a Zone II Guyon’s canal lesion from a Zone I lesion? — A: Zone II is motor-only — patient has intrinsic weakness/clawing but preserved sensation; Zone I involves both motor and sensory fibers. Q: Four RCTs comparing simple decompression vs anterior transposition for cubital tunnel syndrome showed what? — A: No significant difference in outcomes between techniques; simple decompression is preferred as the most cost-effective approach.

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Song (39 pts) : improved pinch (7.0→8.3), SWM, DASH (30.4→19.8), MHQ (55.5→70.7) at 12 mo Subjective scores plateau at 3 mo; objective improvement continues > 12 mo (Giladi) 4 RCTs : no difference between simple decompression and transposition Excellent results 45-57% regardless of technique; simple decompression most cost-effective Trend: transposition declining (67%→16%), in situ rising (~80%) Revision rate: 1.4-19%; predictors: trauma history (OR 7.1), McGowan I (OR 3.2), workers’ comp MABC neuroma in 73% of revision failures; perineural fibrosis in 68% McGowan I patients = OR 3.2 for failure (often other causes: cervical, polyneuropathy, TOS)

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: AAEM criteria; conduction velocity (demyelination) → CMAP amplitude reduction (axonal loss = later) Reduced CMAP at FDI predicts preoperative weakness (Power 2019) 26% with clinical cubital tunnel have no EDX evidence (Kortlever) — diagnosis can be clinical Up to 80% motor neuron pool can be lost with near-normal muscle function (single motor units enlarge 5x to compensate)

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Duchenne sign : ring/small clawing (weak lumbricals/interossei + unopposed extrinsic flexors) Wartenberg sign : small finger abduction (paralyzed 3rd volar interosseous + unopposed EDM) Froment sign : thumb IP flexion with lateral pinch (lost adductor pollicis → compensatory FPL) Nerve stability: “stable” (stays in groove) vs “perching” vs “dislocating” with flexion Elbow flexion-compression test (Novak): highly reliable Scratch collapse test : variable accuracy; ethyl chloride can unmask secondary sites 2PD: abnormal only in severe compression Barrera: For 2PD I always test in order: thumb, index, middle, ring, small. Compare ulnar to radial side of ring finger — that’s your median-ulnar watershed.

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Guyon’s Canal (Ulnar Neuropathy at Wrist)
text: Ganglion = most common cause ; also hook of hamate fracture (Zone II), ulnar artery thrombosis Spares dorsoulnar hand (DCU branches proximal to wrist) Allen test to evaluate ulnar artery patency Non-operative: activity modification, gel-padded gloves; no evidence for splinting/steroids Surgical: open Guyon canal, decompress deep motor branch around hook of hamate; release distal antebrachial fascia proximal to wrist crease

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › History
text: Pain + paresthesia in ulnar distribution (volar/dorsal small + ulnar ring finger) Worse with elbow flexion: sleep, resting on elbow, driving, phone use Advanced: intrinsic weakness, cramping, atrophy

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: US : increased CSA correlates with severity; detects some cases EDX misses (Beekman: 18.5%) MRI : discriminates focal compression + space-occupying lesions

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Medial Epicondylectomy
text: Removes perching prominence; preserves vascularity Risk: medial elbow pain (0-52%), MCL injury, flexion contracture (0-17%)

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Mild/early: activity modification, avoid prolonged flexion Night splinting: rigid orthosis or soft towel block in antecubital fossa x 3-4 weeks

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Operative — Endoscopic In Situ
text: 2-4 cm incision; endoscopic blade divides fascia 10 cm proximal + distal Check for subluxation after release Outcomes equivalent to open (Aldekhayel meta-analysis: 79.8% vs 81.8%)

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Operative — In Situ Decompression (Preferred for Most Cases)
text: 3-6 cm incision between olecranon and medial epicondyle Preserve MABC branches (neuroma in 73% of revision failures — Mackinnon) Release cubital tunnel retinaculum + deep brachial fascia (8 cm proximal) + FCU aponeurosis distally Do NOT dissect circumferentially → causes instability Check stability post-release: perching → evaluate triceps fascia; subluxation → stabilizing flap or transposition

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Operative — Transposition
text: Subcutaneous : excise medial intermuscular septum (proximal AND distal); sling/adipofascial flap to prevent fall-back; preserve FCU motor branches Submuscular : most protected, well-vascularized; often used for revision; Z-lengthen flexor-pronator origin Intramuscular: theoretically straighter; risk of scarring within muscle

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Incorrect diagnosis = critical complication — r/o C8-T1 radiculopathy, thoracic outlet, polyneuropathy before surgery McGowan grade I patients have highest failure rate — low threshold for additional workup Dorso-ulnar sensation affected → compression at elbow (not wrist) 37% nerve hypermobility is normal — don’t transpose for hypermobility alone; 79% do transpose for true subluxation Average 2.2 compression sites missed at revision (Gabel) — complete release from arcade of Struthers through FCU MABC injury during initial surgery → most common source of post-op pain; careful identification + preservation is essential Simple in situ decompression is now the dominant approach — supported by 4 RCTs showing no inferiority to transposition

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: References
text: Power HA, et al. Classifying severity of cubital tunnel syndrome with EDX. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2022;150(1):115e-126e. Mackinnon SE, Novak CB. Neurosurgery. 2005;56(3):522-530.

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Workup › Severity Classification
text: McGowan/Dellon with EDX integration (Power 2022) Clinical exam doesn’t correlate linearly with axonal loss

title: Ulnar Nerve Compression
heading: Treatment › Supercharge AIN-to-Ulnar Motor (SETS)
text: Indication: severe compression, reduced CMAP, spontaneous activity on FDI/ADM EMG, normal PQ EMG Distal forearm incision; AIN harvested at PQ; epineurial window in ulnar motor fascicle ~9 cm proximal to wrist crease Doherty : 73% achieved M3 intrinsic strength Xie RCT : 13% greater pinch strength + lower DASH at 2 yr vs transposition alone Treatment algorithm : injections are not part of cubital tunnel management. Stepwise approach: activity modification → night splinting → surgical decompression. Default to simple in situ release unless nerve subluxes post-decompression.

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Anatomy
text: APL (often multiple slips) + EPB; EPB in separate subcompartment 35-45% Radial sensory nerve branches lie superficial to retinaculum

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Basic Science
text: Tendinosis = chronic degenerative change; pulley/sheath thickening → size mismatch → restricted gliding Often gradual onset preceded by increased activity/use; no clear causal work-tendinopathy link established May coexist with RA, crystalline arthropathy, autoimmune disease

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient has a de Quervain’s injection that fails. What anatomic variant should be suspected, and how is it identified intraoperatively? — A: Separate EPB subcompartment (present 35-45%); must be identified and released as a separate compartment during surgery. Q: What is the Vaughan-Jackson syndrome, and in what direction do ruptures progress? — A: Attritional extensor tendon ruptures from DRUJ arthritis/subluxation, progressing ulnar to radial (EDQ → EDC small → ring → middle). Q: During open A1 pulley release for thumb trigger finger, what structure is at highest risk of iatrogenic injury? — A: The radial digital nerve, which crosses the A1 pulley from ulnar to radial. Q: How much of the A2 pulley can be safely released in conjunction with A1 release for trigger finger? — A: Up to 50% of the proximal A2; beyond that risks bowstringing and requires pulley reconstruction. Q: A patient with RA presents with progressive inability to extend the small and ring fingers. What diagnosis should be considered, and what is the underlying mechanism? — A: Vaughan-Jackson syndrome — attritional rupture of EDQ then EDC tendons from DRUJ synovitis/dorsal ulnar head subluxation.

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Complications
text: Radial sensory nerve injury (usually neuropraxic), incomplete release (missed EPB subcompartment), volar tendon subluxation, painful neuroma

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: ECU Tendinopathy / Instability (6th Compartment)
text: Two categories: tenosynovitis vs instability/subluxation (can coexist) Painful snapping with supination ; pain with resisted ulnar deviation in pronation ECU synergy test : differentiates from intra-articular pathology Subsheath tears may accompany TFCC tears Nonoperative: rest, splint, CSI; instability → pronation + radial deviation splint × 4 weeks Surgical: subsheath release (no instability) or retinacular flap reconstruction (with instability)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: EPL Tenosynovitis / Rupture (3rd Compartment)
text: Extremely rare except in RA or after non-displaced DRF (attritional from ischemia + hematoma at Lister’s tubercle) Prodrome: pain over Lister + triggering on thumb extension Rupture → loss of thumb IP extension + retropulsion Prophylactic decompression if impending; EIP-to-EPL transfer after rupture

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: FCR Tendinitis
text: FCR in fibro-osseous tunnel adjacent to trapezium; associated with STT arthritis , thumb CMC arthritis, CPPD Tenderness at FCR before trapezial entry = highly indicative Nonoperative: NSAIDs, splint, CSI (caution: may weaken tendon → rupture) Surgical: FCR decompression; doesn’t address concomitant STT or CMC pathology Gabel: 90% excellent relief at 44 months

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: FCU Tendinitis / Calcific Tendinitis
text: Repetitive overuse (golfers, racquet sports); ulnar-sided volar forearm pain Calcific tendinitis : rare; FCU most affected — dramatic presentation mimics infection; oblique XR shows pathognomonic calcium Calcific FCU tendinitis is self-limited

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Intersection Syndrome (2nd Compartment)
text: 1st + 2nd compartment tendons cross ~7 cm proximal to wrist Classic in rowers ; swelling + crepitus over dorsal radial distal forearm Nonoperative usually successful : rest, NSAIDs, splint (15-30° wrist extension), CSI at intersection site Surgery rare: retinacular release of 2nd compartment

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger) › Non-operative
text: Oral NSAIDs alone NOT effective Orthosis: 47-93% success (no consensus on design) CSI: 60-90% long-term relief in up to 3 injections; worst outcomes with DM, prolonged/severe duration Complications: skin depigmentation, fat necrosis, tendon weakening, elevated blood glucose in DM Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lidocaine, ~1 mL total volume for trigger finger A1 pulley injection.

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger) › Operative (Open A1 Release — Gold Standard)
text: Protect NV bundles; thumb: radial digital nerve crosses A1 ulnar → radial (HIGH iatrogenic injury risk) Release superficial palmar aponeurosis if residual triggering Percutaneous: long + ring fingers best candidates (safest NV anatomy) A1 + up to 50% proximal A2 release safe biomechanically; > 50% A2 → pulley reconstruction Near-perfect outcomes with open release; minimal recurrence

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: De Quervain’s is the most common UE tendinopathy — always search for EPB subcompartment Incomplete de Quervain’s release = missed EPB subcompartment Vaughan-Jackson: ulnar-to-radial attritional ruptures from DRUJ pathology — think RA Thumb A1 release: radial digital nerve at highest iatrogenic risk Trigger finger: A1 + partial A2 release safe; > 50% A2 requires reconstruction FCR tendinitis often masks underlying STT arthritis Calcific FCU tendinitis is self-limited — aggressive surgery not needed

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: References
text: Scheller A, et al. Long-term results of surgical release for de Quervain’s. Int Orthop. Wolfe SW. Tendinopathies. Green’s Operative Hand Surgery, 7th ed. Gabel G, et al. FCR tendinitis: surgical treatment outcomes. J Hand Surg Am. Cooper HJ, et al. 4th compartment tenosynovitis. J Hand Surg Am.

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: 4th Compartment (EDC + EIP)
text: More common in RA/inflammatory arthropathy Tuck sign : tenosynovitis mass catches in retinaculum during excursion EIP syndrome : distal muscle belly trapped in retinaculum → triggering with active index extension Vaughan-Jackson syndrome : DRUJ arthritis → attritional ruptures ulnar → radial (EDQ → EDC small → ring…)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Treatment
text: Non-operative: - Forearm-based thumb spica × 4-6 weeks - CSI: 70-100% efficacy (high failure rate if EPB subcompartment or triggering) - Splinting alone doesn’t add to injection success Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lidocaine (never Depo-Medrol). For de Quervain’s, approximately 2 mL total volume into the first dorsal compartment. Surgical: - Longitudinal incision; protect radial sensory nerve branches - Complete retinacular division along midline or slightly dorsal (minimize volar subluxation) - Always search for and release EPB subcompartment - 100% resolution at 16-year follow-up (Scheller, 100 patients)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Workup
text: Most common in caregivers of young children + repetitive radial/ulnar deviation Risk factors: pregnancy, age > 40, female, Black race Finkelstein’s test : pain with active radial → ulnar deviation while grasping flexed thumb EPB entrapment test : thumb MCP extension vs palmar abduction — if extension MORE painful → suggests separate EPB subcompartment

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger) › Workup
text: Prevalence up to 3% general, higher in diabetics; thumb + ring most common; middle-aged females A1 pulley enlarges up to 3× normal + intratendinous nodule Associated: CTS, de Quervain’s, Dupuytren’s, RA 4-grade classification : I (pre-triggering) → II (active, self-reduced) → III (passive reduction) → IV (fixed PIP contracture)

title: Wound Management
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: A 45-year-old presents with a clean laceration over the dorsal hand sustained 36 hours ago. What is the most appropriate management? — A: Primary closure; clean wounds can be closed regardless of time since injury. Q: What is the advantage of buried absorbable dermal sutures over transcutaneous sutures for hand wound closure? — A: No skin puncture holes for bacterial entry; no suture removal required; lower risk of staphylococcal pustules. Q: A patient with a volar thumb soft tissue avulsion has exposed distal phalanx. What non-surgical management can achieve complete healing? — A: Daily shower, Vaseline, and Coban dressing; secondary healing with myofibroblast contraction covers exposed bone over ~10 weeks if tissues kept moist. Q: What irrigant is recommended for contaminated open hand wounds? — A: Tap water; no difference in infection rates compared to saline, and it is more practical/cost-effective. Q: What is the primary disadvantage of secondary healing for large volar finger wounds? — A: Scar band contracture at flexion creases inhibiting IP extension.

title: Wound Management
heading: Classification
text: Open wound : exposed raw tissues from disrupted skin cover Closed wound : skin cover restored (e.g., sutured) Clean wound : all exposed tissues alive, no eschar/debris/smell; can be closed Contaminated wound : dead tissue, pus, foreign debris, or bad smell; cannot be closed until converted to clean Subcategories: acute vs chronic, with vs without dead tissue

title: Wound Management
heading: Treatment › Closed Wound Management (Showering)
text: 30 years of evidence: early showering at 24 hours does NOT increase infection — may actually decrease it Instructions: shower next day, hand elevated and quiet, water/mild soap OK, don’t rub wound, apply light clean dressing 3-4 days

title: Wound Management
heading: Treatment › Contaminated Wound Management
text: Sharply excise all dead tissue; irrigate copiously WALANT in procedure room for most debridements — no delay for OR/sedation Tap water = saline for irrigation (no difference in infection rates); tap water preferred for cost Home wound care: daily shower rinse, clean dressing with thick layer of Vaseline Vaseline keeps raw tissues alive (dermis, muscle, bone, tendon) by preventing desiccation; healing wound pushes out remaining Vaseline Barrera: Skip Esmarch exsanguination for infection cases — go straight to tourniquet inflate. Contaminated tissue + milking pressure = proximal spread risk.

title: Wound Management
heading: Treatment › Exposed Raw Tissues
text: Old belief: exposed joint/tendon/bone always needs flap Current : if tissues are alive AND kept moist (Vaseline or VAC), granulation tissue covers all exposed live tissues — skin graft or flap may not be required Critical rule : never let raw live tissues dry, even for a few hours

title: Wound Management
heading: Management Options for Large Open Finger Wounds
text: Option Advantages Disadvantages Secondary healing Avoids further surgery, scarring, cold intolerance, numbness from flap dissection Prolonged healing (weeks), volar crease scar contracture Skin graft (FTSG) Faster healing Donor scar, numb, less abrasion-resistant, may need later revision Flap coverage Avoids contracture on flexor side, fastest return to healed wound Dissection damages skin/fat/nerve/vessels, additional scarring Discuss all three options with patient when all are reasonable

title: Wound Management
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Clean vs contaminated is THE decision point — not time since injury Buried absorbable sutures eliminate suture removal and reduce infection Tap water irrigation is evidence-based and cost-effective Vaseline is the key dressing adjunct for open wounds — prevents desiccation of exposed structures Secondary healing with daily Vaseline + Coban can cover exposed bone/tendon without flap Never leave raw tissue “open to air” — even a few hours causes desiccation necrosis Patient reliability is essential for conservative wound management

title: Wound Management
heading: Treatment › Timing of Closure
text: Old dogma: close within 12-24 hours Current evidence: cleanliness matters more than timing — routinely close wounds open >24 hours if clean Plastic surgeons close chronic open clean wounds with imported flaps regardless of duration

title: Wound Management
heading: Treatment › Transcutaneous vs Buried Sutures
text: Transcutaneous sutures create 2 holes through skin into fat; bacteria enter via holes; cheese-wired dead fat feeds infection; result = staphylococcal pustules at entry points Buried dermal sutures (simple interrupted, absorbable) preferred : no skin holes, no suture removal needed Used routinely for carpal tunnel, trigger finger closure Barrera: CTR postop: dressing off day 5, partial weight-bearing 5 lb, follow-up 10-14 days.

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Pulp: glabrous skin with dense fibrous septae compartmentalizing fat over distal phalanx (P3) Nail unit: germinal matrix (proximal, produces nail), sterile matrix (distal, adherence), eponychium, hyponychium Vascular supply: proper digital arteries → terminal branches at P3 tuft Sensory: proper digital nerves → terminal branches; no large neuromas form at fingertip (distal to PDN branching) P3 tuft fracture nonunion rate: 55% (Da Cruz) Sagittal anatomy of the nail unit: germinal matrix (proximal, under the dorsal nail fold), sterile matrix (distal), eponychium, hyponychium, lunula, and the dorsal/ventral roots over P3. Sagittal anatomy of the nail unit: germinal matrix (proximal, under the dorsal nail fold), sterile matrix (distal), eponychium, hyponychium, lunula, and the dorsal/ventral roots over P3.

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: What is the nonunion rate for tuft fractures of P3? — A: 55%; most are asymptomatic and do not require revision. Q: A patient has a 2 cm volar oblique fingertip amputation of the long finger with exposed bone. What is the workhorse flap? — A: Antegrade homodigital proper digital artery (PDA) flap. Q: What type of skin graft is appropriate for fingertip coverage? — A: Full-thickness skin graft only; STSG cannot withstand fingertip shear forces. Donor site: ulnar palm. Q: After nail bed repair, what prevents split nail deformity from synechiae between germinal matrix and dorsal nail fold? — A: Foil stent (from suture packet) placed beneath the dorsal nail fold.

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Nail deformity : up to 39% with P3 fracture; hook nail from sterile matrix/tuft mismatch Tuft nonunion : 55% of tuft fractures; often asymptomatic; allow 3-4 months before revision Infection : 1-6% baseline; >24h delay with heavy contamination increases risk Hyperesthesia 19-27%, hypoesthesia 24-40%, cold sensitivity 25-73% — time + desensitization (no procedural intervention) Sensibility: directly innervated flaps static 2PD 3.5-4.7 mm; reinnervated junctures 6.3-11 mm TAM: pedicle flaps average 235°

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Map all wounds (glabrous + matrix); trace perfusion pathways to each flap Predict long-term viability

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Workup › History
text: Mechanism: crush (most common) vs sharp vs avulsion (reflexive withdrawal = longitudinal NV injury) Smoking/nicotine, DM, vascular disease — predict marginal necrosis Contamination + delay → consider staged treatment

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Plain radiographs: soft tissue thickness over bone, fracture characterization Acoustic Doppler: evaluate arterial network for flap planning

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Pure crush, no fracture, no open wound : reassurance, pain control, daily active DIP motion, pinch as tolerated; no splint needed Subungual hematoma : no percentage threshold demands nail removal if dorsal cortex intact + nail plate not avulsed Sharp laceration, clean edges, no bone exposure, <15 mm : non-surgical reasonable; average healing 27 days Semi-occlusive moisturizing dressings changed weekly Barrera: Secondary healing with a moist dressing — Vaseline (or bacitracin) under Coban, changed daily — is my default for fingertip injuries and partial amputations, unless there’s a specific operative indication. Patients avoid unnecessary surgery and do better than you’d expect. Hand them Lalonde’s PRS-GO 2022 article (it has the words and the videos) and tell them exactly when to quit: red is raw, pink is healed. Lalonde Secondary-Healing Protocol Lalonde DH, Bouhtiauy J. Secondary healing of fingertip amputations: simple wound care advice for patients. PRS-GO 2022;10:e4020. Open-access full text with patient videos : https://journals.lww.com/prsgo/fulltext/2022/01000/secondary_healing_of_fingertip_amputations__simple.26.aspx Principle: raw tissue kept moist will heal. Skin, fat, nerve, and blood vessels are pulled over the exposed bone/tendon by wound contracture as the defect shrinks closed over 4–8 weeks — no surgery required. Daily instructions for the patient: Shower with a naked finger — don’t aim the nozzle at the tip (it hurts); just let water, with or without soap,

title: Fingertip Injuries
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Soft tissue repair: - Debride devitalized tissue; fit remaining pieces like a puzzle - Small openings (<10 mm wide, 5 mm deep) heal by secondary intention - Matrix repair: identify oblique cleavage planes; foil stent from suture packet in dorsal nail fold to prevent synechiae (split nail) - Sutures: 5-0/6-0 chromic (glabrous), 6-0/7-0 (matrix) Tuft (P3) management: - Options: allow natural position, reduce + pin (0.028” K-wires), or excise - Keep dorsal cortex level to support matrix + nail plate - Distal small fragments embed in scar, typically asymptomatic by ~2 months Numerous small comminuted fragments around the rim of the distal tuft. These typically become embedded in scar and are eventually asymptomatic — no fixation needed. Numerous small comminuted fragments around the rim of the distal tuft. title: Digital Replantation
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Dorsal venous system = dominant digital outflow Dominant (larger) digital arteries : ulnar in thumb/index/middle; radial in ring/small (0.3-0.4 mm larger) Digital artery is dorsal to digital nerve in the finger (reverses in the palm)

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Post-op / Rehab › Anticoagulation
text: No consensus in the literature. Common regimens range from ASA alone to IV heparin gtt for every patient. Practical pattern : Lovenox prophylactic dose while in-house (DVT ppx, not therapeutic) + ASA 81 mg daily × 2 weeks for all IV heparin gtt only if high-risk : known thrombophilia, prior DVT/PE, intraop thrombosis or revision, heavy vein-graft reconstruction, marginal Doppler signal entering recovery Barrera: Anticoagulation (no literature consensus; this is my practice) — Lovenox prophylactic dose in-house + ASA 81 mg PO daily × 2 weeks. Add an IV heparin gtt only if high-risk (thrombophilia, h/o DVT/PE, intraop thrombosis or anastomotic revision).

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Treatment › Arterial Repair Pearls
text: Signs of vascular injury: red line sign (ecchymosis), measles/paprika sign (vasa vasorum ruptures), ribbon/pigtail sign (intimal fractures from traction) Debride back to normal intima; flush with heparinized saline (10,000 U/100 mL) Back-wall first technique : less torsion/manipulation than 0-180° Suture: 9-0 to 11-0 nylon

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Treatment › Artery-Only Fingertip Replantation (Tamai I)
text: Venous anastomosis often impossible distally Alternative outflow: surface bleeding (fish-mouth incisions, nail plate removal), medicinal leeches , pulp reduction Systematic review: 76% survival surface bleeding; 68% leeching 5-10 days for neovascularization; transfusion typically 1+ units (up to 10)

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: Which digital artery is dominant in the thumb? — A: Ulnar digital artery (also dominant in index and middle). Q: What is the single strongest relative contraindication for replantation of an isolated finger? — A: Single digit amputation in Tamai zone II (FDS insertion to DIP) due to tendon adhesions and poor functional outcome. Q: What organism must be covered prophylactically during medicinal leech therapy? — A: Aeromonas hydrophila; treat with ciprofloxacin or 3rd-generation cephalosporin. Q: What are the signs of intimal arterial injury seen under the microscope during replantation? — A: Red line sign (ecchymosis along artery), measles/paprika sign (vasa vasorum ruptures), ribbon/pigtail sign (coiling from traction with intimal fractures). Q: A digit is replanted with arterial repair only (Tamai zone I). What is the expected survival rate with surface bleeding techniques? — A: 76%.

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Overall survival >90% in published series; sharp 91.5%; crush/avulsion 66-68% US average: 5 cases/hospital/year; success as low as 29% at low-volume centers Cold intolerance : 40-100%, near-universal Secondary surgery : 40-60%; most common early = wound healing; late = tenolysis + bony procedures Sensibility: static 2PD 10-12 mm; fingertip replant <7 mm (near-normal) TAM: 129-192° (45-56% of contralateral); Zone I best, Zone II worst Only 50% return to same occupation; 30% don’t return to work at all

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Indications & Contraindications
text: Indications : multiple digits, thumb (any level), wrist/hand amputation, pediatric, single digit zone I Relative contraindications : life-threatening injuries, crush/avulsion, multilevel, single digit zone II (adhesions, poor function), prolonged ischemia, noncompliance Ischemia limits : digits ~12h warm (longer reported); hand/forearm 4-6h warm or 10h cold (muscle necrosis)

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Post-op / Rehab › Leeching Protocol
text: Hirudo medicinalis : bite wound bleeds 3-4 hours (hirudin = antithrombin) Apply every 3-4 hours; 7-10 days for proximal amputations Aeromonas hydrophila in leech saliva — prophylactic ciprofloxacin or 3rd-gen cephalosporin

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Classification › Mechanism
text: Sharp : minimal surrounding damage; best prognosis Crush : bone comminution + bilateral tissue destruction Avulsion : longitudinal NV injury; soft tissue avulsed proximal to fracture; worst prognosis

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Treatment › Multiple Digit Priority
text: Thumb → ulnar digits → radial digits (thumb + small = tip pinch + grasp)

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Treatment › Nerve Repair
text: Primary repair often possible after bone shortening Avoid conduits in replantation (complex soft tissue → extrusion risk) Avoid nerve autograft (donor morbidity if digit fails) Allograft excellent if needed Distal fingertip: nerve repair often not possible AND not required (spontaneous neurotization) Barrera: OR sequence: antibiotics → tourniquet → prep/drape → local → Esmarch + inflate. Max 2 hours per tourniquet run, 20-minute break between; save tourniquet time for the microsurgical portion

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Treatment › Operative Sequence
text: Back-bench prep : start as soon as the part is in the room — before the patient is positioned. Identify and tag arteries, nerves, dorsal veins; debride bone ends; pre-pass K-wires. Parallel time is the cheapest way to shorten ischemia. Skeletal fixation : shorten up to 1 cm; save joints; trans-articular = primary arthrodesis. K-wires or 90-90 interosseous wiring are the workhorses; reserve screws for fracture patterns where they are easy and fast. Flexor tendon repair : modified Kessler core + horizontal mattress epitendinous in the replant setting (gentler on traumatized tendon than a circumferential cruciate) Extensor tendon repair Arteries — may deflate tourniquet here for orientation if needed Nerves Dorsal vein(s) last Barrera: Start back-bench prep on the amputated part as soon as it’s in the OR — before the patient is even in the room. Identify and tag arteries, nerves, dorsal veins under the scope while the patient-side team is positioning and prepping. Parallel time is the cheapest way to compress ischemia. Barrera: Replant intraop sequence — bone (K-wires or 90-90; screws only if the pattern is easy — don’t burn time) → flexor (modified Kessler + horizontal mattress, not cruciate) → extensor → arteries (deflate tourniquet here if needed) → nerves → dorsal vein last. Arteries before nerves before veins.

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Start back-bench prep before the patient is in the room — parallel time is the cheapest ischemia reduction Bone fixation = K-wires or 90-90 IOW; screws only when the pattern makes them fast Flexor repair in the replant setting: modified Kessler + horizontal mattress (not cruciate) — kinder to crushed tendon Intraop sequence: bone → flexor → extensor → arteries → nerves → vein last Red line, measles, and ribbon signs identify extent of vascular injury intraop Reverse vein grafts; distal anastomosis first Avoid circumferential wrap — expose fingertips for monitoring Volume matters: high-volume centers significantly outperform low-volume Post-op monitoring q1h × 24h → q2h × 24h → q4h until discharge — state to floor explicitly so it doesn’t drift to q4h neuro checks Anticoagulation: Lovenox ppx in-house + ASA 81 × 2 weeks for all; IV heparin gtt only for high-risk Cold intolerance is near-universal — counsel patients preop

title: Digital Replantation
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Color + Doppler q1h × 24h → q2h × 24h → q4h until discharge Warming 3-5+ days; bed rest day 1, slow mobilization Arterial loss early → OR immediately (likely technical error) Venous congestion more common postop; controlled bleeding/leeches; revision less likely to succeed Barrera: Flap-check schedule: q1h × 24h, then q2h × 24h, then q4h until discharge. State this explicitly to the floor nurse — without it, the order tends to drift to standard q4h neuro checks and you lose the early-window catch.

heading: Treatment › Vein Grafts
