title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Prehension requires at least 2 painless digits — one movable to grasp + one stable post to pinch (Moran + Berger) 7 prehensile maneuvers: terminal pinch, subterminal pinch, key pinch, directional grip, hook grip, power grasp, span grasp Thumb = 40% of hand function — preserve length first 2nd + 3rd CMC immobile (center of hand); 4th + 5th CMC mobile (palmar arch) Median injury: affects thumb sensation/power, fine motor; ulnar injury: finger intrinsics for object handling

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: What minimum hand function is required for effective prehension? — A: At least 2 painless digits — one movable for grasp and one stable post for pinch. Q: According to the FLOW study, what irrigation method produces the lowest infection rate in open fractures? — A: Normal saline at gravity (low) pressure with no additives. Q: What is the expected grip and pinch strength loss after single ray resection? — A: 20% loss of both grip and pinch strength, regardless of which ray is resected. Q: A patient has a painful neuroma after transradial amputation. What procedure has the lowest rate of symptomatic neuroma recurrence? — A: Regenerative Peripheral Nerve Interface (RPNI) — 0% symptomatic neuromas vs 13% with traction neurectomy. Q: What digit SpO2 value rules out significant vascular injury? — A: SpO2 >95% rules out vascular injury; <84% requires vascular repair.

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: ~75-80% survival; half the strength + motion of unaffected side 94% of severe hand injuries have ≥1 PTSD/ASD sign within 2 months First web space contracture highly limiting → 4-flap Z-plasty (60° most effective) Tenolysis only after passive ROM achieved + active ROM plateaued; wait 3+ months through thick scar

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Treatment › Debridement
text: Organized superficial → deep; sharp excision (scalpel/scissors, NOT scraping/washing) Excise skin/SC until brisk red bleeding at edge Senior surgeon required, NOT delegated to junior

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Amputations › Decision to Amputate
text: Immediate amputation when 4 of 6 systems injured (bone, joint, skin, tendon, nerve, vessel) Injury scoring systems (MESS) NOT validated for upper extremity Patient communication critical — Bastidas demonstrated litigation correlation

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Treatment › Fasciotomies
text: Indicated when dysvascular >6 hours OR crush with significant swelling Hand: interossei via dorsal 2nd + 4th MC incisions; volar thenar + hypothenar; open carpal tunnel Forearm: avoid midline (median nerve coverage challenge)

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Amputations › Finger Amputations
text: PIP-level or proximal phalanx loss = loss of extrinsic flexor power FDS tenodesis to remaining proximal phalanx : enhances MCP flexion + preserves grip strength (82° MCP, 70% grip) Thumb IP amputation: FPL + EPL tenodesis to proximal phalanx Don’t suture flexor + extensor together (depowers tendons)

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Treatment › Irrigation (FLOW Study)
text: Saline + gravity pressure = lowest infection rate No additives (soaps/antiseptics increase tissue necrosis) No high-pressure lavage (drives bacteria deeper) Barrera: Skip Esmarch if infection or tumor — go straight to tourniquet inflate. For mangled extremity cases, save tourniquet time for the microsurgical portion

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Amputations › Neuroma Management
text: Traction neurectomy = standard TMR : transfer transected nerve to motor branch of healthy muscle; 14/15 pain resolution RPNI : thin free muscle graft + nerve insertion; 0% symptomatic neuromas vs 13% traction ; phantom limb pain 51% vs 91%; technically easier than TMR

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Abx within 60 minutes (cephalosporin); delay increases infection rate Stabilize fractures + splint in ED Regional blocks: delay until NV exam by operating surgeon complete No decrease in infection at 8 vs 24h debridement — senior hand surgeon + consistent OR team preferred over rushing

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: ATLS first — life before limb, always Gravity-pressure saline irrigation without additives (FLOW study) Senior surgeon debrides — this is not a junior task Insensate hand has minimal functional value; discuss with patient early RPNI is emerging as superior to traction neurectomy for neuroma prevention Heterotopic replantation: most functional digit → most functional position First web space contracture is a devastating complication — plan coverage early Forearm can be shortened 2 cm without significant rotational loss

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Perfusion Assessment
text: SpO2 >95% rules out vascular injury; <84% requires vascular repair for salvage; in-between = explore Direct pressure for bleeding control preferred over tourniquet; avoid blind clamping/cautery

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Amputations › Ray Resection
text: For amputation at base of P1 or MCP; 3rd or 4th ray closes potential space 20% loss of grip + pinch strength regardless of border vs central Better with early resection (within 14 days)

heading: Treatment › Spare Parts Surgery
text: Fillet flap from non-replantable finger Heterotopic replantation : place most functional digit in most functional position Salvage index finger stump for future pollicization

title: Mangled Hand + Amputations
heading: Treatment › Structure-Specific Management
text: Bone/Joints: - Skeletal fixation first (efficient, not complex); shortening ~1 cm phalanges/MCs tolerated - Forearm shortening up to 2 cm well-tolerated; supination decreases >2 cm, pronation >4 cm - External fixation for severe contamination, multifocal, or speed Perfusion: - Temporary shunts: carotid shunts (heparinized) or trimmed pediatric feeding tubes - Vein grafts: similar caliber, reverse for valve direction , mark direction Nerves: - Insensate digit/hand = minimal value — salvage may be wasted - Repair: debride to healthy fascicles, tension-free, vascularized bed - In blast: zone of injury not immediately apparent — delay nerve resection/grafting ~2 weeks - Nerve tubes inferior; autograft gold standard for mixed nerves Soft Tissue: - Replace like with like; reconstructive elevator > ladder - Reverse radial forearm flap : workhorse for dorsal hand defects - NPWT temporizes but is NOT definitive coverage; decreased infection 5x (prospective RCT)

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Random pattern flaps : subdermal plexus perfusion; length-to-width ratio ≤ 2:1 Axial pattern flaps : named vessel; can mobilize on pedicle; each artery terminates in angiosome; choke arteries + oscillating veins connect adjacent angiosomes Cutaneous (groin), fasciocutaneous (radial forearm), myocutaneous types

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: What is the maximum length-to-width ratio for a random pattern flap? — A: 2:1. Q: A 30-year-old has a 1.2 cm volar thumb tip defect with exposed bone. What is the most appropriate local axial flap? — A: Moberg advancement flap (bi-pedicled, covers distal thumb defects up to 1.5 cm with sensate coverage). Q: What percentage of length gain does a 60° Z-plasty provide? — A: 75% (4-flap Z-plasty at 60° provides 150%). Q: What must be confirmed before elevating a reverse radial forearm flap? — A: Allen test confirming a patent, complete superficial palmar arch for ulnar-dominant hand perfusion.

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Classification — Reconstructive Ladder
text: Primary closure → 2. Delayed primary closure → 3. Skin grafting → 4. Local cutaneous flaps → 5. Fasciocutaneous flaps → 6. Local/distant pedicled flaps → 7. Free tissue transfer

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Arterial insufficiency : pallor, poor refill; check for kinks; if failed → delay flap for choke vessel dilation; ICG angiography to verify Venous congestion : brisk bleeding, firm veins, blue/swelling; severe → free transfer or supercharging Monitoring: clinical judgment + trained nursing remains best

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Forearm-Based Pedicled Flaps
text: Reverse Radial Forearm Flap (RRFF) : - Based on retrograde palmar arch flow; Allen test mandatory - Major perforator cluster 2 cm proximal to radial styloid - Workhorse for dorsal hand defects - Disadvantages: radial artery sacrifice, donor scarring, exposed flexor tendons - RAPF (perforator flap) alternative preserves radial artery Posterior Interosseous Artery (PIA) Flap : no radial sacrifice; designed on line from lateral epicondyle to ulnar styloid; 7-14 perforators; venous congestion is known risk Groin Flap (Smith 1972) : based on SCIA; 2-stage distant pedicled for degloving trauma; divide pedicle at 3 weeks ; defatting in 85%; PE risk >age 50 from prolonged immobilization Always confirm Allen test before any flap that sacrifices the radial artery

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Local Axial Flaps
text: Moberg (bi-pedicled) : distal thumb defects up to 1.5 cm ; both NV bundles preserved; modification = transverse incision at MCP base + V-Y closure to avoid IP contracture Homodigital PDA flaps : Allen test required first; design 4-5 mm larger; preserve thick adipofascial pedicle tissue; PIP flexion contracture risk First Dorsal Metacarpal Artery (FDMA/Kite/Foucher) : dorsal/volar thumb + 1st web space; FDMA = branch of radial artery distal to EPL in snuffbox; 75% runs above FDI; harvest with FDI fascia to ensure FDMA inclusion; preop Doppler to confirm course Reverse DMA (Quaba) : based on distal perforator 0.5-1 cm proximal to MCP; covers defects beyond PIP; don’t skeletonize perforator HTA Flap (Teoh) : lateral skin from adjacent digit; preserves digital nerve + pulp at donor; single-stage; 2PD 3-5 mm; 100% survival in 40-flap series For first web space contractures, 4-flap Z-plasty at 60° is the most effective release — 150% length gain. If severe, plan for coverage with groin flap, reverse radial forearm, or free flap rather than serial Z-plasties.

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Local Random Flaps
text: Indications : areas with skin elasticity + redundancy (dorsum of hand); defects ≤ 2-3.5 cm² Contraindications : gross contamination, infection, significant surrounding tissue damage V-Y Advancement (Atasoy) : distal fingertip defects; ~1 cm advancement; disadvantages = volar pulp scars, decreased sensation Rotation flap : curvilinear around pivot; best for triangular defects; arc = 4x width of defect ; most frequent mistake = too small → tension → ischemia Z-Plasty : contracture release (NOT open wounds); 60° = 75% length gain ; 4-flap Z-plasty = 150% gain — best for first web space contractures Rhomboid (Limberg) : 60°/120° angles; best for dorsal hand defects

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Design flaps 10% larger than defect — tight insetting = ischemia Rotation flap most common error: too small Z-plasty is for contracture release only, never primary wound closure Allen test before any flap that uses or sacrifices the radial or ulnar artery FDMA flap: harvest with FDI fascia — 25% of the time FDMA runs within the muscle Thenar flap: avoid in elderly or patients with arthritis (PIP contracture) Groin flap in patients >50: DVT/PE risk from prolonged immobilization

title: Local + Regional Flaps for Hand Reconstruction

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Most common cause of UE soft tissue defects: trauma Vital structures superficial in UE → commonly exposed Goal: preserve/restore function , not just wound healing Reconstructive elevator (Gottlieb + Krieger) > ladder: choose the most appropriate option, even if more complex

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: According to Godina’s landmark study, what are the infection and flap failure rates when free tissue transfer is performed within 72 hours of injury? — A: 1.5% infection, <1% flap failure. Q: What flap provides the best long-term tendon gliding for coverage over the dorsal hand? — A: Fasciocutaneous flap (e.g., ALT) — better flexibility and gliding than muscle flaps, and easier to re-elevate for secondary reconstruction. Q: What is the maximum amount of fibula that can be harvested as a vascularized free flap? — A: Up to 30 cm; must preserve 6-7 cm of distal fibula for ankle stability. Q: What is the workhorse free flap for functional muscle transfer to restore finger flexion? — A: Gracilis — minimal donor morbidity, 10 cm excursion, can include a skin paddle for monitoring.

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Vascular thrombosis <5% in experienced centers — most devastating complication Inset critical: no tension/compression on pedicle; “comfortable” pedicle course Muscle flaps: continuous implantable Doppler monitoring recommended (hard to assess clinically) Fasciocutaneous: pencil Doppler + clinical exam typically sufficient

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Indications
text: Exposed functional structures (tendon, bone, nerve, vessels, hardware) Prevent contracture over joints with large defects Tissue to allow tendon glide for future tenolysis Poor intrinsic healing (radiation, chronic infection) Free flap specifically when local options unavailable or create more morbidity

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Key Free Flaps
text: ALT (Anterolateral Thigh) — workhorse for large thin coverage: - Pedicle: LCFA descending branch (8-12 cm, 2-2.5 mm) - Up to 15 x 40 cm; primary closure ≤8 cm width - Flow-through option for combined vascular reconstruction - 84% musculocutaneous perforators (intramuscular dissection required) Lateral Arm : thin, pliable; can be innervated (lower lateral brachial cutaneous nerve); very short pedicle Radial Forearm (free) : thin, pliable, long pedicle (10-15 cm); sacrifices radial artery; visible donor scar; can include LABC nerve for sensate flap Scapular/Parascapular : can be osteocutaneous; chimeric with latissimus or serratus on subscapular system; short pedicle, requires lateral positioning Groin/SCIP : historically first free flap; short narrow pedicle; technically challenging thin elevation Latissimus Dorsi : largest single muscle; pedicle = thoracodorsal (6-8 cm, 2-2.5 mm; up to 12 cm if dissected to subscapular); chimeric with serratus ± scapular bone ± ribs Gracilis : minimal donor morbidity; functional muscle transfer for elbow/finger flexion (10 cm excursion); short pedicle (5-6 cm); thin-walled vessels easily damaged by traction Vascularized Fibula : up to 30 cm bone; pedicle = peroneal artery (5-6 cm, 2.5 mm); preserve 6-7 cm fibula distally for ankle stability MFC/Trochlea Flap : pedicle = DGA (7-9 cm, 1.5 mm); corticoperiosteal, corticocancellous, or osteocartilaginous; best for nonunions throughout body; limited to bone defects <5 cm

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Muscle vs Fasciocutaneous Selection
text: Muscle Fasciocutaneous Infection No clinical difference (despite animal 10x bacterial control) Same Contour Thinner after atrophy Difficult to contour primarily Tendon glide Adheres to bed → may restrict Better long-term flexibility Re-elevation Difficult Easier for secondary reconstruction Best use Complex cavitary wounds Over joints/tendons needing glide

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Elevator > ladder in the upper extremity — function, not just wound healing Godina: <72 hours = best outcomes (1.5% infection, <1% failure) ALT is the workhorse for large defects; gracilis for functional muscle transfer Fasciocutaneous flaps are preferred over joints/tendons (better glide, easier re-elevation) MFC flap is the go-to for nonunions with small bone defects 15% of patients have incomplete palmar arch — always verify before dividing recipient Don’t use contralateral uninjured forearm as donor (radial forearm free flap)

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Treatment › Recipient Vessels
text: Arteries : brachial (end-to-side OK), antecubital bifurcation (end-to-end), distal ulnar (workhorse), radial in forearm or snuffbox (confirm Allen test) Veins : cephalic (superficial radial), basilic (superficial ulnar), deep comitantes; antecubital fossa has abundance

text: <72 hours : infection 1.5%, flap failure <1% Common practice: reconstruction within 5 days of trauma Optimal timing = once debridement is definitive + no suspicion of deeper contamination

title: Free Tissue Transfer for Upper Extremity
heading: Workup
text: Plain XR essential; CT for complex wrist; angiography rarely needed acutely Clinical exam + surgical exploration usually sufficient for vascular status Timed Allen test important; CT/MR angiography “insufficient” for palmar arch assessment 15% have incomplete superficial palmar arch — dependent on both radial + ulnar Verify perfusion to each digit (clamp + Doppler) before dividing recipient vessel

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Dermal appendages (hair follicles, sweat glands) contain keratinocytes for regeneration — deeper burns destroy these Jackson’s 3 zones : coagulation (irreversible, central), stasis (potentially recoverable), hyperemia (reversible) Burn injury evolves over 24-72 hours Hand: little soft tissue coverage; volar glabrous skin specialized + difficult to replace; dorsal thin skin → tendon/joint exposure risk

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Treatment › Blister Management
text: Don’t routinely unroof intact blisters (biological dressing) Aspirate if tense/painful; debride if ruptured

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: Name the three zones of burn injury (Jackson model) and which is the critical zone for salvage. — A: Zone of coagulation (irreversible), zone of stasis (potentially salvageable — this is the critical zone), zone of hyperemia (reversible). Q: A chemical burn from hydrofluoric acid is treated with water irrigation. What additional treatment is essential and what systemic complication must be monitored? — A: Topical (and potentially IV/IA) calcium gluconate; monitor for systemic hypocalcemia, which can be fatal. Q: What is the critical core temperature threshold before extremity rewarming in frostbite? — A: Core temperature must be >35°C before extremity rewarming to avoid paradoxical core temperature drop. Q: A patient develops extravasation of doxorubicin from a dorsal hand IV. What is the most important early surgical intervention? — A: Gault flush-out technique within 24 hours — saline flush via multiple small incisions; 89% heal without tissue loss. Q: What is the safe position for hand burn splinting? — A: Wrist 20-30° extension, MCPs 70-90° flexion, IPs fully extended, thumb in maximal palmar abduction.

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Workup › Chemical Burns — Exceptions to Water Irrigation
text: Agent Treatment Phenol Polyethylene glycol (insoluble in water) Elemental Na/K/Li Mineral oil (combusts with water) Dry lye Dust off first Hydrofluoric acid High-flow water → topical calcium gluconate; systemic hypocalcemia , potentially fatal White phosphorus UV light to identify particles; hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Classification
text: Degree Findings Treatment 1st (superficial) Erythema, no blisters Moisturize, aloe vera 2nd superficial partial Blisters, very painful, pink dermis Topical dressings; heals 2-3 wk 2nd deep partial Blisters, painful Topical; excise + graft if not healed 2-3 wk 3rd (full) Leathery, white, insensate Tangential excision + grafting 4th Bone/tendon/nerve/joint Debridement ± amputation

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Frostbite › Classification
text: Superficial (1st-2nd) : white plaque/erythema (1st), clear blisters (2nd) — recoverable Deep (3rd-4th) : hemorrhagic blisters (3rd), hard/insensate/mottled (4th) — tissue loss Hemorrhagic blisters = subdermal plexus disruption = worse prognosis

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Workup › Electrical Burns
text: Resistance: nerve > vessel > muscle > skin/tendon > fat/bone Muscle = largest volume → most thermal injury High voltage >1,000 V ; cardiac arrhythmia (monitor); myoglobinuria → renal failure

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Extravasation Injury › 3 Groups
text: Group Mechanism Examples Treatment Osmotic Protein precipitation K, Ca, contrast Gault flush-out Vasoconstrictive Vessel ischemia Dopamine, NE Phentolamine subq Cytotoxic Direct cell injury Doxorubicin, vinca alkaloids Gault flush-out Gault flush-out within 24h : 89% heal without tissue loss; >24h without flush-out: 52% extensive damage Doxorubicin : cold pack; DMSO topical; dexrazoxane IV within 6h; UV light identifies doxorubicin-laden tissue (reddish-orange fluorescence) Vinca alkaloids : heat (not cold) Recall phenomenon : enhanced necrosis at prior extravasation site with subsequent doxorubicin

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Treatment › Hand Therapy
text: Splint in safe position : wrist 20-30° extension, MCP 70-90° flexion, IP fully extended, thumb max palmar abduction ROM + pressure garments + silicone sheeting Prevention of contracture > correction

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Jackson’s zone of stasis is the critical zone — can be salvaged or lost depending on resuscitation Chemical burns: know the water irrigation exceptions (phenol, alkali metals, dry lye, HF acid) HF acid causes systemic hypocalcemia — can be fatal; needs calcium gluconate Frostbite: core rewarm first, rapid extremity rewarm second; tPA is a game-changer Doxorubicin extravasation: Gault flush-out within 24 hours is the critical window Sheet grafts only for hand burns — mesh grafts produce unacceptable cosmesis

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: References
text: Kowalske KJ, et al. Hand burns. In: ASSH Handthology. Twomey JA, et al. Thrombolysis as an adjunct to the management of frostbite injuries. J Vasc Interv Radiol 2005. Gault DT. Extravasation injuries. Br J Plast Surg 1993. Jackson DM. The diagnosis of the depth of burning. Br J Surg 1953.

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Treatment › Surgical
text: Escharotomy (circumferential constriction): - Forearm: axial along radial + ulnar borders, extend to MCP - Hand: intermetacarpal spaces (avoid extensor exposure) - Digit: midaxial at glabrous/nonglabrous junction Fasciotomy : Δ pressure <30 mm Hg or absolute >30 mm Hg; hand = 2 dorsal (2nd + 4th web), thenar + hypothenar Tangential excision : Weck blade/Goulian knife; endpoint = capillary bleeding Skin grafting : sheet grafting for hand (no mesh for cosmesis); intermediate-thick to thick (0.012+ inch) for less contracture; glabrous donor = foot instep Z-plasty for contracture : 30° = 25%, 60° = 50%, 90° = 75% length gain; 4-flap + 5-flap for web space deepening Barrera: Skip Esmarch exsanguination for burn cases with concern for active infection or tumor. Escharotomy of insensate full-thickness eschar does not require anesthesia — this is a bedside procedure

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Treatment › Topical Agents
text: Silver sulfadiazine : painless, broad-spectrum; can cause leukopenia Mafenide acetate (Sulfamylon) : good eschar penetration; painful; metabolic acidosis risk Mepilex Ag / Acticoat / Aquacel Ag : decreased dressing changes

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Treatment

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Frostbite › Treatment
text: Core temp >35°C before extremity rewarming (avoid paradoxical drop) Rapid rewarming 40-42°C x 15-30 min (hydrotherapy) Oral ibuprofen + topical aloe vera (thromboxane inhibitors) Intra-arterial tPA : 80%+ salvage — greatest advance in frostbite care Avoid early debridement — wait for clear demarcation (3-4 weeks dry gangrene) Tc-99m bone scan: non-uptake → amputation; normal → heal

title: Burns — Thermal / Electrical / Chemical + Frostbite + Extravasation
heading: Workup
text: ABC for major burns; BSA via rule of nines (palm ≈ 1% BSA; entire UE ≈ 9%) 15-20% BSA = physiologic/metabolic effects; inhalational injury = common cause of mortality Circumferential burns → escharotomy if vascular compromise Tetanus prophylaxis

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: FDS : dual origin (medial epicondyle + proximal radius); median nerve; dual blood supply (radial + ulnar arteries) FDP : IO membrane + volar ulna; ulnar artery; dual innervation — ulnar nerve (small + ring), AIN (middle + index) FPL : IO membrane + distal radius; AIN; radial artery dominant Linburg-Comstock anomaly : tendinous connection FDP-index to FPL — 31% unilateral, 16% bilateral; must recognize during exploration Carpal tunnel arrangement: FDP deepest (coronal), FPL most radial, FDS index + small deep to ring + middle Pulley system : 5 annular (A1-A5), 3 cruciate (C1-C3); A2 + A4 = critical (skeletally based); thumb equivalent = oblique pulley Vincula at cruciate pulley level — preserve during repair Healing: intrinsic pathway (epitenon → restores gliding, desired) vs extrinsic pathway (synovial sheath → adhesions)

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Biomechanical Principles
text: Strand count > caliber : 4-0 eight-strand beats 3-0 four-strand by 43% Optimal purchase: 7-10 mm; locks/grasps ≥ 2 mm Gap > 3 mm detrimental to strength accrual Suture: nylon/Supramid preferred for zone I/II; FiberWire too rigid, Ethibond too extendable

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient sustains a Zone I FDP avulsion that retracts to the palm with no bony fragment. What is the Leddy-Packer type, and what is the critical timing concern? — A: Type I; must repair urgently as vincular blood supply is disrupted by retraction past the lumbrical origin. Q: During zone II flexor tendon repair, how many core suture strands are recommended, and what gap threshold is considered detrimental? — A: ≥ 4 strands; gap > 3 mm impairs strength accrual. Q: A 4-0 eight-strand repair is compared to a 3-0 four-strand repair. Which is stronger, and by how much? — A: The 4-0 eight-strand is 43% stronger — strand count is more critical than suture caliber. Q: What is the most important intraoperative check after completing a zone II flexor tendon repair? — A: Digital extension-flexion test — confirm no gap on extension and no impingement on flexion through the pulley system. Q: Which two annular pulleys must be preserved to prevent bowstringing, and what is the maximum total length of pulley that can be safely vented? — A: A2 and A4; up to 2 cm total venting on the palmar aspect is safe.

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Classification
text: Kleinert-Verdan Zones: Zone Anatomy I Distal to FDS insertion (FDP only) II A1 to FDS insertion (“no man’s land”); Tang subzones IIa-IId III Distal TCL to proximal A1 (high NV injury rate) IV Within carpal tunnel V Forearm proximal to CT Thumb: T1-T4 mirror finger zones Leddy-Packer (Zone I FDP avulsions): I = retraction to palm; II = retraction to PIP; III = bony fragment at A4

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Dy systematic review: 6% reoperation, 4% rupture, 4% adhesions Tenolysis for limited active motion despite full passive — wait ≥ 3-6 months Re-rupture → re-repair if early; otherwise two-stage reconstruction > 3 weeks delayed : usually two-stage reconstruction needed

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Loss of resting cascade, absent tenodesis effect → laceration Test FPL, FDS, FDP independently; FDS to small absent ~6% NV exam first (2PD, Semmes-Weinstein, Doppler) US : 83% sens / 85% spec for high-grade zone II partial lacerations 50% rule for partials: < 50% trim edges only; > 50% repair

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Workup › History
text: Ideal repair within 7 days ; hand dominance, mechanism, position at injury Emergency only if digital blood supply compromised

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Operative — By Zone
text: Zone I: - ≥ 1 cm distal stump → direct core + epitendinous repair - < 1 cm stump → direct end-to-end with 10-12 strands of 4-0 nylon (Tang shift away from pullout button) - Bony avulsion fragment → screw, IO wire, or suture Zone II (most variable outcomes): - Standard: ≥ 4-strand repair with 3-0/4-0 braided nonabsorbable + epitendinous - M-Tang 6-strand with sparse peripheral sutures becoming preferred globally - Pulley venting ≤ 2 cm total, palmar cut — no significant bowstringing - Digital extension-flexion test intraop: no gap on extension, no impingement on flexion - FDS repair debated; only FDP in zone IIc (narrowest sheath) Zones III-V: better outcomes; mandatory NV exam; larger gauge sutures FPL: often retracts into carpal tunnel/forearm; 87% good/excellent with 6-strand M-Tang + pulley vents Barrera: OR setup sequence — antibiotics → tourniquet placed → prep/drape → local → Esmarch + inflate. Skip Esmarch exsanguination in tumor or infection cases; elevate only.

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: FDS to small finger absent in ~6% — always test individually Linburg-Comstock can cause unexpected FPL retraction when exploring FDP-index Zone IIc is the narrowest sheath — repair FDP only Gap > 3 mm at repair = detrimental; always check with intraop extension-flexion test Children: repair when possible; 4-week immobilization if non-compliant; 96% excellent outcomes (Sikora) Strand count matters more than suture caliber

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Early active motion preferred — Trumble RCT: place-and-hold > passive (156° vs 128° TAM) Nantong protocol (Tang): - Start day 4-5; 4-6 sessions/day × 15-20 min - 10+ passive ROM cycles → 40-60 runs active flexion to half/two-thirds initial range - Half a fist; avoid extreme flexion; out-of-splint motion OK - Week 3-4: aim full active ROM - Splint: wrist neutral/slight flexion, MCP ~30° flexion Starr systematic review: active = more ruptures (5% vs 4%) BUT better ROM (6% vs 9% stiffness) WALANT: enables intraop active motion check; patient sees repair → better compliance

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: References
text: Tang JB. Recent developments in flexor tendon repair. Hand Clin. (Nantong protocol, M-Tang technique) Trumble TE, et al. RCT: place-and-hold active motion vs passive flexion. J Hand Surg Am. Dy CJ, et al. Complications after flexor tendon repair: systematic review. J Hand Surg Am. Starr HM, et al. Flexor tendon repair rehabilitation: systematic review. Hand. Leddy JP, Packer JW. Avulsion of the profundus tendon insertion. J Hand Surg Am.

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A Boyes grade III patient with joint damage and decreased ROM — is this a single-stage or two-stage reconstruction candidate? — A: Two-stage; single-stage requires Boyes grade I (good tissue, mobile joints, minimal scar). Q: During single-stage flexor tendon reconstruction, should the graft be secured distally or proximally first, and why? — A: Distal first — easier finger wound closure before the digit is flexed by proximal tensioning. Q: What complication results from a flexor tendon graft that is tensioned too tight? — A: Quadriga — the tight graft limits excursion of all FDPs (shared muscle belly), reducing adjacent digit flexion. Q: What is the ideal time window for tenolysis after flexor tendon reconstruction? — A: ≥ 3 months and ≤ 1 year post-healing, once the patient has plateaued in therapy with full passive but limited active motion.

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Classification
text: Boyes Preoperative Classification: Grade Condition Implication I Good — minimal scar, mobile joints Single-stage candidate II Notable scar, mild contracture Likely two-stage III Joint damage, decreased ROM Two-stage IV Nerve damage Two-stage V Multiple systems (II+III+IV) Two-stage

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Tendon rupture ~7% PIP motion loss: ~30% lose ≥ 30° Need for tenolysis after reconstruction: 12-47% Quadriga : graft too tight / distal adhesions → all FDPs limited (single muscle belly) Paradoxical extension : graft too loose → lumbricals drive IP extension DIP/PIP flexion deformity (8-55°) nearly universal Wide-awake tensioning helps avoid Quadriga and paradoxical extension

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Workup › History
text: Prior repair details, timing, mechanism, hand dominance, functional demands Document TAM, TAF, TAE, DPC (active + passive) TAM “normal” = 260° (MCP included) or 175° (PIP + DIP only) Assess digital cascade with wrist flex/ext

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: XR for arthritis, fracture, deformity MRI/US with caution — pseudotendon can be misread as intact tendon

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Operative — Single-Stage Reconstruction
text: Indications: Intact flexor sheath + pulley system, flexible digit, failed primary repair or delayed presentation Both FDS + FDP injured → reconstruct FDP only Intact FDS + functional PIP → reconstructing FDP may do more harm (except young high-demand 10-21 yo) Pass graft via pediatric feeding tube or tendon passer Distal fixation : direct suture to remnant preferred (Tang: 10-12 strands 4-0 nylon); alternatives = pullout button, bone tunnel, screw, suture anchor Proximal : Pulvertaft weave (≥ 2-3 weaves + cross-stitching) in palm or distal forearm Secure distal first → easier wound closure before flexion Tensioning : restore digital cascade; slightly tighter (stretches over time); gradually more flexion index → small

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Operative — Two-Stage Reconstruction (Hunter)
text: Indications: Substantial sheath disruption, severe trauma/crush, failed primary repair or grafting Stage 1: - Silicone rod implant (4 mm typical) creates pseudosheath (mesothelial cell-lined) - Anchor distally to ≥ 1 cm FDP remnant if possible - Therapy: wound healing, reduce inflammation, minimal motion (excess → synovitis) - Infection rate ~15% Stage 2 (8-16 wk, later preferable): - Pull rod from distal end → pass tendon graft through pseudosheath - Slight extra tension for anticipated loosening - Pulvertaft weave proximally Modified Paneva-Holevich (preferred by some): - Stage 1: rod placed + FDS/FDP sutured as loop in palm - Stage 2: rod removed, pedicled FDS flap used as graft — no additional donor tendon needed; one side already healed WALANT preferred for flexor tendon reconstruction — enables intraop active motion assessment, real-time tensioning, and patient education Barrera: For tumor or infection cases, skip Esmarch exsanguination — elevate only.

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Patient Selection
text: ≥ 1 uncompromised digital nerve required Contraindications : NV impairment, intractable flexion contractures, noncompliance Preoperative aggressive therapy program — improves motion AND tests compliance Discuss alternatives: arthrodesis, amputation, transfer, tenodesis, no surgery

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Hierarchy: primary repair > tenolysis > single-stage graft > two-stage (final attempt) Intact FDS with functional PIP — think twice before reconstructing FDP in low-demand patients Preserve ≥ 3 pulleys for single-stage; A2 + A4 most important Modified Paneva-Holevich avoids a separate donor tendon harvest Children: wait until ≥ 6 yo; avoid bone tunnels (physis); modified Paneva-Holevich preferred

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Pulley Reconstruction
text: Indications: Severe bowstringing, multiple pulley injury, flexion lag; full passive motion via therapy first Reconstruct A2 + A4 minimum (± A3) Best graft material : extensor retinaculum (pre-existing synovial gliding surface) Harvest proximal to Lister’s tubercle (more robust) A2 reconstruction: graft under extensor tendon; A4: graft over conjoined extensor Techniques: Bunnell (1 wrap), Lister (least resistance), Karev belt-loop (strongest but decreases ROM) Avoid bone drill holes (phalangeal fracture risk) Postop: external pulley ring bolster × 4-6 weeks

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: References
text: Hunter JM. Staged flexor tendon reconstruction. J Hand Surg Am. Tang JB. Distal fixation techniques in flexor tendon reconstruction. Hand Clin. El-Shebly AA, et al. Pulley reconstruction with extensor retinaculum. J Hand Surg. Boyes JH. Flexor tendon grafting in the fingers and thumb. JBJS.

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Tendon Graft Options
text: Graft Type Absent % Length Palmaris longus Extrasynovial 25% 16 cm Plantaris Extrasynovial 19% 35 cm EDL 2nd toe Extrasynovial < 1% 35 cm FDL 2nd toe Intrasynovial < 1% 12 cm Intrasynovial biologically superior (fewer adhesions) but clinical evidence not definitive Palmaris + plantaris most common (minimal donor morbidity) Suitable graft found in 80-85% of patients

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Tenolysis
text: Best ≥ 3 months and ≤ 1 year post-healing Prerequisite: full passive but limited active motion; therapy plateau Wide-awake surgery preferred (real-time active motion assessment) Results: 50-70° TAM improvement in 80% of patients; 20% no gain or loss Start therapy within first few days postop — most motion achieved in first week

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Extrinsic extensors form dorsal hood at MCP with sagittal bands to volar plate; centralize tendon + extend P1 Long extensor trifurcates distal to P1 → central slip (→ middle phalanx) + 2 lateral slips Lateral bands (intrinsic + lateral slips) → terminal tendon → distal phalanx Triangular ligament prevents dorsal subluxation of lateral bands; transverse retinacular ligament prevents dorsal migration at PIP ORL : present < 50%; most often ulnar side ring finger Prime MCP flexors = intrinsics (tendons volar to MCP axis, dorsal to PIP/DIP axes) Grip strength markedly decreased with extensor paralysis Quadriga concept : finger extensors function as single muscle unit — basis for relative motion splinting Wrist Compartments: # Contents Pearl 1 APL + EPB EPB separate subcompartment 35-45% 2 ECRL + ECRB 3 EPL Angles around Lister’s tubercle 4 EDC + EIP EIP deepest, shortest belly 5 EDM Usually bifid 6 ECU Always in separate subsheath EDC to small finger absent < 50% (junctura tendinum substitutes) Extensor digitorum brevis manus : aberrant muscle (PIN innervation); may be sole index extensor — do NOT excise Thumb: EPL = primary central extensor; no lumbricals/interossei; APB (radial) + adductor (ulnar) → dorsal aponeurosis → IP extension

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient presents with a painful, stiff PIP joint after a dorsal laceration over the proximal phalanx. On exam, passive DIP flexion is more difficult with PIP extended than flexed. What does this indicate? — A: Boutonniere deformity (positive Boyes test) — lateral band dorsal subluxation tethers the terminal tendon with PIP extension. Q: A 30-year-old presents 2 weeks after a closed sagittal band rupture with extensor subluxation at the middle finger MCP. What is the best initial treatment? — A: Relative motion extension splint for 6 weeks — acute splinting within 3 weeks has a 95% success rate. Q: After non-displaced distal radius fracture, a patient develops inability to extend the thumb IP joint. What is the diagnosis and optimal treatment? — A: Attritional EPL rupture at Lister’s tubercle; EIP-to-EPL tendon transfer. Q: On exam, a patient has difficulty with passive PIP flexion when the MCP is extended, but PIP flexion improves with MCP flexed. Is this intrinsic or extrinsic tightness? — A: Intrinsic tightness (positive Bunnell test); extrinsic tightness shows the opposite pattern. Q: A bony mallet fracture involves 40% of the articular surface with no DIP subluxation. What is the recommended treatment? — A: DIP extension splint 24/7 for 6-8 weeks — even large bony fragments respond to splinting when the joint remains congruent.

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Classification
text: Finger Zones (odd = joint, even = bone): Zone Location Key Structure I DIP Terminal extensor III PIP Central slip V MCP Sagittal bands VII Retinaculum Synovial sheath Thumb: TI (IP) through TV (retinaculum)

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: MCP extension contracture from prolonged splinting (most common) Bunnell test (intrinsic tightness): MCP extended → passive PIP flexion difficult vs Extrinsic tightness : MCP flexed → PIP flexion harder Tenolysis: wait ≥ 4 months; therapy must be at plateau Wong systematic review (zones IV-VII): TAM relative motion 205-236° vs dynamic 191-214° vs static 79-202°

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Odd zones = joints, even zones = bone segments — easy mnemonic Modified Elson test is the best diagnostic for central slip injury Mallet: splinting works even for large bony fragments without DIP subluxation Sagittal band: splint within 3 weeks = 95% success; delay drops to ~50% Fight bite at zone V — always explore for joint penetration; septic joint develops quickly Extensor digitorum brevis manus is NOT pathology — do not excise Bunnell vs extrinsic tightness test: opposite patterns of MCP-dependent PIP flexion

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: References
text: Doyle JR. Extensor tendons — acute injuries. Operative Hand Surgery (Green’s). Peelman JN, et al. Sagittal band injuries treated with splinting. J Hand Surg Am. Wong AL, et al. Rehabilitation of extensor tendon injuries zones IV-VII: systematic review. Hand. Ishiguro T, et al. Extension block pinning for mallet fractures. J Hand Surg Br. Curtis RM. Capsulectomy of the interphalangeal joints. J Bone Joint Surg Am.

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone I-II — Mallet Deformity
text: Doyle Classification: I = closed ± avulsion; II = open laceration; III = open + tissue loss; IVa = pediatric physeal; IVb = 20-50% articular; IVc = > 50% + volar subluxation Closed (Type I): - DIP extension splint 24/7 × 6-8 weeks + gradual daytime weaning; leave PIP free - Even large bony fragments respond to splinting alone - Outcomes: 7.6° extensor lag, 12.8% complication rate Bony mallet with DIP subluxation: - Extension block pinning (Ishiguro) : 0.045 K-wire 45° to P2 head as block + second retrograde K-wire across DIP; remove 4-6 weeks Open (Type II/III): 5-0 monofilament tendon repair + K-wire DIP pinning Chronic mallet → swan neck: Fowler tenotomy (divide central extensor at PIP); wait ≥ 6 months; SORL reconstruction or FDS volar PIP tenodesis for fixed deformity

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone III — Central Slip / Boutonniere
text: Initial presentation may be subtle — lateral bands can extend PIP early Modified Elson test : PIP fully flexed against resistance; rigid DIP extension = positive (central slip injury) Acute closed: PIP extension splint 6-8 weeks continuous + active DIP flexion hourly; then part-time 4-6 weeks Acute open: < 50% → wound care + early motion; complete → ORIF with 4-0/5-0 + PIP pinning in extension × 5-6 weeks Chronic boutonniere: - Boyes test : passive DIP flexion harder with PIP extended (vs pseudoboutonniere) - Conservative first — serial casting/splinting → relative motion flexion splint × 3 months - Surgical outcomes unpredictable; worse with PIP fixed flexion, age > 45, prior surgery - Curtis stepwise approach : TRL release → tenolysis → central slip reinforcement

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone V — Sagittal Band Injuries
text: Closed sagittal band rupture: radial side middle/ring most common Acute (< 3 wk): relative motion extension splint × 6 weeks — 95% success (Peelman) 3 wk delay: only ~50% succeed with splinting → surgical repair Fight bite : always evaluate for MCP joint penetration; aggressive I&D + IV antibiotics + delayed closure

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone VI (Dorsum of Hand)
text: Thicker tendons; 3-0 core suture; > 80% good/excellent regardless of postop protocol Loss of MCP flexion = most frequent complication

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone VII-VIII
text: EPL rupture after non-displaced DRF → EIP-to-EPL transfer (optimal) Zone VIII: don’t wait > 4 weeks — muscle contracture becomes permanent Relative motion splinting is increasingly preferred for zones V-VI — leverages the quadriga concept, keeping the injured tendon in relative extension while permitting near-normal hand function and therapy

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Anatomy
text: APL (often multiple slips) + EPB; EPB in separate subcompartment 35-45% Radial sensory nerve branches lie superficial to retinaculum

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Basic Science
text: Tendinosis = chronic degenerative change; pulley/sheath thickening → size mismatch → restricted gliding Often gradual onset preceded by increased activity/use; no clear causal work-tendinopathy link established May coexist with RA, crystalline arthropathy, autoimmune disease

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient has a de Quervain’s injection that fails. What anatomic variant should be suspected, and how is it identified intraoperatively? — A: Separate EPB subcompartment (present 35-45%); must be identified and released as a separate compartment during surgery. Q: What is the Vaughan-Jackson syndrome, and in what direction do ruptures progress? — A: Attritional extensor tendon ruptures from DRUJ arthritis/subluxation, progressing ulnar to radial (EDQ → EDC small → ring → middle). Q: During open A1 pulley release for thumb trigger finger, what structure is at highest risk of iatrogenic injury? — A: The radial digital nerve, which crosses the A1 pulley from ulnar to radial. Q: How much of the A2 pulley can be safely released in conjunction with A1 release for trigger finger? — A: Up to 50% of the proximal A2; beyond that risks bowstringing and requires pulley reconstruction. Q: A patient with RA presents with progressive inability to extend the small and ring fingers. What diagnosis should be considered, and what is the underlying mechanism? — A: Vaughan-Jackson syndrome — attritional rupture of EDQ then EDC tendons from DRUJ synovitis/dorsal ulnar head subluxation.

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Complications
text: Radial sensory nerve injury (usually neuropraxic), incomplete release (missed EPB subcompartment), volar tendon subluxation, painful neuroma

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: ECU Tendinopathy / Instability (6th Compartment)
text: Two categories: tenosynovitis vs instability/subluxation (can coexist) Painful snapping with supination ; pain with resisted ulnar deviation in pronation ECU synergy test : differentiates from intra-articular pathology Subsheath tears may accompany TFCC tears Nonoperative: rest, splint, CSI; instability → pronation + radial deviation splint × 4 weeks Surgical: subsheath release (no instability) or retinacular flap reconstruction (with instability)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: EPL Tenosynovitis / Rupture (3rd Compartment)
text: Extremely rare except in RA or after non-displaced DRF (attritional from ischemia + hematoma at Lister’s tubercle) Prodrome: pain over Lister + triggering on thumb extension Rupture → loss of thumb IP extension + retropulsion Prophylactic decompression if impending; EIP-to-EPL transfer after rupture

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: FCR Tendinitis
text: FCR in fibro-osseous tunnel adjacent to trapezium; associated with STT arthritis , thumb CMC arthritis, CPPD Tenderness at FCR before trapezial entry = highly indicative Nonoperative: NSAIDs, splint, CSI (caution: may weaken tendon → rupture) Surgical: FCR decompression; doesn’t address concomitant STT or CMC pathology Gabel: 90% excellent relief at 44 months

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: FCU Tendinitis / Calcific Tendinitis
text: Repetitive overuse (golfers, racquet sports); ulnar-sided volar forearm pain Calcific tendinitis : rare; FCU most affected — dramatic presentation mimics infection; oblique XR shows pathognomonic calcium Calcific FCU tendinitis is self-limited

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Intersection Syndrome (2nd Compartment)
text: 1st + 2nd compartment tendons cross ~7 cm proximal to wrist Classic in rowers ; swelling + crepitus over dorsal radial distal forearm Nonoperative usually successful : rest, NSAIDs, splint (15-30° wrist extension), CSI at intersection site Surgery rare: retinacular release of 2nd compartment

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger) › Non-operative
text: Oral NSAIDs alone NOT effective Orthosis: 47-93% success (no consensus on design) CSI: 60-90% long-term relief in up to 3 injections; worst outcomes with DM, prolonged/severe duration Complications: skin depigmentation, fat necrosis, tendon weakening, elevated blood glucose in DM Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lidocaine, ~1 mL total volume for trigger finger A1 pulley injection.

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger) › Operative (Open A1 Release — Gold Standard)
text: Protect NV bundles; thumb: radial digital nerve crosses A1 ulnar → radial (HIGH iatrogenic injury risk) Release superficial palmar aponeurosis if residual triggering Percutaneous: long + ring fingers best candidates (safest NV anatomy) A1 + up to 50% proximal A2 release safe biomechanically; > 50% A2 → pulley reconstruction Near-perfect outcomes with open release; minimal recurrence

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: De Quervain’s is the most common UE tendinopathy — always search for EPB subcompartment Incomplete de Quervain’s release = missed EPB subcompartment Vaughan-Jackson: ulnar-to-radial attritional ruptures from DRUJ pathology — think RA Thumb A1 release: radial digital nerve at highest iatrogenic risk Trigger finger: A1 + partial A2 release safe; > 50% A2 requires reconstruction FCR tendinitis often masks underlying STT arthritis Calcific FCU tendinitis is self-limited — aggressive surgery not needed

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand

text: Scheller A, et al. Long-term results of surgical release for de Quervain’s. Int Orthop. Wolfe SW. Tendinopathies. Green’s Operative Hand Surgery, 7th ed. Gabel G, et al. FCR tendinitis: surgical treatment outcomes. J Hand Surg Am. Cooper HJ, et al. 4th compartment tenosynovitis. J Hand Surg Am.

heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: 4th Compartment (EDC + EIP)
text: More common in RA/inflammatory arthropathy Tuck sign : tenosynovitis mass catches in retinaculum during excursion EIP syndrome : distal muscle belly trapped in retinaculum → triggering with active index extension Vaughan-Jackson syndrome : DRUJ arthritis → attritional ruptures ulnar → radial (EDQ → EDC small → ring…)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Treatment
text: Non-operative: - Forearm-based thumb spica × 4-6 weeks - CSI: 70-100% efficacy (high failure rate if EPB subcompartment or triggering) - Splinting alone doesn’t add to injection success Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lidocaine (never Depo-Medrol). For de Quervain’s, approximately 2 mL total volume into the first dorsal compartment. Surgical: - Longitudinal incision; protect radial sensory nerve branches - Complete retinacular division along midline or slightly dorsal (minimize volar subluxation) - Always search for and release EPB subcompartment - 100% resolution at 16-year follow-up (Scheller, 100 patients)

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: De Quervain’s Tenosynovitis (1st Compartment) › Workup
text: Most common in caregivers of young children + repetitive radial/ulnar deviation Risk factors: pregnancy, age > 40, female, Black race Finkelstein’s test : pain with active radial → ulnar deviation while grasping flexed thumb EPB entrapment test : thumb MCP extension vs palmar abduction — if extension MORE painful → suggests separate EPB subcompartment

title: Tendinopathies of the Forearm, Wrist, and Hand
heading: Stenosing Tenosynovitis (Trigger Finger) › Workup
text: Prevalence up to 3% general, higher in diabetics; thumb + ring most common; middle-aged females A1 pulley enlarges up to 3× normal + intratendinous nodule Associated: CTS, de Quervain’s, Dupuytren’s, RA 4-grade classification : I (pre-triggering) → II (active, self-reduced) → III (passive reduction) → IV (fixed PIP contracture)

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Benign Tumors › Aneurysmal Bone Cyst
text: 80% in 1st 2 decades; metacarpals + proximal phalanges; USP6 translocation XR: expansile, sclerotic border, bony septae; MRI fluid/fluid levels = classic Marginal curettage + bone graft; high recurrence; cryosurgery/argon beam ↓ recurrence Avoid RT (radiation-induced sarcoma risk)

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Benign Tumors

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Workup › Biopsy
text: Most important step — errors lower when done at definitive treating institution Open biopsy: GA (not regional — tumor spread risk), no exsanguination (elevate 3-5 min), tourniquet 250 mmHg, small longitudinal incision, place where excisable at definitive op Frozen section for non-osseous only — bone needs decalcification (days) Core needle: ~90% accuracy, less contamination; risk = sampling error Barrera: For tumor cases in the OR, skip Esmarch exsanguination — elevate only. Standard sequence: antibiotics → tourniquet placed → prep/drape → local → elevate + inflate (no Esmarch).

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A 35-year-old woman presents with an expansile lytic lesion of the distal radius with cortical thinning. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what imaging workup is required? — A: Giant cell tumor; treat as malignancy with chest CT, bone scan or PET, and local MRI + CT. Q: A patient with multiple enchondromas and soft tissue hemangiomas with phleboliths on X-ray has what syndrome, and what is the risk of malignant transformation? — A: Maffucci’s syndrome; 50-100% malignant transformation risk requiring lifelong surveillance. Q: A 22-year-old presents with a proximal phalanx enchondroma that fractures through the lesion. Should you perform curettage and grafting acutely? — A: No — heal the fracture first, then perform curettage + bone graft. Early treatment during fracture healing increases complication rates. Q: What distinguishes BPOP (Nora’s lesion) from osteochondroma on imaging? — A: BPOP lacks medullary continuity with the underlying bone, whereas osteochondroma has cortical and medullary continuity with native bone. Q: What is the most common primary bone tumor of the carpus, and where does it most often occur? — A: Osteoid osteoma; scaphoid is the most common carpal location.

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Malignant Tumors › Chondrosarcoma — Most Common Hand Malignancy
text: 5th-6th decade; 26% diagnosed > 10 years after onset XR: lytic, cortical destruction, stippled calcification, indistinct borders Radioresistant + chemoresistant → surgery only High-grade → wide en bloc resection / ray amputation Low-grade (atypical cartilaginous tumor): curettage + cryo may preserve function — Meftah: 90.7% recurrence-free at 25 years

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Classification
text: Enneking Staging: Stage Grade Site Mets IA Low (G1) Intracompartmental (T1) M0 IB Low Extracompartmental (T2) M0 IIA High (G2) T1 M0 IIB High T2 M0 III Any Any M1 Surgical Margins: Intralesional (through tumor) → Marginal (reactive zone) → Wide (normal tissue cuff) → Radical (entire compartment)

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Benign Tumors › Enchondroma — Most Common Bone Tumor of Hand
text: 70% of hand bone lesions; proximal phalanx > MC > middle phalanx Asymptomatic; presents with pathologic fracture or incidental finding XR: medullary, sharp sclerotic margins, expansile, punctate calcification Growth after skeletal maturity = malignant transformation concern Solitary → chondrosarcoma: ~1% risk Ollier’s disease (multiple, non-hereditary): ~30% malignant transformation → annual surveillance Maffucci’s syndrome (enchondromas + hemangiomas with phleboliths): 50-100% transformation Treatment: observe if asymptomatic; acute fracture → heal fracture first then curettage + graft Curettage + autograft: 4.5% recurrence; allograft comparable; Ca phosphate cement biomechanically superior

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Malignant Tumors › Ewing’s Sarcoma
text: t(11;22) EWS-FLI-1 fusion; < 1% in hand; 1st-2nd decade Fever, anemia, leukocytosis — misdiagnosed as infection Histology: round cell, PAS-positive (glycogen) Wide excision + neoadjuvant chemo; 5-yr DFS > 70%

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Benign Tumors › Giant Cell Tumor of Bone
text: 3rd-4th decade; 85% after age 20; hand 2%, distal radius 14% (3rd most common GCT site) Distal radius = most common primary site for GCT metastatic to lung Treat as malignancy — chest CT, bone scan/PET, local MRI + CT Campanacci: I (contained) → II (cortical expansion) → III (cortical perforation) Curettage alone: 49-79% recurrence — NOT recommended Adjuvants (PMMA, phenol, cryo, argon, ethanol) ↓ recurrence ≤ 27%; PMMA reduces recurrence 8× Campanacci III → wide excision + reconstruction (vascularized fibula if > 6 cm) Pronator quadratus = volar tumor barrier at distal radius Bisphosphonates + denosumab = potential medical adjuvants

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Workup › History + Exam
text: Pain, growth pattern, occupation, family history Size, mobility, location, firmness; adjacent joint ROM; skin changes, venous engorgement Neuro exam (compression from soft tissue extension); SWM (2.83 = normal); pulses (accentuated → malignancy proximity) Labs: CBC, chemistry, LFTs, UA; SPEP/UPEP for lytic lesions

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Plain XR always — whole bone, joints above + below Cortical breakthrough = malignant or aggressive benign (GCT) 50% cortex destruction → pathologic fracture risk (midshaft loses 90% strength) Local CT: 1 mm cuts (larger cuts miss cortical breakthrough) MRI: soft tissue extension; T2 enhancement (also blood/pus); fat bright on T1 + T2 Staging (if malignancy/GCT suspected): CT chest/abd/pelvis, bone scan or PET

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Malignant Tumors

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Malignant Tumors › Metastatic to Hand
text: Rare; lung > kidney > head/neck (lung > 40%); metacarpals ~50% of hand mets Median survival ≤ 6 months; treatment = pain + function (ray/transverse amputation)

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Benign Tumors › Osteoid Osteoma
text: Only 2% of OO in hand/wrist → frequently missed (avg 13.5 mo diagnostic delay) NSAID-responsive night pain; proximal phalanx most common in hand Most common primary bone tumor of carpus (scaphoid = most common carpal location) CT: pathognomonic round lucent nidus + sclerotic rim (25% missed on plain XR) Excision preferred; RFA suboptimal in hand (NV thermal injury risk) Osteoblastoma = nidus > 1.5 cm, histologically identical

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Malignant Tumors › Osteosarcoma — 2nd Most Common Hand Malignancy
text: Hand cases present later in life; frequently low-grade; better survival than other sites XR: lytic/blastic/mixed; Codman triangle periosteal reaction Wide excision (often amputation) + adjuvant chemo (MTX, doxorubicin, ifosfamide, cisplatin) Tumor necrosis > 90% post-neoadjuvant = favorable

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Benign Tumors › Other Benign
text: Osteochondroma : cortical continuity with native bone (pathognomonic); no malignant degeneration in hand; simple excision. Masada classification for forearm deformity in MHO (I = ulnar OC + shortening; II = radial OC + radial head dislocation; III = distal radius OC) BPOP / Nora’s lesion : no medullary continuity (vs osteochondroma) — key distinguishing feature Fibrous dysplasia : GNAS mutation; ground-glass with sclerotic margins; nonoperative + bisphosphonates Chondroblastoma : epiphyseal, chicken wire calcification; curettage + graft

title: Primary Bone Tumors of the Hand and Wrist
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Enchondroma is the most common hand bone tumor; chondrosarcoma is the most common hand bone malignancy GCT at distal radius: treat as malignancy; curettage alone = unacceptable recurrence; add PMMA Osteoid osteoma: frequently missed in hand — think of it with NSAID-responsive night pain in a young patient BPOP vs osteochondroma: look for medullary continuity (present in OC, absent in BPOP) Biopsy at the treating institution — Mankin showed ↑ complications at referring centers Ray amputation = workhorse for hand sarcomas

Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Benign Tumors

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Biopsy
text: Poor biopsy → amputation; Mankin : 17.3% complication rate, 20% altered subsequent treatment Tourniquet without exsanguination ; longitudinal incision incorporable into definitive resection FNA: high false-negative, cannot evaluate architecture — useful for recurrence only Core needle preferred to FNA; non-diagnostic → repeat or open Excisional biopsy for small superficial finger/hand lesions — must excise to negative margins Barrera: For soft tissue tumor excision in the hand, skip Esmarch exsanguination — elevate only.

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A 40-year-old presents with a firm, painless, slow-growing nodule on the volar aspect of the index finger that is fixed to deeper structures. X-ray shows cortical scalloping of the proximal phalanx. What is the most likely diagnosis? — A: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (GCTTS); the bone erosion, volar digit location, and fixation to deep structures are classic. Q: A patient with NF-1 presents with a rapidly enlarging, painful mass along the ulnar nerve in the forearm. What diagnosis must be ruled out, and what imaging modality helps differentiate? — A: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST); F-18 FDG-PET distinguishes MPNST from benign neurofibroma. Q: What is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of the hand, and what benign condition is it frequently misdiagnosed as? — A: Epithelioid sarcoma; frequently mistaken for infection or inflammatory process due to its slow-growing nodular/ulcerative presentation. Q: A 55-year-old woman has a painful subungual lesion of the ring finger with cold intolerance. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what two exam findings support it? — A: Glomus tumor; Love’s pin test (point tenderness) and Hildreth’s sign (decreased pain with elevation + tourniquet inflation). Q: The landmark Rosenberg 1982 trial demonstrated what equivalence between limb-sparing surgery + radiation and amputation for soft tissue sarcomas? — A: Equivalent overall survival (70% vs 71%); limb salvage had higher local recurrence (19% vs 6%) but preserved functio

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Cutaneous Malignancies
text: SCC : 2nd most common cancer worldwide; 1.9-5.2% lymphatic spread; wide excision or Mohs BCC : excellent prognosis; raised papule + central ulceration ± telangiectasias; UV = greatest risk Melanoma : most aggressive cutaneous; acral lentiginous = 29-61% of hand melanomas ; subungual variant; BRAF testing; sentinel lymph node biopsy; wide excision (1-2 cm margins)

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Tumor-Like Lesions › Epidermal Inclusion Cyst
text: Traumatic implantation of epithelial cells; fingertip in laborers Intraosseous distal phalanx variant may mimic malignancy/infection Marginal excision; ~10% recurrence

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Tumor-Like Lesions › Ganglia — Most Common Hand/Wrist Soft Tissue Tumor
text: 50% of all hand masses; 2nd-4th decade Dorsal wrist 70% (arise from dorsal SL ligament), volar wrist 30% 50-60% dorsal wrist ganglia resolve spontaneously Aspiration: 11-85% recurrence (steroids don’t help) Open excision (dissect stalk + adjacent capsule); arthroscopic: 11% recurrence Female + preop pain → most likely persistent postop pain

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Benign Tumors › Glomus Tumor
text: Nailbed/periungual/pulp; ring finger most common; middle-aged women Classic triad: cold intolerance + pain + focal tenderness Love’s pin test + Hildreth’s sign (decreased pain on elevation + tourniquet) US or MRI confirms; marginal excision

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › History + Exam
text: Painless mass, often long-standing; recent change in size or pain = red flag Large + deep + increasing = best malignancy predictor (Nandra); pain alone not useful Refer all superficial > 5 cm or any deep-seated mass to subspecialist Risk increases with age; dorsal wrist sarcoma may mimic ganglion

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Plain XR always (calcifications, osteophytes, pressure erosion) MRI = best for STS — T1 hypo, T2 hyper; Gd guides biopsy to vascular non-necrotic area Specific MRI diagnosis possible only 24% of the time (Kransdorf) F-18 FDG-PET: metastatic detection, benign vs malignant nerve sheath, neoadjuvant response assessment

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Malignant — Soft Tissue Sarcomas › Key Subtypes
text: Epithelioid sarcoma : slow-growing nodule/ulcer mistaken for infection; hand 75% 5-yr DFS; > 5 cm = 25% survival Synovial sarcoma : t(X;18); children/adolescents; chemo-sensitive ; 30% peripheral calcification; hand 68% 5-yr DFS Clear cell sarcoma : “malignant melanoma of soft parts”; t(12;22) EWS/ATF1; 20% regional lymph node mets AMFS : distal extremities; high local recurrence due to infiltrative margins; RT improves control MPNST : ~50% from NF-1; NF-1 lifetime risk 8-13%; wide excision; 5-yr survival as low as 40%

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Benign Tumors › Lipoma
text: ~50% of all soft tissue tumors; deep UE = 22% May cause nerve compression (CTS from carpal tunnel lipoma, PIN entrapment from parosteal radial lipoma) MRI: isointense to SC fat; marginal excision; ~5% recurrence

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Malignant — Soft Tissue Sarcomas

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Benign Tumors › Neurofibroma
text: Within fascicles → harder to excise than schwannoma 90% sporadic; ~10% NF-1 (cafe au lait, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules) Plexiform nearly exclusive to NF-1; can undergo malignant transformation PET-CT distinguishes MPNST from neurofibroma

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Benign Tumors › Other Benign
text: Nerve lipomatosis (fibrolipomatous hamartoma) : median nerve 85%; simple decompression only; macrodactyly in 1/3 Fibroma of tendon sheath : low MRI signal all sequences; common recurrence in fingers Infantile digital fibromas : pathognomonic intracellular inclusion bodies; 80% in 1st year; may spontaneously regress

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Malignant — Soft Tissue Sarcomas › Overview
text: Epithelioid sarcoma = most common hand STS (23%); synovial sarcoma 15% Most common UE STS overall: undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma > liposarcoma > myxofibrosarcoma > synovial Hematogenous → lung; regional lymph nodes 2-5% (except rhabdo, epithelioid, synovial, clear cell, angiosarcoma) Rosenberg 1982 : resection + RT = amputation for survival (70% vs 71%); ↑ local recurrence with limb salvage (19% vs 6%)

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Ganglion = most common hand mass; ganglia resolve spontaneously 50-60% of the time GCTTS is the 2nd most common hand soft tissue tumor — not a ganglion; check for bone erosion Glomus tumor triad: cold intolerance, pain, focal tenderness — Love’s pin test + Hildreth’s sign Schwannoma: shell out with microscope; target sign on MRI is 100% specific Epithelioid sarcoma = most common hand STS — easily mistaken for infection or ganglion Poor biopsy at a referring institution may force amputation — biopsy at treating center when possible Acral lentiginous melanoma: disproportionately common in hand — always biopsy pigmented subungual lesions

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Benign Tumors › Schwannoma (Neurilemoma)
text: Most frequent benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor; ulnar nerve most common in UE Antoni A (cellular) + B (myxoid) areas; S-100 positive ; true capsule Mobile transverse, not longitudinal; multiple = NF-2 MRI target sign on T2 (specificity 100%, sensitivity 59%) Shell out with microscope ; postop dysfunction 2.5-30%

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Benign Tumors › Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor (GCTTS)
text: 2nd most common hand soft tissue tumor; volar digits most common Painless firm slow-growing nodule fixed to deep structures; may erode bone Al Qattan: Type I (pseudocapsule) vs Type II (non-encapsulated, satellite nodules → higher recurrence) Marginal excision; recurrence 4-44%; ↑ with bone invasion, DIP involvement, tendon/capsule involvement

title: Soft Tissue Tumors of the Hand and Upper Extremity
heading: Malignant — Soft Tissue Sarcomas › Treatment Principles
text: Ray amputation = workhorse for hand STS; Pradhan: 6% local recurrence (ray amp) vs 42% (limb salvage) Preop RT: thicker pseudocapsule, easier NV dissection; lower dose/field/complications than postop Unplanned excisional biopsy: 83% have residual disease — re-excision not associated with adverse outcome (Houdek)

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: SLIL has 3 regions: dorsal (strongest, greatest yield strength), proximal (membranous fibrocartilage), palmar Dorsal SLIL is the primary restraint to translation; dorsal + palmar both resist rotation DCSS (dorsal capsulo-scapholunate septum) — X-shaped crossed fibers linking extrinsic and intrinsic ligaments; critical to the “dorsal SL complex” Tear progression: volar → membranous → dorsal (Mayfield) Dorsal fibers intact → minimal kinematic change; dorsal torn → substantial instability Secondary stabilizers : RSC ligament, scaphocapitate ligament, scaphotrapezial ligaments — attritional failure over time leads to static malalignment End-stage: SLAC arthritis (predictable degenerative pattern: radial styloid → scaphoid fossa → capitolunate → pancarpal)

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: Which portion of the scapholunate interosseous ligament is the strongest and most important for carpal stability? — A: The dorsal portion (greatest yield strength and primary restraint to translation). Q: A patient with a positive Watson scaphoid shift test has an SL angle of 72° on lateral radiograph and no arthritis. What stage of Garcia-Elias classification is this? — A: Stage 4 (complete SL tear, not repairable, reducible rotary subluxation, no arthritis). Q: In the Mayfield progressive perilunar instability model, what is the typical sequence of SLIL tear progression? — A: Volar → membranous → dorsal. Q: What is the SLAC arthrosis degenerative pattern in order of involvement? — A: Radial styloid-scaphoid → scaphoid fossa → capitolunate → pancarpal (radiolunate usually spared). Q: What muscle re-education program is recommended for non-operative management of SL instability? — A: Co-contraction of ECRL, APL, and FCR (dart-thrower’s motion muscles) with inhibition of ECU.

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Classification
text: Geissler arthroscopic grading (I-IV) : I = attenuation/hemorrhage, no midcarpal incongruity; II = slight gap (< probe width); III = probe passes through gap; IV = gross instability, 2.7 mm scope passes through Garcia-Elias staging (1-6) : progression from partial tear with intact dorsal SL → irreducible malalignment → SLAC arthrosis EWAS/IWAS classification (I-V) : pre-dynamic → dynamic → static instability; subdivides stage III into A (volar), B (dorsal), C (complete SLIOL tear, reducible)

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Arthroscopic techniques show excellent early/midterm results vs historical open methods, but no RCTs Open capsulodesis: associated with ROM loss Tendon reconstruction: difficulty balancing tendon length; multiple techniques exist because none is clearly superior Fusions (intercarpal or wrist) eliminate normal kinematics and may lead to adjacent arthrosis

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Watson scaphoid shift test : thumb on scaphoid tuberosity, wrist from ulnar to radial deviation → dorsal clunk with release; painful clunk = pathologic (present in 25-32% of asymptomatic wrists bilaterally) Positive only if dorsal SL ligament is completely disrupted Dorsal pain during the maneuver is of primary importance

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Workup › History
text: Any wrist trauma can cause acute SL injury; high association with distal radius fractures and radial styloid fractures Suspect SL injury when fracture line exits near SL interval

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: PA/lateral + grip views : Terry Thomas sign (SL gap > 3 mm pathologic, > 5 mm definitive), scaphoid ring sign (foreshortened flexed scaphoid), disrupted Gilula’s lines, triangular lunate Lateral : SL angle > 60° = SL dissociation; DISI pattern Carpal height index (proximal lunate → distal capitate / 3rd MC length) quantifies collapse MRI : sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.90 — cannot reliably exclude intrinsic ligament tears Arthroscopy remains gold standard for diagnosis, staging, and treatment planning

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Most SL tears never reach surgical care Garcia-Elias selective muscle re-education: activate ECRL, APL, FCR (SL-friendly muscles); inhibit ECU Dart-thrower’s motion rehabilitation (minimal SL movement through this arc) Best for IWAS stage I; may temporize in some stage II injuries

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Healing potential diminishes with time : acute (best), subacute 3-6 wk (reduced), chronic > 6 wk (minimal primary healing) Treatment by IWAS stage: Stage I : PRP or physical therapy; ADCLR if refractory Stage II (A/B/C) : ADCLR (arthroscopic dorsal capsuloligamentous repair) ± AVCLR if persistent volar instability Stage III : wide ADCLR ± AVCLR Stage IV : wide ADCLR or ligament reconstruction with tendon graft/synthetic bracing Stage V (DISI) : 360° arthroscopic ligamentoplasty or open ligamentoplasty (modified Brunelli), BTB repair K-wire fixation : SL + SC ± LT pins; maintain 6-8 weeks for soft tissue healing Chronic without arthritis : same goal of restoring dorsal SL complex anatomy via ADCLR or reconstruction SLAC wrist (Garcia-Elias stage 6) : salvage — PRC, 4-corner arthrodesis, total wrist arthrodesis

title: Scapholunate Ligament Injuries and Reconstructions
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Dorsal SL complex = SLIL + DCSS + extrinsic ligaments — all must be addressed for stable repair Always check for secondary stabilizer insufficiency (RSC, scaphocapitate ligaments) Watson test has high false-positive rate — correlate with pain and asymmetry Grip views and dynamic fluoroscopy can unmask dynamic instability missed on static films SL angle > 60° on lateral is the key radiographic finding When multiple reconstruction options exist and none is clearly superior, it means the problem is unsolved

heading: References
text: Messina JC et al. The EWAS classification of scapholunate tears. J Wrist Surg. 2013;2(2):105-109. Mathoulin C et al. Scapholunate injuries: challenging existing dogmas. J Hand Surg Eur Vol. 2021;46(1):5-13. Berger RA. Anatomy of the ligaments of the wrist. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2001;(383):32-40. Garcia-Elias M et al. Three-ligament tenodesis for SL dissociation.
