title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform): no tendon attachments — intercalated segment; position dictated by geometry + ligaments Distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate): rigid platform with negligible intercarpal motion Gilula’s lines : smooth concentric arcs along proximal/distal row joint surfaces on PA; disruption = instability Extrinsic ligaments : volar (RSC, LRL, SRL, ulnocarpal complex) > dorsal (DRC, DIC) in structural strength; dorsal ligaments more proprioceptive Space of Poirier : capsular weakness between RSC and LRL — lunate dislocates volarly through here SLIL : dorsal strongest; LTIL : volar strongest Dart-thrower’s motion (DTM) : natural wrist axis (radial extension → ulnar flexion); minimal proximal row motion through this arc

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: In Mayfield’s progressive perilunar instability, what structure fails in stage III? — A: The lunotriquetral interosseous ligament. Q: A patient with midcarpal instability demonstrates a painful clunk as the wrist moves into ulnar deviation with the proximal row snapping from flexion into extension. What is this sign called? — A: The catch-up clunk (palmar midcarpal instability). Q: What is the reported nonunion rate for lunotriquetral arthrodesis? — A: 41% (Shin series). Q: A perilunate fracture-dislocation with a scaphoid waist fracture is classified as what type of arc injury? — A: Greater arc injury. Q: What surgical option for palmar midcarpal instability best preserves dart-thrower’s motion? — A: Radiolunate fusion.

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Adaptive (CIA)
text: Most commonly from distal radius malunion (dorsal tilt → DISI → midcarpal catch-up clunk) Treatment: corrective osteotomy of distal radius; 3D virtual planning available

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Complex (Perilunate Injuries)
text: Mayfield stages (radial → ulnar) : I = SL disruption; II = capitate dislocation (space of Poirier opens); III = LT dissociation; IV = lunate dislocation Lesser arc = purely ligamentous; greater arc = fractures through surrounding bones (most commonly transscaphoid) PLIND (perilunate injuries non-dislocated): no capitate-lunate dislocation on lateral; midcarpal osteochondral loose bodies are a clue Up to 25% historically missed; lateral radiograph most diagnostic (“spilled teacup” sign) ORIF : combined volar + dorsal approach. Volar first (CTR + volar capsule [space of Poirier] repair), then dorsal (joystick K-wires to reduce the SL, then 0.062” K-wires for definitive stabilization). Arthroscopic-assisted fixation feasible for PLIND and select PLD (Herzberg stages 1-2A) Post-op: cast 2 months → wrist brace + gentle motion; buried K-wire removal at 3 months Despite severity, 10-15 yr outcomes often satisfactory; delay in treatment = worst prognostic factor Barrera: Perilunate repair construct — combined volar + dorsal approach. Start volar: CTR (median nerve is almost always under pressure), then repair the volar capsule (space of Poirier). Go dorsal: joystick K-wires into scaphoid + lunate to reduce the SL under direct vision, then 0.062” pins for definitive stabilization. Cast 2 months, transition to wrist brace + gentle motion, buried K-wire removal at 3 months.

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Classification
text: Larsen (1995) — 6 parameters: chronicity, constancy, etiology, location, direction, pattern CID (carpal instability dissociative): within a row (SL, LT) CIND (carpal instability nondissociative): between rows (midcarpal, radiocarpal) CIC (carpal instability complex): perilunate injuries spanning both CIA (carpal instability adaptive): secondary to extracarpal pathology (distal radius malunion)

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Nondissociative (CIND) › Combined Midcarpal Instability (CMCI)
text: Young women with laxity; VISI deformity + dorsal subluxation on provocative testing May respond to volar ligamentous reefing (Apergis: 13/14 excellent); but at 5-8 yr follow-up, no difference surgical vs nonsurgical

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Nondissociative (CIND) › Dorsal Midcarpal Instability (DMCI / CLIP Wrist)
text: Dorsal capitate subluxation on lunate (CIND-DISI) Pain with heavy lifting + power grasp in supination Johnson-Carroll: space of Poirier obliteration (6 excellent/11 outcomes) Treatment: primarily nonsurgical

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Lunotriquetral Interosseous Ligament Injury
text: Less common than SL; often associated with TFCC tears and ulnar impaction Geissler classification applies (same as SL) VISI pattern (lunate flexion) — only with complete LTIL + secondary stabilizer failure Cadaveric: 30% LTIL perforation in patients > 60 yo Exam : LT ballottement (Reagan test), LT shear (Kleinman test), LT compression; ulnar-sided wrist pain Imaging : disrupted Gilula’s arcs I/II, proximal triquetral migration; diastasis rare even with instability Treatment ladder : Conservative: immobilization (pisiform-supported cast), therapy, CSI Arthroscopic debridement + pinning (80% success, Osterman series) Ligament reconstruction (distally based ECU strip through bone tunnels) — 69% 5-yr survival (Shin) LT arthrodesis: 41% nonunion rate — generally avoided Ulnar shortening osteotomy: effective when ulnocarpal abutment coexists (83% good-to-excellent, Mirza) Barrera: For suspected TFCC injuries with associated LT symptoms, start with the standard ladder: 4 weeks brace → Wrist Widget + OT → MRI without contrast → CSI → surgery as last resort. Most stable-DRUJ injuries respond to immobilization and bracing. The LT component often improves in parallel with TFCC-directed conservative treatment.

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Nondissociative (CIND) › Palmar Midcarpal Instability (PMCI)
text: Most common CIND; often in generalized ligamentous laxity “Catch-up clunk” : proximal row lags in flexion during ulnar deviation → snaps into extension “Kettle sign”: difficulty holding heavy objects in ulnar deviation Radiographs often normal; dynamic fluoroscopy demonstrates clunk Treatment : primarily nonsurgical (6+ months); ECU/FCU strengthening, pisiform-padded orthosis Surgical: dorsal capsular plication (von Schroeder: durable improvement at 35 months); radiolunate fusion preserves DTM; soft tissue reconstruction has high failure rate (6/9 in Lichtman series)

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Always get a true lateral radiograph — most perilunate injuries are diagnosed here PLIND lesions: look for midcarpal osteochondral loose bodies as a diagnostic clue LT arthrodesis has unacceptably high nonunion (41%) — reconstruction or ulnar shortening preferred Midcarpal instability is primarily nonsurgical — commit to 6 months of therapy before considering surgery For radiocarpal fracture-dislocations, protect the volar ligament repair for 3 full months Dart-thrower’s motion rehab is relevant across multiple instability patterns

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Radiocarpal Instability / Fracture-Dislocations
text: High-energy; dorsal dislocation more common Dumontier classification : type 1 (< 1/3 scaphoid facet, RSC avulsion) vs type 2 (> 1/3 facet fragment) Type 1: volar ligament repair + dorsal spanning plate protection (3 months before plate removal) Type 2: ORIF of radial styloid fragment restores stability

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: References
text: Mayfield JK et al. Carpal dislocations: pathomechanics and progressive perilunar instability. J Hand Surg Am. 1980;5(3):226-241. Shin AY et al. Treatment of isolated LT ligament injuries: comparison of arthrodesis, reconstruction, and repair. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 2001;83(7):1023-1028. Herzberg G et al. Perilunate dislocations: a multicenter study. J Hand Surg Am. 1993;18(5):768-779. Wolfe SW et al. Carpal instability nondissociative. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2012;20(9):575-585. Dumontier C et al. Radiocarpal dislocations: classification and proposal for treatment. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2001;83-A(2):212-218.

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: DRUJ : diarthrodial trochoid joint; intrinsically unstable; ulnar head (convex, 10 mm curvature) articulates with sigmoid notch of radius (concave, 15 mm curvature) Sigmoid notch morphology (axial plane): flat face (42%), C-type (30%), S-type (14%), ski slope (12%) Tolat coronal types : type I parallel (55%), type II oblique (33%), type III reverse oblique (12%) Ulnar fovea : center of forearm rotation axis; attachment site for deep RUL fibers (ligamentum subcruentum) TFCC components : central articular disc, dorsal + volar RULs, meniscus homologue, ulnar collateral ligament, ulnocarpal ligaments, ECU subsheath floor RULs = primary DRUJ stabilizers; each has superficial (styloid) and deep (foveal) components; both must be injured for severe unidirectional instability Forearm rotation : anatomic arc 150-170° (full passive max pronation → max supination); functional arc 140-150° (Morrey, Sennwald) — the range used for ADLs and the target for reconstruction < 10% ulnar head contact at extremes of rotation; max contact (60%) at neutral Force transmission : radius carries majority; ulna 3-34% depending on ulnar variance Barrera: When teaching forearm rotation, distinguish the anatomic arc (150-170°) from the functional arc (140-150°) . Textbooks conflate the two. The functional arc is what predicts disability and what you’re trying to restore in DRUJ reconstruction or distal radius malunion correction. A patient who loses 30° from anatomic max still keeps a working arc.

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Associated Injury Patterns
text: Galeazzi fracture : DRUJ instability in 55% if fracture < 7.5 cm from articular surface; stabilize radius first, then assess DRUJ Essex-Lopresti : radial head fracture + IOM rupture + DRUJ disruption; ulnar-positive variance is a clue; radial head replacement + DRUJ repair ± IOM reconstruction Distal radius malunion : most common cause of chronic DRUJ dysfunction; dorsal angulation > 20-30° and radial shortening > 3-5 mm → DRUJ instability

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: Which Palmer class TFCC tear causes DRUJ instability and involves avulsion from the ulnar attachment? — A: Class IB (ulnar avulsion/peripheral tear). Q: A Galeazzi fracture is defined as a fracture of the distal third of the radius with what associated injury? — A: Dislocation of the DRUJ (dorsal or volar). Q: What position of immobilization provides maximal DRUJ stability after reduction of a dorsal DRUJ dislocation? — A: Supination. Q: What is the gold standard imaging study for evaluating DRUJ instability? — A: CT with bilateral comparison in neutral, supination, and pronation. Q: In an Essex-Lopresti injury, what three structures are disrupted? — A: Radial head, interosseous membrane, and DRUJ (TFCC).

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Classification
text: Palmer classification of TFCC tears : Class I (traumatic) : IA = central perforation (no DRUJ instability); IB = ulnar avulsion (can destabilize DRUJ); IC = distal avulsion (ulnocarpal ligaments); ID = radial avulsion Class II (degenerative) : IIA = wear; IIB = wear + chondromalacia; IIC = perforation + chondromalacia; IID = + LT perforation; IIE = + ulnocarpal arthritis

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Ballottement/shuck test : stabilize radius, translate ulna dorsal-palmar in neutral, pronation, supination; compare contralateral Piano key sign : pronated forearm, press ulna volarly → springs back like piano key DRUJ compression test : compress ulna against sigmoid notch + rotate forearm → pain/crepitus Fovea sign : press soft spot between FCU, ECU, triquetrum, ulnar head → pain = TFCC pathology Table-top test : push up from seated → dorsal dimple sign = instability

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Workup › History
text: Dorsal/volar dislocation mechanism: hyperpronation → dorsal; hypersupination → volar Associated injuries: distal radius fracture (most common), Galeazzi fracture, Essex-Lopresti injury Ulnar styloid fractures accompany 60% of distal radius fractures; base fractures with > 2 mm displacement or foveal involvement may destabilize DRUJ

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: True lateral : pisoscaphocapitate relationship; ulna normally 2 mm dorsal to radius; > 6 mm = instability CT (gold standard) : bilateral comparison in neutral/supination/pronation MRI/MR arthrography : foveal attachment assessment; sensitivity debated Arthroscopy : trampoline test (central disc tension), hook test (foveal competence), suction test

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Acute isolated DRUJ dislocation: closed reduction + above-elbow immobilization 4-6 weeks in position of stability (dorsal dislocation → supination; volar → pronation) Subacute/chronic: wrist brace, FCU/ECU strengthening Barrera: For TFCC injuries with a stable DRUJ, use the standard treatment ladder: 4 weeks rigid brace → Wrist Widget + OT → MRI without contrast if still symptomatic → CSI (Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido, never Depo) → surgery only as last resort with positive MRI and refractory symptoms.

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: TFCC Repair - Peripheral repair: outside-in arthroscopic technique; debride synovitis, PDS sutures through capsule + disc - Foveal repair (deep): arthroscopic bone tunnel repair (preferred) or open anchor into fovea - Open foveal repair (Barrera technique): hockey stick incision → double opposing inverted L capsulotomies with transverse limbs at the joint interface to protect the TFCC → big bite of TFCC with 2-0 PDS → two bone tunnels with 1.6 mm K-wire from fovea out the ulnar neck → pass suture through tunnels → tie down with forearm in neutral rotation → dorsal capsulorrhaphy / tightening for added stability Barrera: Open foveal repair construct: hockey-stick incision, double opposing inverted L capsulotomies (transverse limbs at the joint interface to protect the TFCC), big bite of TFCC with 2-0 PDS , two bone tunnels with a 1.6 mm K-wire from the fovea out the ulnar neck , tie down with forearm in neutral , then dorsal capsulorrhaphy for added DRUJ stability. The inverted-L design is the part residents miss — draw it on the skin before incision. - Comparable outcomes open vs arthroscopic DRUJ Ligament Reconstruction (Adams procedure) - Indication: chronic instability with irreparable TFCC - Palmaris longus tendon graft through bone tunnels in radius (dorsal-to-volar) and ulna (fovea-to-lateral neck) - Graft passed around ulnar neck in opposite directions, tensioned in neutral rotation, tied - Post-op: long-arm orthosis → cast; short-arm at 4 wk; activities at 4 mo; heavy

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Both dorsal and volar RULs must be injured for complete unidirectional instability After distal radius ORIF, always check DRUJ stability intraoperatively Ulnar styloid tip fractures are generally benign; base fractures may destabilize the DRUJ The hook test is the most sensitive/specific arthroscopic test for foveal detachment (Atzei) CT is superior to lateral radiographs for diagnosing DRUJ subluxation (10° rotation can falsely normalize lateral) When reconstructing the DRUJ, address any sigmoid notch deficiency or distal radius malunion first

heading: References

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: A 28-year-old manual laborer with dorsal wrist pain has ulnar-negative variance and a sclerotic lunate with intact cortex on x-ray. Gadolinium MRI shows homogeneous proximal enhancement. What is the recommended initial surgical treatment? — A: Radial shortening osteotomy (B1 disease, ulnar-negative, viable lunate). Q: What Viegas lunate type is more prevalent in Kienböck disease? — A: Type I (no hamate facet). Q: In Preiser disease with advanced scaphoid collapse and OA, what is the preferred salvage procedure? — A: Three-corner fusion with triquetral excision. Q: What percentage of cadaveric metacarpal heads lack a central arteriole, predisposing to Dietrich disease? — A: 35%. Q: What is the maximum recommended resection for radial shortening osteotomy in Kienböck disease? — A: 2 mm (> 4 mm associated with poor outcomes).

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Classification › Capitate — Milliez Classification
text: Group I (proximal), Group II (body), Group III (whole bone)

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: All Kienböck evidence is level IV / small retrospective — no quality RCT exists Bain series (31 pts, 10-yr f/u): 23% required further surgery (mostly hardware removal); no salvage procedures, infections, or nonunions

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Workup › History
text: Kienböck: dorsal wrist pain worse with extension; age 20-40, M:F 2:1; average 1-2 years of symptoms before diagnosis Pediatric Kienböck: often regresses with conservative care (< 12 yo)

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Plain radiographs : 3 views; assess Lichtman stage, ulnar variance, carpal collapse CT : fragmentation, coronal fracture, perilunate arthritis Gadolinium-enhanced MRI : Schmitt viability patterns — normal enhancement vs ischemic (maintained perfusion) vs partial necrosis (reparative) vs necrotic (no enhancement) 4D-CT : dynamic kinematics; SPECT-CT : bone scan sensitivity + CT anatomy

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Classification › Kienböck — Lichtman-Bain Algorithm
text: Combines osseous staging + arthroscopic assessment + Schmitt vascular (ceMRI): - B1 (intact cortex + cartilage): protect/unload - B2 (localized disease): reconstruct - B3 (advanced lunate disease): salvage - C1 (carpal instability, intact articulations): stabilize - C2a (radiolunate compromised): bypass or fuse - C2b (radioscaphoid compromised): PRC if lunate facet OK - C3 (KDAC — Kienböck disease advanced collapse): salvage

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Lunate (Kienböck Disease)
text: “Keystone” of wrist — load-bearing intercalated segment; 5 articulations, no muscle attachments Viegas classification : Type I (35%, no hamate facet) — more prevalent in Kienböck, coronal fracture-prone; Type II (65%, hamate facet present) — may be protective Zapico classification : Type 1 trapezoidal (negative ulnar variance, nutcracker susceptibility); Type 2 rectangular (neutral); Type 3 pentagonal (positive) Proximal subchondral bone plate only 0.1 mm thick — first and most severely affected region Blood supply: mainly palmar (radiocarpal + intercarpal arches); single arterial supply → increased AVN risk (Gelberman 1980) Pathogenesis (“compartment syndrome of bone”): repetitive loading → venous occlusion → interstitial edema → sinusoidal tamponade → ischemia → necrosis → repair/fracture/fragmentation

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Pediatric (< 15 yo) : nonoperative first — most resolve with splinting Ages 16-20 : nonoperative trial then consider unloading Elderly (> 70 yo) : nonoperative; consider synovectomy Splinting 4-12 weeks (recent: 12 wk cast for < 17 yo without collapse); NSAIDs, PT

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Treatment › Operative (by Lunate/Wrist State)
text: Unloading (B1 disease) : - Radial shortening osteotomy : for ulnar-negative; 2 mm resection optimal (> 4 mm = poor outcome); volar locking plate - Capitate shortening : for ulnar-neutral/positive; single cut at middle/distal third; headless screw - Camembert osteotomy (wedge from ulnar radius) = most complete unloading per FEA - Core decompression of radius (Illaramendi): 22 pts, no further surgery at 10 yr Reconstruction (B2/B3) : - PRC : for less active, older patients; grip 68% contralateral; capitate-radius arthritis in 87% (often asymptomatic) - Radioscapholunate fusion : excise distal scaphoid pole (improves motion + union), excise triquetrum for graft - Scaphocapitate fusion : bypasses lunate; requires functional scaphoid fossa - VBG (vascularized bone graft): 4+5 ECA or medial femoral trochlea; for B1-B2 with ulnar-neutral/positive Salvage (C3) : - Total wrist fusion (10-15° extension + slight ulnar deviation) - Wrist hemiarthroplasty + PRC For suspected Kienböck, gadolinium-enhanced MRI (Schmitt classification) directly informs whether the lunate has viable perfusion and changes the treatment algorithm.

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Other AVN Sites
text: Scaphoid (Preiser) : retrograde blood supply → proximal pole vulnerability; dominant hand, F > M Capitate : retrograde supply like scaphoid; do not osteotomize proximal to waist (risk to subarticular plexus) MC head (Dietrich) : 3rd MC most common; 35% of cadavers lack central arteriole; M:F 3:2, peak 3rd decade

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: At-risk lunate: Viegas type I + Zapico type 1 + negative ulnar variance + flat radial inclination Kienböck is NOT synonymous with ulnar-negative variance — later studies show inconsistent association Capitate AVN: never osteotomize proximal to the waist (retrograde blood supply) Pyrocarbon lunate replacement is not routinely recommended (instability concern) Dietrich disease of the MC head may coexist with Freiberg disease (metatarsal head AVN)

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Treatment › Preiser Disease
text: Conservative: immobilization, steroid, electrical stimulation Advanced collapse → 3-corner fusion (preferred — excise triquetrum for graft + better ulnar deviation)

title: AVN of Hand and Wrist
heading: Classification › Preiser — Herbert-Lanzetta Staging
text: Normal x-ray, abnormal CT Increased density proximal pole + osteopenia Fragmentation ± pathologic fracture Fragmentation + collapse + OA

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Scaphoid = “intercarpal connecting rod” between proximal and distal rows (Gilford 1943) SLAC pattern (Watson 1984): SL injury → scaphoid volar flexion + lunate extension → progressive degenerative cascade Stage I : radial styloid–scaphoid Stage II : scaphoid fossa Stage III : capitolunate (capitate/hamate migration into lunate fossa) Stage IV : pancarpal Radiolunate articulation typically spared (congruous hemisphere) — basis for 4CF SNAC (scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse): analogous pattern from scaphoid nonunion Other etiologies: inflammatory arthritis, LT injury, Kienböck, posttraumatic, OA

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: In SLAC arthritis, which articulation is typically spared and serves as the basis for 4-corner arthrodesis? — A: The radiolunate articulation. Q: What is the most important structure to preserve during proximal row carpectomy to prevent ulnar carpal translation? — A: The radioscaphocapitate (RSC) ligament. Q: A patient with stage II SLAC wrist, type I lunate, preserved proximal capitate, and a 30 pack-year smoking history. PRC or 4CF? — A: PRC (smoker → higher nonunion risk with 4CF; preserved capitate + type I lunate = ideal PRC candidate). Q: What two nerves are excised in partial wrist denervation? — A: Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) and anterior interosseous nerve (AIN). Q: What is the nonunion rate after total wrist arthrodesis? — A: Less than 5%.

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › 4-Corner Arthrodesis (4CF) with Scaphoid Excision
text: Indications : SLAC/SNAC all stages, preserved radiolunate articulation, capitate head AVN, RSC incompetency Contraindications: radiolunate arthrosis, Kienböck, active infection Must correct DISI (flex wrist over towel → neutral lunate rotation → radiolunate pin) Fixation: headless compression screws or recessed dorsal circular plate Post-op : cast 6-8 weeks; no > 5 lb until 12 weeks 3-corner / lunocapitate (LC) arthrodesis : fewer bones in fusion mass → lower nonunion risk; excise triquetrum → easier reduction + eliminates pisotriquetral arthritis source

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Point tenderness localization, provocative maneuvers (Watson shift, LT ballottement, intercarpal shear, compression) Evaluate DRUJ, tendon pathology, neuropathy, pisotriquetral joint, thumb CMC/STT joints Grip strength comparison

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Workup › History
text: Pain, loss of motion, progressive wrist dysfunction Timing of pain: morning → inflammatory; evening → posttraumatic/OA Prior wrist trauma (may be remote), previous injections, smoking history

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: PA, lateral, oblique sufficient for most patients CT: bone quality assessment; MRI: specific articulation involvement (motion-sparing decision-making) Direct inspection at surgery (open or arthroscopic) remains superior to all imaging

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: First-line regardless of stage: splinting, PT (strengthening + stabilization), activity modification, CSI Trial of 3-6 months before surgical intervention Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo). Intra-articular injections can be both diagnostic and therapeutic — complete but temporary relief confirms the pain generator and justifies proceeding to the appropriate motion-sparing procedure.

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Partial Wrist Denervation
text: PIN + AIN neurectomy through small dorsal incision; excise 1-2 cm of each 85% satisfaction; 90% would choose same treatment again Option for pancarpal arthritis where comorbidities preclude major surgery Excise AIN as distal as possible to avoid pronator quadratus denervation

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Radiolunate articulation is usually spared in SLAC/SNAC — always inspect it RSC ligament integrity is critical for PRC; if damaged, convert to 4CF or pin For 4CF, correct the DISI deformity before final fixation — otherwise impingement is inevitable Smokers have higher nonunion risk with any arthrodesis — PRC may be safer Type I lunate + type I capitate = best PRC candidates (smallest radius mismatch) Denervation is an underutilized, minimally invasive option for any wrist arthritis

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › PRC vs 4CF Decision-Making
text: PRC preferred : preserved proximal capitate, Kienböck, smokers (no fusion to fail) 4CF preferred : preserved proximal lunate, stages III-IV SLAC/SNAC, capitate AVN, RSC incompetency PRC: better motion; 4CF: better grip strength; conversion to total wrist fusion: 4CF 10% vs PRC 5% 4CF: 10-20% higher complication rate (nonunion, radiocarpal impingement)

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Proximal Row Carpectomy (PRC)
text: Indications : SLAC I-II, perilunate sequelae, Kienböck — with preserved proximal capitate and lunate fossa cartilage Contraindications: stage III-IV SLAC/SNAC, capitate head AVN, RSC ligament insufficiency (ulnar carpal translation) Capitate morphology matters : type II lunate (hamate facet) → V-shaped or spherical capitate → greater mismatch with lunate fossa → higher degeneration rate Technique: dorsal approach, ligament-sparing capsulotomy, PIN neurectomy; remove scaphoid first (assess RSC integrity) No radial styloidectomy (protects RSC ligament origin) Post-op : volar orthosis 3-6 weeks → PT at 3 months Outcomes : > 85% survival free of revision at 20 years; progressive radiocapitate arthritis (does not correlate with clinical deterioration) Diseased capitate options: capsular interposition (Eaton), OATS plug from lunate/triquetrum, pyrocarbon resurfacing

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Radioscapholunate (RSL) Arthrodesis
text: Indication: radiolunate ± radioscaphoid arthrosis with spared midcarpal joints Distal scaphoidectomy improves flexion/radial deviation + union rate (0% vs 5% nonunion) Dart-thrower’s motion generally preserved Progressive radiographic midcarpal arthrosis does not correlate with clinical deterioration

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Total Wrist Arthrodesis
text: Gold standard for pancarpal arthritis; slight extension + ulnar deviation Precontoured dorsal plate, 3rd MC → radius; fix distally first PRC can be added to reduce fusion joints + provide autograft Nonunion < 5%; tendon irritation ~15% (most common reoperation) “Functional wrist ROM” for ADLs: 35° flex-ext, 25° radial-ulnar deviation — these are lost

title: Intercarpal and Radiocarpal Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Total Wrist Arthroplasty (TWA)
text: 4th-generation implants (Universal 2, ReMotion, Maestro): 5-yr survival > 90%, complications < 10% Best for low-demand, older patients with pancarpal arthritis ± ipsilateral elbow/shoulder arthritis Goal: ~70° arc of motion, balanced stability 10-yr survival: 92% (revision as endpoint), 75% (including radiographic loosening)

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: DRUJ = bicondylar articulation; ulna is the stable unit around which radius + carpus rotate Forearm rotation 150-180° at DRUJ; bony constraints provide only 20% of stability ; 80% from soft tissues Ulnar head : seat (articulates with sigmoid notch) + dome/pole (articulates with TFCC disc) 220° of head covered with articular cartilage (dual articulation) Ulnar variance: neutral → 82% force through radius, 18% through ulna; +2.5 mm → 42% through ulna; -2.5 mm → 4% through ulna DOB (distal oblique bundle) : present in 40% of specimens; part of distal IOM; contributes to DRUJ stability Sigmoid notch inclination varies; cartilaginous thickness may neutralize radiographic inclination differences

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis, DRUJ arthrosis, and risk of ulnar carpal translation needs surgical treatment. What procedure preserves the ulnocarpal buttress? — A: Sauvé-Kapandji procedure. Q: What is the primary advantage of the hemiresection interposition technique (Bowers) over the Darrach procedure? — A: Preservation of the TFCC attachments (foveal and styloid), reducing stump instability. Q: In a modified Darrach procedure with ECU stabilization (Sotereanos), what is done to the ulnar stump to prevent radial impingement? — A: Oblique radial osteotomy of the ulnar stump combined with ECU tendon stabilization through a bone tunnel. Q: What percentage of DRUJ stability is provided by bony constraints vs soft tissue? — A: 20% bony, 80% soft tissue. Q: What is the minimum proximal ulnar length required for the Aptis total DRUJ prosthesis? — A: 11 cm.

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Fovea sign : press interval between ulnar styloid and pisiform → sensitive + specific for TFCC/UT pathology Piano key sign : volarly directed pressure on ulnar head in pronation → springs back with pain Grind test : compress + rotate DRUJ → pain/crepitus = arthrosis DRUJ compression test : compress ulna against radius → pain Table-top test : push up from seated → dorsal dimple sign Compare ROM, grip strength, and stability to contralateral side

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Failed Darrach Salvage
text: Achilles allograft interposition (Sotereanos) : rolled tendon “pillow” (5 x 3 cm) sutured between radius and ulna; VAS 8.1 → 1.3, arc improved 69°, grip improved 72% at 7-yr f/u Ulnar head replacement or total DRUJ replacement for more severe cases

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Workup › History
text: Pain localized to DRUJ, limited forearm ROM Difficulty with doorknobs, keys, opening jars; grinding/snapping with rotation Progressive worsening over years; increasing distal ulnar prominence

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: PA + lateral (neutral rotation): joint space narrowing, sclerosis, osteophytes, ulnar variance Scheker: dynamic weighted PA demonstrates radioulnar convergence under load CT : articular surface detail, subluxation, 3D fracture orientation MRI: soft tissue pathology, early arthritis; 3-phase bone scan for early/multifocal disease Kakar-Garcia-Elias “four-leaf clover” algorithm : systematically evaluate bony deformity, cartilage damage, TFCC injury, ECU stability

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Implant Arthroplasty
text: Partial Ulnar Head (Eclypse, First Choice): - Replace ulnar seat; preserve styloid + TFCC - Requires intact sigmoid notch + TFCC; press-fit stem - Limited long-term data; bony erosion in 50% at 5 years (rheumatoid) Total Ulnar Head (uHead, Herbert ceramic): - Complete head replacement; no inherent stability — needs soft tissue support + intact sigmoid notch - Also for failed Darrach/salvage - Survival 82-87% at 5-10 years; 35% require additional procedures (Kakar) Total DRUJ Arthroplasty (Aptis semiconstrained): - Replaces ulnar head, sigmoid notch, and TFCC function - Linked device → does not require soft tissue stability - Survival 93-100% at 5 years; complication rate 28-31% (ECU tendinitis, heterotopic bone, loosening) - Requires ≥ 11 cm proximal ulna for stem

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Activity modification, OT, NSAIDs, immobilization (must include elbow to eliminate forearm rotation) Intra-articular injection: 0.25 mL 1% lidocaine + 20 mg triamcinolone — significant improvement in DASH/pain/ROM at 1, 3, 6 months (Nam) Barrera: CSI = Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido (never Depo). For DRUJ arthritis, an intra-articular injection doubles as a diagnostic test — complete temporary relief confirms the DRUJ as the pain generator. Repeated steroid injections should be discouraged.

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Darrach: resect minimum bone; more resection = more stump instability + convergence Sauvé-Kapandji: proximal osteotomy must be < 35 mm from radiocarpal joint to maintain stump stability HIT requires intact TFCC — always assess preoperatively For young, active patients: Sauvé-Kapandji or HIT preferred over Darrach Radiographic convergence after Darrach is common (50%) but rarely symptomatic (8%) One-bone forearm = ultimate salvage for multiply failed forearm reconstruction

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: References

title: DRUJ Arthritis
heading: Treatment › Surgical Options
text: Darrach Procedure (Distal Ulnar Resection) - Osteotomy just proximal to sigmoid notch; resect entire ulnar head - Best for low-demand patients; contraindicated if ulnar carpal translation risk (inflammatory arthritis without radiocarpal stabilization) - Modified Darrach (Sotereanos): oblique radial osteotomy + ECU tendon stabilization → 14/15 pain-free, no impingement at 37 months - Complications: radioulnar convergence (radiographic in 50%, symptomatic in 8%), ulnar stump instability, extensor tendon rupture - Long-term: sustained results at 12.8 years (Grawe), VAS 0.1 at rest; resect minimum bone to clear sigmoid notch Hemiresection Interposition (Bowers/HIT) - Resect ulnar seat only; preserve styloid + foveal TFCC attachment - Requires intact or reconstructable TFCC - Interpose dorsal capsular flap ± tendon graft to prevent convergence - Less convergence risk than Darrach; 75% favorable results - Contraindication: irreparable TFCC (loses advantage over Darrach) Matched Distal Ulnar Resection (Watson) - 270° arc convex resection matching sigmoid notch curvature - 97 wrists over 21 years — excellent results in isolated DRUJ problems Sauvé-Kapandji Procedure - DRUJ arthrodesis + proximal ulnar pseudarthrosis (10-15 mm resection gap) - Preserves ulnocarpal buttress + TFCC attachments; controls ulnar variance precisely - Best for: rheumatoid arthritis (prevents ulnar carpal translation), young active patients, chronic DRUJ instability - Fixation: 1-2 cannulated compression scre

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Wrist arthroscopy = gold standard for diagnosing intra-articular and ligamentous conditions Confined space requires precise portal placement — being a few mm off limits access + damages cartilage Traction : 4.5-5.5 kg (10-12 lb) via finger traps; apply traction BEFORE drawing portal landmarks

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: What is the most sensitive and specific arthroscopic test for foveal TFCC detachment? — A: The hook test (Atzei). Q: During arthroscopic wafer procedure for Palmer class IIC degenerative TFCC tear, what is the maximum amount of ulnar head bone that should be removed? — A: Less than 4 mm. Q: A Geissler grade III interosseous ligament tear is defined by what finding on midcarpal arthroscopy? — A: A probe can be inserted into the gap between carpal bones and twisted 90°. Q: What is the recommended starting point for dorsal percutaneous arthroscopic scaphoid screw placement? — A: The middle third of the SLIL insertion on the proximal pole of the scaphoid. Q: During arthroscopic dorsal ganglionectomy, what structure must be protected while debriding dorsal capsule? — A: The scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) — debride dorsal to it, not through it.

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Arthroscopic Assessment › Carpal Instability (Geissler Classification)
text: Grade Radiocarpal Midcarpal I Loss of concavity (bulge) Retained alignment II Convex ligament Rotatory malalignment; probe fits but can’t twist III Gap between bones Probe inserted + twisted 90° IV Detached / “drive-through” Scope passes freely RC → MC Rimington cadaveric study : physiologic laxity broader than originally described (48% had Geissler III SLIL) — cannot diagnose pathologic instability in isolation

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: TFCC Injury Management (Palmer Classification) › Class IA (Central Perforation)
text: No DRUJ instability; debride unstable flap if failed splint/CSI Do not debride volar/dorsal RULs (critical DRUJ stabilizers)

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: TFCC Injury Management (Palmer Classification) › Class IB (Ulnar Avulsion)
text: Outside-in technique : scope 3-4, sutures through ECU sheath floor + disc; 2-0 PDS; tie in supination All-arthroscopic (FasT-Fix) : PLL blocks with pretied sliding knots; 11/12 excellent at 1 yr (Yao) Foveal tears : transosseous sutures or suture anchors into fovea Barrera: For TFCC peripheral tears (Palmer IB), I follow the conservative ladder first: 4 weeks rigid brace → Wrist Widget + OT → MRI without contrast → CSI → arthroscopic repair as last resort. Most stable-DRUJ TFCC injuries respond to bracing. Reserve surgery for refractory symptoms with positive MRI.

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: TFCC Injury Management (Palmer Classification) › Class IC (Distal/Ulnocarpal Avulsion)
text: Includes ulnotriquetral split tears (Berger) Outside-to-inside repair with meniscal Mender II needle; 84% good/excellent at 21 months (Clark)

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: TFCC Injury Management (Palmer Classification) › Class ID (Radial Avulsion)
text: Treatment controversial — radial TFCC is relatively avascular Repair has NOT shown functional improvement over debridement

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: TFCC Injury Management (Palmer Classification) › Class II (Degenerative)
text: IIA/IIB (no perforation): ulnar shortening osteotomy IIC (perforation): ulnar shortening OR arthroscopic wafer procedure (debride < 4 mm ulnar head bone through central tear) IID (LT perforation): ulnar shortening (traction reduces LT instability) IIE: treat DRUJ arthritis Wafer vs ulnar shortening : similar outcomes; wafer has lower complication rate (11% vs 35%) and better grip strength

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Other Arthroscopic Applications › Distal Radius Fractures
text: Threshold for congruity: historically 2 mm, recent evidence supports 1 mm Arthroscopy: direct visualization + concurrent SL/TFCC injury diagnosis and treatment Abe series: 35% had > 2 mm residual step-off after fluoro-only reduction

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Setup and Portals › Dorsal Wrist Portals
text: Portal Location Use 3-4 Between 3rd/4th compartments, 1 cm distal to Lister tubercle Primary radiocarpal viewing 4-5 Ulnar to 4th compartment, in line with ring finger Radiocarpal working 6-R Radial to ECU Radiocarpal alternative; TFCC debridement 6-U Ulnar to ECU Radiocarpal alternative 1-2 Proximal snuffbox Radial styloid access; radial artery + SBR nerve risk Radial midcarpal 1 cm distal to 3-4 Midcarpal viewing; STT access Ulnar midcarpal 1 cm distal to 4-5 Midcarpal viewing; easier landmark Midcarpal portals: needle inserted horizontally (vs sloping for radiocarpal) 1-2 portal : highest risk — blunt dissection mandatory (radial artery + superficial radial nerve)

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Setup and Portals › DRUJ Portals
text: Proximal DRUJ : between EDM and ECU; 1.9 mm scope; wrist in supination, reduced traction Only DRUJ arthroscopy can confirm foveal attachment integrity (Atzei)

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Arthroscopic Assessment › Foveal TFCC Tests
text: Hook test : displace ulnar edge centrally with probe — easy displacement = foveal incompetence (most sensitive/specific) Trampoline test : compress central disc — loss of buoyancy = positive Suction test : negative pressure to assess laxity

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Other Arthroscopic Applications › Ganglionectomy
text: Dorsal ganglions: usually overlie SLIL; portal adjacent to (not through) ganglion Excise 1 cm dorsal capsule adjacent to SLIL until extensors visible — stay dorsal to SLIL Recurrence: 0-10% (systematic review: 8% arthroscopic vs 10% open; statistically equivalent)

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science › Key Arthroscopic Anatomy
text: TFCC components : central articular disc, dorsal + volar RULs (superficial → styloid, deep → fovea), ulnocarpal ligaments, meniscus homologue, UCL, ECU subsheath floor Peripheral 10-40% of articular disc is vascularized (ulnar artery branches) — peripheral tears CAN heal Prestyloid recess : normal synovial pouch — do not confuse with peripheral tear Ligament of Testut (radioscapholunate): vestigial neurovascular structure, not a true stabilizer

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Draw portals AFTER applying traction (landmarks shift) Mark veins before tourniquet inflation Dry arthroscopy: avoids fluid extravasation risk; better for mini-open combined procedures 1-2 portal = highest-risk portal (radial artery + SBR nerve) Geissler grading alone cannot diagnose pathologic instability — correlate clinically For TFCC class ID (radial tears): debridement may equal repair in outcomes Arthroscopic scaphoid fixation: use screw at least 4 mm shorter than measured length

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Other Arthroscopic Applications › Scaphoid Fractures
text: Dorsal percutaneous technique: starting point = middle third of SLIL insertion on proximal pole Screw at least 4 mm shorter than measured Nonunion with cystic changes: ream + inject DBM through bone biopsy needle → 14/15 healed Humpback nonunion (Wong/Ho): correct DISI, morselized bone graft via midcarpal portal, fibrin glue, release traction for capitate compression → 90% union at 14 weeks

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Other Arthroscopic Applications › TM (Thumb CMC) Arthroscopy
text: 1-R (volar) + 1-U (dorsal) portals; 1.9 mm scope; fluoroscopy confirms placement Radial artery within few mm of EPB at TM joint — high injury risk Badia classification: Stage 1 (intact cartilage) → 2 (ulnar eburnation) → 3 (diffuse full-thickness loss) Partial trapeziectomy: 3-4 mm bone removed ± suture button suspensionplasty (Mini TightRope) Edwards: excellent outcomes at 4 years without interposition (fibrocartilage cap forms) Synovectomy alone independently associated with secondary arthroplasty → couple with partial trapeziectomy

title: Wrist and Hand Arthroscopy
heading: Setup and Portals › Volar Portals
text: VR (volar radial): through FCR sheath, between RSC + LRL ligaments → visualizes volar SLIL VU (volar ulnar): ulnar to FDS, protect ulnar NV bundle → visualizes volar LTIL Inside-out: volar ulnar midcarpal is 3.7 mm from ulnar artery; volar radial midcarpal is 1 mm from median nerve
